World.title: El Jalapeño: Guadalajara residents to receive contaminated water at ‘very affordable rates,’ state officials say
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUADALAJARA — State water authorities assured Guadalajara residents Monday that while the tap water delivered to hundreds of thousands of homes currently features a rust-colored hue, a gritty texture and a distinct metallic aroma, it remains an unbeatable value at 80% off the standard rate.

The discount, approved by the Jalisco state Congress, applies to roughly 600 neighborhoods supplied by the Intermunicipal System of Potable Water and Sewerage Services (SIAPA). Officials noted the price adjustment reflects a consumer-first framework where utility fees scale directly with fluid quality, ensuring citizens never overpay for a lack of clarity.

“We recognize the water arriving at your kitchen sink may not technically meet international definitions of ‘potable,’ but from an inflation-adjusted perspective, this is a remarkable savings opportunity,” said SIAPA spokesperson Fernando Morales, gesturing toward a pitcher of dark amber tap water. “I mean, this water is an amazing bargain, considering what we’re charging for it.”

Under the new policy, state human rights officials will inspect taps across 750,000 households to confirm whether municipal output crosses the threshold from clear drinking water into the deeply discounted sediment class. Residents whose water accidentally runs entirely transparent will, unfortunately, remain locked into the full 100% price rate.

Both quality-dependent fee structures will continue to fund SIAPA operations, including drainage maintenance, administrative overhead and the specialized team tasked with explaining why a bad deal on usable water becomes a fantastic deal when the water is unusable.

Local civic groups, who originally petitioned under the slogan “If there is no clean water, no payment,” expressed quiet amazement at the legislative response. State officials, however, urged the public to focus on the economic upside rather than minor daily inconveniences like boiling laundry.

“Paying zero pesos for murky water would suggest the service has no value,” Morales added, reassuring reporters that the billing software was functioning properly. “By charging a modest 20%, we allow citizens to enjoy the financial triumph of securing hundreds of gallons of industrial-grade sludge at wholesale clearance rates.”

World.title: Mexico’s critically endangered axolotl proves an international success
World.content:
The remarkable axolotl is native to the lakes and wetlands of highland Mexico. It is closely related to salamanders, but unlike its amphibian cousins, it does not undergo a complete metamorphosis, remaining an aquatic creature throughout its life. This is reflected in the name, axolotl being a Nahuatl word that has been translated as “water servant” or “water dog.” They have become critically endangered due to a combination of factors, including the loss of habitat and the pollution of the waters that remain available to them. The introduction of carp and tilapia into the lakes to provide fish for the local market also proved a disaster as these predators took a heavy toll on axolotl eggs and juveniles. It is uncertain how many axolotls survive in the wild, but it is probably no more than 1,000, and perhaps much fewer.

The thriving axolotl pet trade

Ironically, while they are disappearing in the wild, there are hundreds of thousands of axolotls being kept as pets in aquariums around the world. It is easy to see why axolotls attract pet owners, for they are amusing animals to look at with their fringed gills and what appears to be an endless smile. Their popularity has increased recently thanks to their appearance in animated movies and video games, most notably Minecraft. They are generally considered good pets in that they are not dangerous in any way, and any diseases they might carry do not pass to humans. Another bonus is that they can live up to 15 years under optimal conditions, so you get value for money.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by We’re All Primos! (@wereallprimos)

Even if they are released into the wild, which they never should be, they are unlikely to become a threat to native wildlife. And they do occasionally get released. In April 2026, a young girl looking for frogs and fish in a British river made the first documented discovery of an axolotl living in the wild in Europe. On the downside, they are sensitive animals that require a lot of care, which includes providing a gentle flow of cool water and ensuring minimal light exposure. Anybody keeping them needs to invest in specialized tank filters and be prepared to make frequent water changes. It is feared that many captive axolotls experience stress due to poor living conditions.

Legal controls and regulations

In addition to the ethical demands of keeping axolotls, there are also legal considerations. As a critically endangered species, they have been added to Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, or CITES. This means that international trade in these animals is strictly controlled, and restrictions and regulations can change from country to country. In Mexico, you must purchase your axolotl from a certified breeder and have authorization from the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources to keep them. However, regulations can change from place to place. For example, while axolotls can be kept in many U.S. states, owning one as a pet is illegal in California, Maine, New Jersey and Virginia.

A major concern is not that axolotls make dangerous or difficult pets, but that captivity is changing the animals. A feature that has always attracted considerable attention is the axolotl’s healing ability. It does not heal by scarring, but is capable of tissue regeneration. Entire limbs and tails can regrow over a period of months, and in certain cases even organs can be replaced. Much of the stock now available in the pet trade is thought to have originated from a small number of wild axolotls that were collected for medical research in the late 1880s.

Captive breeding programs

As few if any animals are now captured in the wild, the captive gene pool is small, and it is feared that this has made pet axolotls susceptible to genetic defects that might include a weakened immune system, poorly developed digestive systems and underdeveloped gills. In the wild, axolotls develop different colors but are typically a dark brown, tan or gray, often with dark spots, a color combination that helps them blend into the muddy waters of their native lakes.

In captivity, breeding pairs are deliberately chosen to produce colors thought attractive to the pet trade. At one point, it was thought that captive axolotls might even have been crossbred with tiger salamanders. The result is strains of animals that might look like axolotls but do not necessarily represent any animals found in the wild. Releasing a pink or albino axolotl into a Mexican lake would be like putting a pack of dachshunds into the Serengeti and pretending they are African hunting dogs.

Conservation efforts

This is a vital issue, for if the pet trade has any higher goal, then it is the dream that one day captive stock might be returned to the Mexican lakes. This is one reason that an Axolotl Museum and Amphibian Conservation Center has been opened in Chapultepec Zoo. A recent experiment in releasing captive axolotls has proved remarkably successful. In April 2025, captive-bred axolotls were released into the artificially created wetland of La Cantera Oriente and the animals seemed to do well. They carried small trackers, and not only did all survive the initial release, but those later captured and weighed had put on weight, showing they were successfully hunting. It might work in the axolotl’s favor that they are optimistic eaters, taking anything from worms to insect larvae.

Attempting to protect populations in the heartlands of Lake Xochimilco is even more ambitious. A decade-long project led by the Ecological Restoration Laboratory of the National Autonomous University of Mexico’s Biology Institute has attempted to do just that. The axolotl has lived alongside humans for many generations and has adjusted to the traditional farming methods practiced since Mexica times. Therefore, the project involved working with local farmers to restore chinampas, those small agricultural islands that once fed the great city of Tenochtitlán.

Hope for the future

It was hoped that these would both provide a haven for axolotls and support sustainable agriculture for the local people. A major problem is that the waters of Xochimilco are no longer flushed clean with spring water from the mountains, so biofilters have to be built. These are stacks of volcanic rocks and reedy plants placed around the chinampas to clean the water and provide shelter from predator fish.

After the early promise with such projects, there was a concern when a couple of adult axolotls were seen to be taken by egrets. This raises the possibility that captive-bred axolotls might lack the survival instincts of those brought up in the wild. However, where there is goodwill, there is hope. Since 2018, Feb. 1 has been celebrated as National Axolotl Day, drawing attention to one of Mexico’s most charming, remarkable and endangered animals.

World.title: The men’s World Cup is over, now Mexico’s women are ready for their moment
World.content:
With the 2026 edition of the men’s World Cup behind us — in which Mexico became the first country to host the sporting event on three separate occasions (1970, 1986 and 2026), leaving an indelible impression on fans worldwide who openly celebrated Mexico’s culture, gastronomy and spirited fandom — the “summer of North American soccer” is coming to a close. Well, sort of. It’s not completely over.

Luckily for fans of fútbol (also known as fút or balompié in Mexico), on-pitch action will resume with a different set of national heroes, as Mexico and the rest of the globe prepare for the upcoming 2027 Women’s World Cup.

World Cup qualifying has already begun

View this post on Instagram A post shared by FOX Sports MX (@foxsportsmx)

Though the tournament won’t actually take place until next summer — hosted in Brazil, marking the first time the FIFA women’s edition will take place on Latin American soil since debuting in 1991 — the race for the trophy is already underway.

Last winter, World Cup qualifying games began; this fall, North American qualifiers, which determine which teams from the region will compete in the World Cup, will conclude.

Here’s a look at Mexico’s national women’s squad and how they have fared so far on their historically arduous journey for sporting glory.

A history of women’s professional soccer in Mexico

Like all women’s sports around the globe, Mexico’s Liga MX Femenil is relatively new and lags behind its male counterpart league in terms of financial support, national investment, media coverage and, as a result, fandom. Despite those barriers, it has been celebrated as a highly successful effort.

The league was announced in late 2016 and officially played its first game in 2017. Since then, it has quietly developed into one of the world’s leading women’s leagues, with the Associated Press reporting that “women’s pro soccer is thriving in Mexico” and The New York Times citing it as the most-watched women’s league on the planet.

That said, it hasn’t been a path without systemic and cultural resistance. Instances of gender bias, sexism and a massive gap in pay and resources have endured. Last summer, Mexican men’s national team legend and former superstar Javier “Chicharito” Hernández was fined by the Mexican Football Federation for demeaning comments on social media that portrayed women as “failing” and “eradicating masculinity,” prompting a response from President Claudia Sheinbaum. In 2023, former Club América Femenil player Scarlett Camberos chose to leave the team and country due to excessive sexual harassment and cyberstalking.

Liga MX Femenil and the birth of the FIFA Women’s World Cup

Though Liga MX Femenil — both its successes and its accentuated reminder of Mexico’s machismo — is relatively nascent, pro women’s soccer in Mexico can be traced back to 1970. Before FIFA’s involvement, an unofficial Women’s World Cup existed as a series of international events independently sponsored by various nations. In those times, Mexico finished in third place at the 1970 World Cup in Italy and ended as runner-up in the largely erased 1971 World Cup in Mexico. It is estimated that the 1971 final at Estadio Azteca drew 110,000 fans. Unofficial tournaments continued throughout the 1980s under non-FIFA-sanctioned entities like the Chinese Taipei Football Association.

Pressure for an official FIFA Women’s World Cup mounted, crescendoing in 1986 when Norwegian delegate Ellen Wille famously urged FIFA to legitimize a women’s tournament in a speech that “changed the course of women’s football,” according to the BBC. In 1988, FIFA organized a trial tournament, the FIFA Women’s Invitation Tournament in China. Overwhelming success resulted in the debut of the official Women’s World Cup in 1991 in China.

Surprisingly, since the FIFA era of the World Cup began, Mexico’s women’s team hasn’t shown much promise. That is finally changing.

The road to the 2027 World Cup is off to a perfect start

In February, Mexico’s women’s team kicked off its World Cup campaign in the preliminary qualifying rounds of the Concacaf W Championship. Concacaf is the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, representing one of FIFA’s six continental governing bodies, which divides competition into regional tournaments that funnel teams into the World Cup every four years. Under this format, all North American, Central American and Caribbean teams face off, with the four quarterfinal winners earning direct berths to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Currently, Mexico is among the remaining eight North American countries with a chance to secure a World Cup ticket this year. It can do so by defeating Haiti on Nov. 28 at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Texas.

Mexico’s women haven’t reached a World Cup since 2015. Unlike the Mexican men’s national team — which has qualified 18 times dating back to 1930 — the women have appeared only three times (1999, 2011 and 2015). While the Women’s World Cup has taken place only nine times compared to 23 for the men, El Tri Femenil has struggled to assert regional dominance, holding a 33.3% qualification rate compared to the men’s nearly 80% rate over a much longer period.

A thus-far ‘flawless’ qualifying journey

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Concacaf W (@concacafw)

However, this World Cup cycle is proving to be different: Mexico’s women have been perfect in their qualifying run, an unprecedented feat. In 2023, Mexico also went undefeated for the first time at the Pan American Games in Santiago, Chile, en route to claiming its first gold medal, proving this current team’s success is no fluke.

El Tri has topped Group A of the Concacaf W Championship qualifiers with a flawless 12 points — going unbeaten in four matches and scoring 36 goals while conceding zero. That places them among the continent’s strongest units and makes them favorites to advance. While they have primarily played lower-ranked competition — such as Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, which Mexico defeated 14-0, and Puerto Rico — the core of the 2023 Pan American Games roster remains intact, leading many to consider this the best women’s team Mexico has ever fielded.

‘The Sorceress’ and other Mexico stars to watch

The roster is headlined by Lizbeth “La Maga” Ovalle (whose nickname translates to “The Sorceress”). Having debuted professionally in 2017, the winger — originally from Aguascalientes, who gained fame as one of Mexico’s top scorers with Tigres UANL — set a record in 2025 by signing a US $1.5 million contract with the Orlando Pride of the National Women’s Soccer League, making it one of the most lucrative deals in women’s soccer history. That same year, Ovalle won the FIFA Marta Award for “Best Goal of the Year” at The Best FIFA Football Awards ceremony for her spectacular “scorpion kick” goal.

Behind Ovalle, Mexico boasts a depth of experience and skill with team captain Rebeca Bernal and the formidable striker Charlyn Corral, one of Mexico’s all-time leading goal scorers. Complementing the veteran leadership is “Concacaf Best Young Player” award winner Alice Soto, a 19-year-old dynamic midfielder who debuted professionally at age 13 and has been scoring in Liga MX Femenil ever since.

Why upcoming qualification matters

Against Haiti, Mexico can automatically claim a direct spot in the 2027 World Cup. A loss would send the team to a playoff round for a second chance.

Haiti is coming off its inaugural appearance in the 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand. Les Grenadières, as they are known, are a rising team led by attacking duo Melchie Dumornay and Nérilia Mondésir, supported by a defense that has allowed only one goal during qualifiers.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mente Mujer (@mentemujer_)

Though the Women’s World Cup does not begin until next June, the matches will stream on Netflix for the first time, with Mexico’s women primed for their deepest run in tournament history. Furthermore, the 2031 Women’s World Cup will be co-hosted by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica, marking the first time Mexico will host the FIFA women’s event.

Until then, El Tri Femenil hopes to deliver the nation its first World Cup trophy — regardless of gender.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: US crimes against Mexico from an immigrant’s perspective
World.content:
There is nothing like living outside of your native country to make you reflect on the meaning of its actions, especially if your native country happens to be the United States of America.

Living in Mexico, of course, makes you an automatic representative of your country. This is not a fair position to be in, but it is the story of immigrants everywhere. For the most part, I benefit from my country of origin: whereas plenty of people in the U.S. might look down on an immigrant from Mexico, here it is the opposite. Most people expect me to be cool and interesting, and maybe a little sneaky, scary or both.

We may all be individuals, but the human brain only has so much capacity to think of people as individuals. Gather too many foreign individuals into the same place, and the borders between us blur and blend until we are collectively “others.”

Proud and ashamed

Many things about the U.S. make me very, very proud to be from there: like jazz music, the advancement of civil rights and feminism. First in flight. Customer service agents who are mostly empowered to actually help you. Clean public restrooms with toilet paper, for free!

Other aspects of my home country, however, make me feel deeply, deeply ashamed. A less-than-stellar record when it comes to genocide and enslavement, for example. And oh, Lord, influential religious leaders who would love to send us back to those “good old days.” Deliver us!

When it comes to current events, our treatment of immigrants is at the top of my list right now.

In case you have been protecting your peace more than I have and have abstained from the news, here is a sad summary: Donald Trump returned to office with as much of a mandate as you could suppose to reduce the “out of control” immigration in the U.S.

The killing of innocents and deportation of US citizens

More Latinos in the U.S. than ever voted for him. Strangely, they seemed to believe his promise that he would only target and deport “the criminals” among them. Who would not get behind that?

As it turns out, there are a lot fewer “immigrant criminals” than most people thought. So, unfortunately for the law-abiders, the net was pretty much immediately cast much, much wider to meet detention quotas set by the administration. It caught mothers and fathers taking their children to school. It caught lots and lots of people here legally, papers be damned. It caught those who were brought as children and have known no other life than that of an American.

On top of the generalized horror of being torn from one’s life, there is the very suspicious fact that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been extremely cagey, caught in lies more than once. It is a fight every time a local official wants to enter a (privately run) detention facility. Those who have come out of them have described the places as unfit for human beings. Rotting food, freezing temperatures and medical needs that are ignored. It is not hard to imagine how over 50 people have died since detentions were ramped up upon Trump’s return, some by suicide. Seventeen of these deaths have been of Mexican nationals (14 in custody, three during “operations”).

A lack of institutional control

Then, of course, there are the vehicle stops and shootings under extremely suspicious circumstances. One of the latest, of course, was that of a Mexican national, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who turned out not to even be ICE’s target. ICE’s story is that he tried to “weaponize his vehicle” against them. Witnesses say it was quite the opposite. The feds had to be blocked from deporting the witnesses. Weird behavior from an institution that has nothing to hide, right?

In short, things are truly out of control.

The U.S. and Mexico are supposed to be allies. What is going on here?

‘A general lack of accountability’

The main thing that is going on, I believe, is that the wrong people are in charge. Unhappy people voted them in, believing their lies about what the source of their unhappiness actually stemmed from. A threadbare social safety net paired with barely-there labor laws that are happy to let people simply fall through the net and onto the concrete pavement? Nah, that cannot be it … transgender people and immigrants, that is who is hurting you!

Social media — what was supposed to bring us together — and a general lack of accountability to the truth that the internet age has wrought have been excellent at getting people all riled up for stupid reasons.

The U.S. is really pushing it with Mexico right now.

Can Mexico do anything about it?

I personally think that is doubtful, but who knows? I have been wrong before. But if ICE cannot even be held accountable for its on-camera killings of U.S. citizens, who is going to put a boot on its neck over immigrant killings?

And when the offending country has been essentially in charge of international justice for decades, it is hard to tap the brakes. After all, who do you go to for help when the police themselves are corrupt?

Mexico, of course, understands this conundrum in a literal sense. But Mexico also does not claim to be the distributor of justice for the world, either.

Of all the words I might use to describe Mexicans, “proud” would be in the top five. While it seems that a few insults here and there will always be tolerated because of the particular power dynamic the two countries have, you cannot just start letting its citizens die and not even apologize for it.

Mexico files criminal complaints

Claudia Sheinbaum, thankfully, is not letting this go. Criminal complaints, cease-and-desist letters to the private companies in charge of detention, the United Nations. They are going at it from all angles.

The Secretariat of Foreign Affairs is “filing a criminal complaint against whoever is responsible.”

But, gosh. “Whoever is responsible.” Hmm. There is our first issue right there.

Would that be the president, for insisting that as many immigrants be tossed out of the U.S. as possible? Stephen Miller, the architect of the whole thing? Agency heads? Those who hire and “train” (or don’t) ICE officers? The private companies who feel no need to provide adequate living conditions? The offending/negligent immigration officers themselves? It truly is a long list of candidates.

The known reality, of course, is that in the end, it is unlikely anyone will be held to account. I mean, we cannot even get the U.S. to acknowledge that it dropped a bomb on an Iranian girls’ school, killing hundreds of children. Sanctity of life, indeed.

‘The twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty’

How are we supposed to get anyone who has been given “free rein” to carry out the president’s signature plan to play fair?

One of the biggest crimes that humans commit against each other is allowing the twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty to go on … and right now, those twin monsters have the full backing of the U.S. federal government.

This is what happens when you remove the shackles of accountability from institutions filled with the kinds of people who see the world as a fight between those who hunt and those who get hunted.

And many people who work in ICE fancy themselves hunters; they like to prey on people who are running or scared, or just trying to stay out of trouble’s way. They are hunted by the same types of people who used to catch (and torture) runaway slaves. They sniff out fear and relish the capture.

So here we are, many of us, living in a country that has welcomed us in ways that the U.S. would not dream of welcoming our neighbors. It is a strange and sad position to be in. It is also worth remembering that the tables could always turn.

We are the “others” here, after all.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Santa Cruz Marimba Ensemble Heads to Global Percussion Stage
World.content:
Cultural Heritage & Global Recognition

The Marimba and Percussion Ensemble from the University of Costa Rica’s Santa Cruz campus will perform at the PAS International Convention. —The Event. The Percussive Arts Society convention runs from 11 to 14 November in Indianapolis, United States. —A National First. It marks the first time traditional Guanacastecan marimba music will sound at this premier global percussion gathering. —The Director’s View. Director Raziel Acevedo Álvarez calls the PAS convention “el Mundial de Percusión,” or the World Cup of percussion. —Proven Track Record. The group has previously performed in Mexico, Guatemala, France, Poland, Portugal, Nicaragua, and Peru.

A Costa Rica marimba ensemble from the University of Costa Rica’s Santa Cruz campus will bring the traditional sound of Guanacaste to the world’s most prestigious percussion stage this November, marking a milestone for the country’s cultural diplomacy and musical heritage.

A World Stage for Guanacaste’s Rhythms

The Ensamble de Marimbas y Percusión del Recinto de Santa Cruz has accepted an invitation to the Percussive Arts Society International Convention in Indianapolis. The event runs from 11 to 14 November and gathers many of the planet’s most accomplished percussionists.

Director Raziel Acevedo Álvarez framed the invitation in competitive terms that resonate globally. He described the PAS convention as “el Mundial de Percusión,” explicitly comparing it to a World Cup for the percussion world.

Why the Invitation Matters for Costa Rica

The University of Costa Rica confirmed this will be the first time traditional Guanacastecan marimba music features at the PAS convention. The selection rests on the ensemble’s high artistic level and its dedicated work in researching and diffusing the region’s musical traditions.

For a small Latin American nation, placing a university cultural group on this stage carries soft-power value. It positions Costa Rica’s heritage alongside conservatoire-trained ensembles from wealthier countries, opening doors for future cultural exchange and tourism interest in the Guanacaste province.

The Road to Indianapolis

The Santa Cruz campus ensemble did not arrive at this moment by chance. The group has built a serious international résumé through concerts, conferences, and recitals across Costa Rica and beyond.

Previous invitations have taken the musicians to Mexico, Guatemala, France, Poland, Portugal, Nicaragua, and Peru. That sustained programme of performance and documentation of Guanacaste’s marimba traditions created the platform needed for PAS recognition.

What the Ensemble Brings to the Convention

The group focuses on the traditional marimba of Guanacaste, an instrument and repertoire distinct from the chromatic orchestral marimba more common in international percussion circles. Their programme will present rhythms and melodies rooted in Costa Rica’s Pacific Northwest.

The UCR news release noted that the invitation also reflects the challenge of preparing and presenting this material in a U.S. context. The ensemble must transport instruments, adapt to a new acoustic environment, and communicate the cultural context of each piece to an international audience.

The Investment and Expat Read-Through

Cultural milestones like this reinforce Costa Rica’s brand as a country that invests in education and the arts. The University of Costa Rica’s regional campuses, including Santa Cruz, serve as cultural anchors that boost quality of life in areas attractive to expats and retirees.

Guanacaste already draws significant foreign investment in tourism and real estate. International recognition of its cultural output adds another layer to the province’s appeal, distinguishing it from other sun-and-surf destinations in the region.

What to Watch Next

The ensemble’s performance in Indianapolis will be closely watched by cultural institutions back home. A strong showing could generate additional funding for the group and inspire similar university programmes across Central America.

The PAS convention itself runs across four days in November. Organisers typically release a detailed schedule closer to the date, and the Costa Rican ensemble’s slot will be one to track for those attending or following Latin American percussion.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Percussive Arts Society International Convention?

The PAS International Convention is widely regarded as the premier global gathering for percussionists. It brings together performers, educators, and industry professionals for concerts, clinics, and exhibitions.

The University of Costa Rica’s ensemble director has called it the “World Cup of percussion” due to the calibre of participants it attracts each year.

Why is this a milestone for Costa Rican marimba music?

This marks the first time the traditional Guanacastecan marimba will be featured at the PAS convention. The invitation validates years of research, documentation, and performance work by the Santa Cruz campus ensemble.

It places a distinctly Costa Rican musical tradition on a stage normally dominated by conservatoire and orchestral percussion styles.

Where has the Santa Cruz Marimba Ensemble performed before?

The ensemble has built an international profile with performances in Mexico, Guatemala, France, Poland, Portugal, Nicaragua, and Peru. These appearances, combined with extensive work inside Costa Rica, helped the group reach the artistic level required for the PAS invitation.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — July 27, 2026

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife







If You Only Go to One Place Pedra do Sal Samba (Monday Edition) If you have only one place to go tonight, make it the historic Pedra do Sal. This open-air, free samba gathering is Rio’s most authentic and welcoming ‘roda de samba’, where locals, musicians, and visitors pack the cobblestone square. It starts early enough for a new arrival and is the perfect gentle, joyful intro to Rio’s musical soul.







Tonight at a Glance —Pedra do Sal Free, open-air traditional samba in the birthplace of the genre. Crowd is an easy mix of locals, tourists and musicians. Arrive by 7 pm on Monday. —Quartinho Bar Intimate, artsy living-room bar in Botafogo for inventive cocktails and an effortlessly cool, LGBTQ+ friendly crowd before heading to Lapa. Best from 9 pm. —Bar Bukowski Long-standing rock ‘n’ roll dive bar in Botafogo, perfect for cheap drinks, a mixed local-expat crowd, and live bands when on. Good late-weekday fallback. —Mãe Joana Eclectic, pet-friendly Botafogo bar with bold cocktails, occasional art shows and a young, creative, LGBTQ+-inclusive scene. A warm-up hideout. —Arcos da Lapa Circuit No fixed venue, just follow the throng along Rua Mem de Sá. Party on the street with caipirinhas from carts, then dip into any pulsing samba bar. Just stick to the main strip.







Tonight, Monday 27 July 2026, Rio’s best move is to let the old-school samba of Pedra do Sal welcome you in the early evening, then migrate to Botafogo’s cool bars before diving into the chaotic joy of a Lapa street party. The circuit is as classic as it gets: an authentic, sprawling, open-air jam in the port zone, followed by hipster-bars-turned-samba-dens, all navigated safely with Uber and a little local know-how.







Tonight across Rio de Janeiro. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight







Roda de Samba ao Ar Livre — at Pedra do Sal, 7 pm (gathering); music from 8 pm. This is the quintessential Rio Monday night. The birthplace of samba fills with a democratic, joyful crowd for a free, acoustic street roda. It is friendly, unpretentious, and the single best cultural reset for a jet-lagged newcomer.







Artsy Pre-Club Drinks — at Quartinho Bar, 9 pm onwards. Botafogo’s hottest little bar offers a dimly-lit, erotic-art-clad haven for craft cocktails. A hip, chatty LGBTQ+ friendly crowd spills onto the pavement, making it a perfect transitional stop before Lapa gets loud.







Eclectic Bar Social — at Mãe Joana, 9 pm onwards. A few doors down, Mãe Joana’s whimsical decor and bold drinks draw a creative young crowd. If there’s a DJ or samba jam scheduled tonight, it’s the best spot to loosen up mid-week in Botafogo.







Rock Bar Night — at Bar Bukowski, 11 pm onwards. If Monday brings a live rock cover band, Bukowski’s grungy Botafogo bunker is a sure bet for affordable beers, a heavy dose of AC/DC, and chatting to Carioca rockers and international stragglers who don’t want the night to end.







Lapa Street Party — at Rua Mem de Sá / Arcos da Lapa, 11 pm to 3 am. Lapa doesn’t need a headliner to be electric. The street IS the venue. Grab a caipirinha from a cart, dodge the dancers, and let the thumping bass from open-doored bars like Rio Scenarium guide you.







The Circuit: When to Go Where







Warm-up (7 pm – 10 pm): Start at Pedra do Sal in Saúde for free outdoor samba. Grab a beer and a pastel, soak up the sunset music, and don’t be shy to squeeze into the circle.







Botafogo Shift (9 pm – 12 am): Take an Uber to the Rua Nelson Mandela/Voluntários da Pátria axis. Hit Quartinho Bar or Mãe Joana for a speak-easy vibe and crafted cocktails among Rio’s creative class.







Lapa Late-Night (11 pm – 3 am): Uber to the Arcos da Lapa. Walk Rua Mem de Sá, let the sound bleed from venues like Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema wash over you, and join the street carnival.







Weekend Pre-Game (Thursday onwards): Thursday belongs to Baixo Gávea’s student street chaos, while Friday and Saturday nights see Botafogo’s deck bars and Lapa’s live houses hit their explosive peak.







Post-Beach Sunset (Daily): In Ipanema and Leblon, start at a beach kiosk like Barraca do Uruguai for a post-sunset caipirinha before moving to Rua Dias Ferreira’s upscale bars for a quieter Monday alternative.







Scenes & Sounds







Samba — The spiritual heartbeat of Rio. In intimate botecos or vast street rodas, the percussion and cavaquinho rattle your bones. Highly participatory; don’t worry if you can’t clap on the two perfectly. Where: Pedra do Sal (Mondays), Carioca da Gema, Rio Scenarium (Lapa), and weekend street parties in Centro.







MPB and Jazz — A softer, more contemplative Brazilian sound. Perfect for date nights where you can actually talk. Expect velvety Portuguese vocals over acoustic guitar. Where: Beco das Garrafas (Copacabana), Vinícius Bar (Ipanema), and Blue Note Rio (Lagoa).







Funk and Baile — High-octane, bass-heavy Brazilian funk parties. Raw, sweaty, and deeply local. Best to attend with a Brazilian friend who knows the dynamics unless you are at a controlled club night. Where: Parties in Vidigal and Rocinha (go with locals), or club nights in Lapa and Centro.







Electronic — A smaller but dedicated scene. From sweaty underground booths to poolside day parties, house and techno dominate. Where: D-Edge (Barra), Fosfobox (Copacabana), and roving daytime parties like Surreal Park.







Forró — The sexy, close-dancing folk forró from the Northeast. Partner dancing is essential; classes often precede the party, making it a great solo activity. Where: Feira de São Cristóvão (the mammoth indoor market) and dedicated forró houses in Lapa.







Pick Your Night







Solo and safe: Pedra do Sal. It is impossible to feel lonely here. The crowd is a natural blend, it ends early enough for an easy Uber home, and the open-air space feels secure and communal.







Date night: Quartinho Bar into Rio Scenarium. The intimate, dimly-lit cocktail spot sets a romantic tone, followed by the multi-level antique wonderland of Rio Scenarium for dancing among beautiful things.







Meet locals: Baixo Gávea. Specifically a Thursday, but tonight, Botafogo’s bars like Bukowski or Mãe Joana are where groups of Carioca friends decompress and are open to chatting at the bar.







Chill and conversation: Leblon’s Rua Dias Ferreira. A sophisticated, low-volume Monday. Hit Boteco Belmonte for chopp (draft beer) and impeccable empadinhas at a pavement table with an upscale local crowd.







Dance till sunrise (future weekend): D-Edge or Fosfobox. For future reference, these are the bunkers for electronic music. Not peak on a Monday, but on weekends, they run past 5 am for the truly relentless.







Where to Go







Pedra do Sal — Saúde (Porto Maravilha) A sacred historical site and the most genuine ‘roda de samba’ you will find. Crowd spans all ages, races, and orientations; tourists mingle seamlessly with die-hard sambistas. Tonight: Traditional free outdoor ‘Roda de Samba’ starting around 8 pm. No tickets, no walls, just pure music. Best time: Mondays, 8 pm to midnight. Arrive by 7 pm to get a spot on the steps and snag a beer before the crush. Cost: Free entry. Beer from street vendors: ~R$10. Caipirinhas: ~R$20. Cash useful, some vendors take PIX. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde, Rio de Janeiro Instagram: @pedradosaloficial Getting there: Uber direct (set pickup/dropoff on Rua Sacadura Cabral). VLT tram to Parada dos Museus is also an option before dark. Good to know: No booking; just show up. Very casual.







Quartinho Bar — Botafogo An intimate lounge with risqué art and a decadent living-room feel. It draws a sophisticated, LGBTQ+ friendly, and effortlessly cool crowd for cocktails before the real party starts. Tonight: Opens at 7 pm. Check their Instagram for Monday DJs or themed nights; otherwise, a reliable, chatty cocktail standby. Best time: Weekdays 8 pm–1 am. Peak vibe around 10 pm. Cost: Craft cocktails: R$35–R$50. Comanda tab system. Card and PIX accepted. Address: Rua Conde de Irajá 95, Botafogo, Rio de Janeiro Instagram: @quartinhobar Getting there: Botafogo metro station (10-min walk). Use Uber late at night. Good to know: Walk-in friendly on weekdays; a short wait possible after 10 pm.







Bar Bukowski — Botafogo Rio’s legendary rock temple. Dark, loud, sticky floors, but incredibly fun. Great for a low-stakes night of pool, cheap beer, and a cross-section of Carioca subcultures. Tonight: Likely open with DJ rock sets or a live cover band. Confirm programming on Instagram. Doors open 9 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday, 11 pm until very late. Monday is a quieter ‘check first’ night. Cost: Entry may be free or R$20 on band nights. Beer: R$12–R$18. Comanda system operates. Address: Rua Álvaro Ramos 270, Botafogo, Rio de Janeiro Instagram: @barbukowski Getting there: Short walk from Botafogo metro. Uber recommended for return. Good to know: No booking generally; dress code is strictly casual/alternative.







Mãe Joana — Botafogo Whimsical decor and a vibrant, pet-friendly garden space make this one of Botafogo’s most loved hangouts. A creative, younger crowd and excellent signature drinks. Tonight: Open from 6 pm. Usually features ambient DJ sets or acoustic music on weekdays. Best time: Tuesdays to Fridays from 8 pm. Cost: Cocktails ~R$38. Bar snacks available. Card accepted. Address: Rua Conde de Irajá 181, Botafogo, Rio de Janeiro Instagram: @maejoanabar Getting there: Near Botafogo metro. Ride-share is safest post-midnight. Good to know: Walk-ins welcome.







Rio Scenarium — Lapa A three-story antique shop turned nightlife wonderland. It is touristy, yes, but absolutely unmissable for the visual spectacle and quality samba/MPB bands. Crowd is half tourist, half local. Tonight: Open tonight. Monday lineups usually feature a quality samba or MPB group. Check their Instagram for tonight’s exact band and set time, likely 9 pm. Best time: Any night it’s open, 9 pm arrival to beat the queues. Music starts ~10:30 pm. Cost: Entry: R$40–R$80. Comanda card system strictly enforced. Drinks: R$25+. Card OK. Address: Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro, Rio de Janeiro Instagram: @rio_scenarium Website: www.rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Uber direct to door. Do not wander the surrounding dark streets on foot. Good to know: Highly recommended to book a table via their website; otherwise queue early.







Carioca da Gema — Lapa A smaller, grittier, and more local alternative to Rio Scenarium right across the street. Intense samba sessions in a cozy, sweaty atmosphere. Tonight: Roda de Samba tonight typically from 9:30 pm. Confirm on Instagram for the specific group. Best time: Monday to Saturday. Music peaks at 11 pm. Cost: Couvert Artístico: R$30–R$50. Beer/Drinks: affordable. Comanda system. Address: Av. Mem de Sá 79, Lapa, Rio de Janeiro Instagram: @cariocadagema Getting there: Uber to the Arcos da Lapa, a short walk on the main drag. Good to know: Shows up early (9 pm) for a table; no booking needed for standing.







Boteco Belmonte — Leblon The quintessential upscale Rio boteco chain. Perfect for a ‘zero anxiety’ night. Impeccable draft beer, classic empadinhas, and a flawlessly executed steak sandwich among a well-heeled local crowd. Tonight: Open from midday until 1 am. A reliable standby for a quiet, high-quality Monday meal and drink. Best time: Weekdays 7 pm–11 pm for a lively but not chaotic atmosphere. Cost: No entry fee. Chopp ~R$15. Dishes R$40–R$90. Card and PIX accepted. Address: Rua Dias Ferreira 521, Leblon, Rio de Janeiro Phone: +55 21 2274-8379 Instagram: @botecobelmonte Getting there: Uber drop-off at the door. Anjos do Leblon metro is a 20-min walk. Good to know: No booking; grab a free pavement table.







Fosfobox — Copacabana A subterranean club (‘a caixinha’) that is a legendary alternative to mainstream beats. Great for rock, indie, and retro pop after-hours in a labyrinth of basement rooms. Tonight: Usually a ‘Quiet Monday’. Verify on Instagram, but it’s typically a weekend destination. If open, it’s a reliable late-late option. Best time: Friday/Saturday, 1 am to 5 am. Cost: Entry R$30–R$60. Comanda card. Cash and card. Address: Rua Siqueira Campos 143, Loja 22A (Galeria), Copacabana Instagram: @fosfobox Getting there: Metro Siqueira Campos (5 min). Uber for leaving. Good to know: Pay at door.







Cobal do Humaitá — Humaitá/Botafogo Border A massive renovated market hall housing a collection of bars and restaurants with shared outdoor tables. It is an easy, sure-fire bet for large groups or solo drinkers to blend in. Tonight: Open until late. Best for starting the night. Grab a beer from multiple different vendors under the same roof. Best time: Weekdays 6 pm–11 pm. A lively but contained after-work crowd. Cost: Variable by stall. Beer ~R$12–R$18. Card accepted everywhere. Address: Rua Voluntários da Pátria 446, Humaitá Instagram: @cobaldohumaita Getting there: Easy Uber drop. 15-min walk from Botafogo metro. Good to know: No booking; free seating.







Neighbourhoods at a Glance







Botafogo: The hipster hub. Edison bulbs, craft beer on Voluntários da Pátria, and an unpretentious local crowd that bridges the South Zone’s beach and the city’s grit.







Lapa: High-octane, sweaty, historical bohemia. The arches loom over a non-stop street party that smashes tourists, suburban Cariocas, and samba purists together on the same sticky cobblestones.







Saúde (Porto Maravilha): Revitalised docklands. The crowd is a cultural purist mix; you come specifically for live music venues like Pedra do Sal and Trapiche Gamboa, not for a pub crawl.







Leblon: Polished and wealthy. Rua Dias Ferreira is the dining spine, complete with designer glasses and sidewalk tables where the only danger is the price tag on the wine.







Copacabana: Tourist-heavy but genuine nightlife density. A mix of old-school piano bars in Beco das Garrafas, dive clubs like Fosfobox, and mega kiosks on the pavement.







Gávea: University mayhem. On Thursday, the entire student body seems to flood the Baixo Gávea triangle, clutching plastic cups and causing a beautiful, youthful gridlock.







LGBTQ+ Tonight







Quartinho Bar (Botafogo) — Not an exclusively gay bar, but a deeply queer-friendly, artsy gathering spot. The living-room intimacy and erotic art collection make it a magnet for Rio’s creative LGBTQ+ community to start their night.







Buraco da Lacraia (Lapa) — A delightfully chaotic, slightly grimy Lapa dive famous for its over-the-top drag shows and late, late nights. Expect Brazilian pop, outrageous hosting, and zero judgement. A proper ‘sauna’ of people and fun.







The Week International (Centro) — The mega-club of note in Zona Portuária. Primarily a weekend draw, this huge, sleek space hosts massive gay parties and international DJs. Check the schedule, as it’s not a Monday stronghold but iconic.







Money & How Paying Works The Comanda Card: In most clubs (Rio Scenarium, Fosfobox), you receive a paper or plastic tab at the entrance. EVERYTHING you consume is notched onto this card, and you pay at the cashier before leaving. Losing the card results in a brutal, non-negotiable fine (often R$300+), so lock it in your pocket. Couvert Artístico: This is a cover charge for live music, not a ticket you buy in advance. It appears as a R$20–R$50 charge on your comanda or bill simply because a band is playing. It is separate from your food and drink. Cash vs. Card: Rio’s nightlife is plastic and PIX-friendly. You can use credit/debit cards for everything in established venues. Keep about R$100 in small cash, however, to buy caipirinhas from street vendors in Lapa or a pastel at Pedra do Sal. Tipping: A ‘serviço’ charge of about 10% is usually already included as the ‘couvert’ line on your final food/drink bill in table-service bars. You do not need to add bulk cash on top, though rounding up the final total for good service is a welcome grace note.







Getting Home Safe







Metrô Closing Time: The subway (MetrôRio) shuts down sharply at midnight (00:00) Monday through Saturday. The last trains depart the termini around 23:45; do not rely on it to get you home from Lapa at 1 am.







Uber vs. Taxi: Always, always use Uber or 99 to get home after dark, or to bridge neighbourhoods. Open the app inside the venue, verify the license plate, and wait in the doorway. Never hail a street taxi when you’ve had a drink.







Safe Pickups: In Lapa, set your pickup pin outside a major landmark like the Petrobras building or a well-lit bar entrance on Rua Mem de Sá, not a side alley. At GIG airport, Uber picks up at Gate D, Departures Level (2nd Floor).







Keep the Phone Hidden: When walking in crowded street areas like Lapa or even busy Ipanema crossings, don’t scroll with your arm stretched out. Window grabs from bikes or simply opportunistic snatch-and-grabs in a crowd happen. Duck into a doorway or bar to check the map.







Neighbourhood Bridges: Do not walk from Botafogo to Lapa or Copacabana to Botafogo at night. The tunnels and empty streets connecting them are not safe on foot. Spend the R$20 on an Uber for door-to-door peace of mind.







Frequently Asked Questions







What time should I arrive at Pedra do Sal?







Get there for 7 pm. The sun is dipping, the roda starts loosely at 8 pm, and it allows you to grab a cold beer before the density of the crowd squeezes the square. It’s respectful and fun to see the warm-up.







Is it safe around Lapa at night for a foreigner?







Yes, on the main strip (Rua Mem de Sá). It is a massive, policed party. Side streets, however, can quickly become sketchy. Stick strictly to the lit, busy roads where people are drinking, and don’t try to explore the dark ‘charming’ back alleys.







Do the clubs in Botafogo have a dress code?







No ties or suits needed anywhere. Rio nightlife is ‘casual chic’. For guys, a plain t-shirt, well-fitting jeans and clean sneakers open every door. Dress like a stylish European tourist, not a boardwalk tourist. Flip-flops (chinelos) will get you turned away from some Lapa clubs.







Sources: metrolinehub.com, planrio.com, supervia.com.br

Social Distortion Santiago will bring the iconic California punk-rock band to Teatro Caupolicán on 17 November 2026, adding a heavyweight name to Chile’s increasingly busy international concert calendar and signalling continued promoter appetite for the Andean market.

A Veteran Act Lands in Santiago

Social Distortion, fronted by Mike Ness since 1978, carved out a distinctive space between punk aggression and rockabilly swing. The band’s catalogue spans four decades and includes staples such as “Story of My Life,” “Ball and Chain,” and “Reach for the Sky.”

A South American date is a relative rarity for the group, whose touring has historically concentrated on North America and Europe. The Santiago stop suggests a broader regional routing that promoters have been quietly assembling.

For Chilean fans of punk and alternative rock, the show represents a chance to see a band that influenced generations of musicians but has seldom visited the Southern Cone. The booking also fits Teatro Caupolicán’s pattern of hosting legacy punk and hard-rock acts.

Teatro Caupolicán: Santiago’s Mid-Size Powerhouse

Teatro Caupolicán sits on San Diego street in central Santiago and has operated as a performance space since 1936. Its roughly 4,500-capacity configuration makes it the go-to venue for international acts that are too large for clubs but not filling stadiums.

The theatre has hosted everyone from Iggy Pop and The Offspring to Brazilian heavyweights like Sepultura. Its calendar for 2026 already includes ChileTerror Fest II in late November, underscoring its role as a hub for rock and metal programming.

The venue’s location, a short walk from the Universidad de Chile metro station, makes it accessible for both Santiago residents and visitors staying in the city centre. Surrounding bars and restaurants in the Barrio San Diego area typically see a surge in business on concert nights.

Chile’s Live-Music Economy Keeps Climbing

Chile’s concert industry has posted a strong recovery since the pandemic shutdowns of 2020–2021. Major international tours by artists including Coldplay, The Weeknd, and Karol G have drawn sell-out crowds, with ticket spending comfortably exceeding 2019 benchmarks.

Promoters are increasingly viewing Santiago as a reliable anchor for South American tours, alongside São Paulo, Buenos Aires, and Bogotá. The city’s combination of disposable income, a music-hungry audience, and modern logistics infrastructure makes it attractive for routing decisions.

For investors watching the Latin American entertainment sector, the steady stream of international bookings is a positive signal. It points to stable consumer confidence and a regulatory environment that, while not frictionless, allows large-scale events to proceed with manageable risk.

What the Social Distortion Santiago Date Means for Expats

Santiago’s expat community, concentrated in neighbourhoods such as Providencia, Las Condes, and Ñuñoa, has long complained about being bypassed by touring acts that stick to Brazil and Argentina. Each new international booking chips away at that grievance.

English-language live music also serves as a cultural anchor for professionals and families posted to Chile. A Social Distortion show offers a slice of familiarity in a city where day-to-day life unfolds in Spanish, and it tends to pull together a cross-section of Chileans and foreigners.

The concert adds to a quality-of-life narrative that relocation consultants and corporate HR departments use when selling Santiago as a destination. Access to global cultural events is a tangible factor in retention for multinational assignments.

Ticket Outlook and What to Watch

Ticket prices have not been officially published, but comparable rock shows at Teatro Caupolicán in 2025 and 2026 have ranged from CLP 45,000 to CLP 90,000 (approximately US$50 to US$100). VIP packages, if offered, would likely push above that band.

Sales are expected to launch through PuntoTicket, the dominant ticketing platform for Chilean venues. Readers should monitor Social Distortion’s official channels and the Teatro Caupolicán website for the on-sale announcement, as punk and legacy rock shows in Santiago have been known to sell out quickly.

The broader question is whether this date is a one-off or part of a larger Latin American swing. If additional dates surface in Lima, Buenos Aires, or São Paulo, it would confirm that promoters see a viable regional circuit for acts of Social Distortion’s profile — a development worth tracking for anyone with a stake in Latin America’s live-entertainment market.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Social Distortion playing in Santiago, Chile?

Social Distortion are scheduled to perform at Teatro Caupolicán in Santiago on 17 November 2026. The date is part of a Latin American tour leg, though additional regional stops have not yet been confirmed.

How can I buy tickets for the Social Distortion Santiago concert?

Tickets are expected to go on sale through PuntoTicket, the primary ticketing platform for Teatro Caupolicán. Exact on-sale dates and price tiers have not been announced, so checking the venue’s official site and Social Distortion’s social media is the best way to stay informed.

What is the capacity of Teatro Caupolicán?

Teatro Caupolicán holds approximately 4,500 people, making it one of Santiago’s premier mid-size concert venues. It is located on San Diego street in the city centre and is easily reached by metro.

World.content:
Fiscal Oversight

Colombia’s Comptroller General issued a formal fiscal risk warning after a sharp rise in public-sector contracts. —The numbers. 14,414 contracts worth approximately COP 4.55 trillion (USD 1.1 billion) were signed in a post-election-law surge. —Direct contracting. The Comptroller flagged a notable increase in direct contracting, bypassing competitive bidding processes. —Core concerns. Weak budget planning, contract concentration, and pressure on public cash flow and control capacity were cited. —Preventive measure. The notice was sent to the Ministry of Finance and other national government entities as an early alert.

Colombia’s Comptroller General has issued a formal fiscal risk warning after a surge of 14,414 public-sector contracts worth COP 4.55 trillion (USD 1.1 billion) under the Petro administration, signalling potential strain on the nation’s fiscal sustainability.

What Triggered the Fiscal Risk Warning

The Comptroller General’s office flagged the surge after a post–Ley de Garantías spike in government contracting. The electoral guarantee law restricts public-sector hiring and contracting ahead of elections, and its expiration often unleashes a backlog of deals.

The 14,414 contracts were concentrated in a matter of weeks, with direct contracting growing especially fast. Direct contracting allows entities to award work without competitive bidding, a practice that oversight bodies have long warned can reduce transparency and value for money.

The Comptroller’s Specific Concerns

The warning letter, sent to the Ministry of Finance and other national entities, listed four main risks. Weak financial and budget planning topped the list, alongside the rising share of direct contracting and the concentration of contracts among a narrow group of recipients.

The office also pointed to mounting pressure on public cash flow and the state’s ability to control spending quality. The alert was framed as preventive, not punitive — an early signal meant to prompt corrective action before the pattern hardens into a structural fiscal problem.

The Petro Administration’s Spending Push

President Gustavo Petro has made expanded public investment a centrepiece of his agenda, arguing that state spending must drive Colombia’s transition away from fossil-fuel dependence. His administration has pushed infrastructure, social programmes, and energy-transition projects that rely heavily on public procurement.

Critics say the contract surge reflects a broader pattern of loosening fiscal discipline. The Comptroller’s warning lands as Colombia’s government already faces a tight fiscal path, with tax revenues under pressure and debt-service costs rising in a high-rate global environment.

What the Fiscal Risk Warning Means for Investors

For bondholders and portfolio investors, the alert adds a new layer of near-term uncertainty. Colombia’s fiscal rule, which limits the structural deficit, has been a cornerstone of investor confidence, and any sign that spending is outpacing planning raises questions about compliance.

Direct contracting also carries governance risks that institutional investors track closely. A perceived weakening of procurement standards can affect sovereign credit assessments and the risk premiums demanded on Colombian peso and dollar-denominated debt.

The Latin America Read-Through

Colombia’s experience mirrors a wider regional tension between activist governments and fiscal watchdogs. From Peru to Chile, independent comptrollers and central banks have clashed with executives eager to accelerate public spending, often with direct contracting as the flashpoint.

For expats and business operators inside Colombia, the warning is a reminder that the institutional checks built into the 1991 constitution remain active. The Comptroller General is an autonomous body, and its willingness to issue a public alert suggests oversight institutions are still functioning, even as political pressure on them grows across the region.

What to Watch Next

The Ministry of Finance’s formal response will be the first signal of how seriously the administration takes the alert. A detailed plan to tighten procurement oversight and return to competitive bidding would calm markets; silence or dismissal would likely deepen concern.

Investors should also watch for any follow-up from the Comptroller’s office, including specific audits of high-value direct contracts. Any finding of material irregularities could shift the political debate in Congress, where Petro’s coalition already faces resistance on fiscal reform.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a fiscal risk warning in Colombia?

A fiscal risk warning is a formal preventive alert issued by the Comptroller General’s office to government entities. It flags spending patterns or budget practices that could threaten the country’s fiscal sustainability if left unaddressed, and it is designed to prompt corrective action before a crisis develops.

Why did direct contracting increase under the Petro administration?

The surge followed the expiration of the Ley de Garantías, an electoral law that restricts government contracting ahead of elections. Once the restriction lifted, a backlog of projects moved forward, and the administration used direct contracting to accelerate spending on infrastructure and social programmes central to its agenda.

How does this affect Colombia’s credit rating and investment climate?

The warning adds near-term uncertainty for bondholders and rating agencies that track Colombia’s fiscal rule compliance. A sustained rise in direct contracting and weak budget planning could pressure sovereign credit assessments and widen risk premiums on Colombian debt, though the alert itself is preventive and does not yet signal a breach of fiscal targets.

World.content:
Chile · Regulation · Business

Chile’s REP Law is entering a decisive phase for electronics and battery recycling decrees. —TRAEE’s role. It is the first collective management system in formation for electrical and electronic waste under the REP Law. —Compliance shift. The move signals a transition from voluntary pilots to structured, binding compliance mechanisms for major retailers. —Battery focus. Duracell’s inclusion is strategic ahead of a specific Supreme Decree for battery collection and valorisation goals.

Four major consumer-facing companies have joined Chile’s TRAEE collective waste system, positioning themselves ahead of binding TRAEE REP Law decrees that will soon mandate recycling targets for electronics and batteries.

The TRAEE platform and its regulatory moment

TRAEE, which stands for Transformación de Residuos de Aparatos Eléctricos y Electrónicos, is the first collective management system in formation for electrical and electronic waste under Chile’s REP Law (Law 20.920). Incubated by the Santiago Chamber of Commerce (CCS), it has until now operated as a voluntary, pre-regulatory platform running pilots with municipalities and recyclers.

That status is changing rapidly. The Ministry of Environment is preparing decrees that will set mandatory collection and valorisation goals for electrical and electronic equipment (AEE) and batteries, triggering a 24-month window for producers to form and gain approval for formal management systems.

Why Cencosud, Falabella and Tottus are moving now

For large retailers that sell high volumes of electronics and batteries, joining TRAEE at this stage is a calculated compliance move. Romina Reyes, TRAEE’s manager, has noted a typical operational limbo of six to eight months between new partners joining and formal approval of a management plan by the Ministry.

Early adhesion allows Cencosud, Falabella and Tottus to co-design the collective system they will later depend on for legal compliance. It also helps ensure the system has the scale, geographic reach and financial backing to meet future targets, reducing the risk of non-compliance once decrees take full effect.

Duracell and the coming battery decree

Duracell’s entry is particularly strategic. Batteries are explicitly foreseen as a priority product under the REP Law, and a dedicated Supreme Decree for battery collection and valorisation goals is under preparation.

TRAEE is transitioning to serve a new combined priority product category called “Pilas + RAEE” (P+RAEE). Having a global battery brand inside the system strengthens its capacity to handle this combined stream and embeds Duracell in a multi-sector solution rather than leaving it to manage isolated compliance efforts.

The broader REP Law timeline

Chile’s REP Law creates a binding framework where producers and importers of priority products must organise and finance the management of their post-consumer waste. Implementation has been gradual, with mandatory targets for tyres and packaging beginning in 2023.

Textiles are expected to be declared a new priority product, with goals still to be set by decree. The next wave will cover electrical and electronic equipment and batteries, and stakeholders describe this fifth year of implementation as critical for determining whether the REP system advances or stagnates.

What this means for investors and the market

The adhesion of major retailers to TRAEE signals that Chile’s extended producer responsibility regime is moving from pilot phase to enforceable reality. For investors in Chilean retail and consumer goods, this means compliance costs will become a visible line item, but early movers may gain operational advantages and reputational capital.

Competition authorities, including the FNE and TDLC, oversee collective systems under the REP Law to ensure they operate autonomously and do not hinder competition. That oversight is particularly relevant when major retailers coordinate through a single system, and governance and transparency will be closely watched as TRAEE scales up.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the REP Law in Chile?

The REP Law (Law 20.920) is Chile’s extended producer responsibility framework. It requires producers and importers of priority products—including electronics, batteries, packaging and tyres—to organise and finance the collection and recycling of their post-consumer waste, with binding targets set by decree.

Why are retailers joining TRAEE now?

The Ministry of Environment is preparing decrees that will set mandatory recycling targets for electronics and batteries. Joining TRAEE before those decrees take effect allows companies to co-design the collective system, secure geographic coverage and avoid the six-to-eight-month operational limbo that follows formal adhesion.

What does Duracell’s participation mean for battery recycling in Chile?

Duracell’s entry strengthens TRAEE’s capacity for the new combined “Pilas + RAEE” category. A dedicated Supreme Decree for battery collection and valorisation goals is under preparation, and having a global battery brand inside the system aligns it with upcoming binding obligations.

Rolling Stones guitarist Ronnie Wood will bring a career-spanning live show to Santiago’s Movistar Arena on 10 November 2026, his only scheduled performance in Chile.

A Rare Solo Appearance from a Rock Institution

Ronnie Wood, a two-time Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee, will headline the Movistar Arena in Santiago on 10 November 2026. The concert, first reported by Chilean outlet The Clinic, marks a rare solo outing for the guitarist away from the Rolling Stones machine.

Wood will be joined by Irish vocalist Imelda May, a long-time collaborator known for her rockabilly and blues-infused style. The pairing suggests a setlist that draws deeply from Wood’s six decades of recording, spanning his work with the Faces, the Jeff Beck Group, and his solo catalogue.

The show is tied to the release of Fearless: The Anthology, a compilation that curates highlights from Wood’s extensive career. For Chilean fans, the date represents a concentrated dose of rock history delivered by one of its most enduring sidemen and frontmen.

Santiago’s Growing Pull as a Live-Music Capital

The booking reinforces Santiago’s position as a priority stop on South American tour itineraries. Movistar Arena, with its roughly 15,000-seat capacity, has become the city’s go-to indoor venue for international legacy acts seeking a controlled, high-production environment.

Chile’s live-music market has matured significantly over the past decade. Promoters now routinely route major tours through Santiago alongside São Paulo and Buenos Aires, a shift driven by rising disposable income in certain demographics and a concert-going culture that supports premium ticket pricing.

For the broader Latin America desk, the Wood date is a data point in a larger story: the region’s biggest cities are competing aggressively for high-value cultural tourism. A single arena show by a Rolling Stone generates hotel nights, restaurant spending, and media attention that extends well beyond the box office.

What the Ronnie Wood Santiago Show Means for Investors and Expats

For expats and business travellers based in Chile, the concert is a high-profile cultural event on the 2026 calendar. It signals that Santiago continues to attract the kind of talent that makes a city feel globally connected, a factor that weighs into corporate relocation and retention decisions.

From an investor perspective, the live-entertainment sector in Chile has shown resilience even through political and economic cycles. Venues like Movistar Arena operate with international-standard infrastructure, and the pipeline of confirmed acts for 2026 suggests promoter confidence in consumer demand holding firm.

The Wood–May pairing also highlights a trend toward curated, narrative-driven tours rather than full-scale stadium productions. These formats carry lower overhead and can be profitable at mid-sized venues, a model that suits markets like Chile where the population base is smaller but the willingness to pay for premium experiences is high.

The Imelda May Factor and the Setlist Appeal

Imelda May’s presence elevates the show beyond a standard retrospective. The Dublin-born singer has collaborated with Wood on multiple projects and brings her own devoted following, particularly among fans of roots-rock and Americana.

Their on-stage chemistry typically allows Wood to move between guitar and vocal duties while May handles lead singing on select tracks. For the Santiago audience, the format promises a dynamic evening that covers Faces-era rave-ups, Stones deep cuts, and material from Wood’s solo albums.

The Fearless: The Anthology framing gives the tour a clear narrative hook. Rather than promoting a single new record, Wood is packaging his entire body of work, a strategy that resonates with older demographics who value legacy and with younger listeners discovering the catalogue through streaming.

Ticketing and What to Watch Next

Ticketing details for the Ronnie Wood Santiago concert have not yet been published, but Movistar Arena events in Chile typically follow a structured rollout. Presales are often tied to specific bank cards or promoter mailing lists, with general sales opening on the PuntoTicket platform shortly after.

Demand is likely to be strong given the exclusivity of the date. With no other Chilean shows on the itinerary, the single Santiago appearance will draw fans from across the country and potentially from neighbouring Argentina, where the Rolling Stones themselves have historically played larger stadiums.

The key watchpoint for the industry is whether this solo tour expands into a broader Latin American leg. If the Santiago show performs well, promoters in São Paulo, Buenos Aires, and Mexico City will almost certainly push for additional dates, turning a one-off into a regional run.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Ronnie Wood performing in Santiago, Chile?

Ronnie Wood is scheduled to perform on 10 November 2026 at the Movistar Arena in Santiago. The date was confirmed by Chilean media and is his only announced show in the country.

Who is performing with Ronnie Wood at the Santiago concert?

Irish singer Imelda May will join Ronnie Wood on stage for the Santiago performance. The two have collaborated previously, and May’s vocal style complements the blues and rock material drawn from Wood’s six-decade career.

How can I buy tickets for Ronnie Wood’s Santiago show?

Official ticketing information has not yet been released. Based on standard practice at Movistar Arena, tickets will likely be sold through PuntoTicket, with presale windows announced via the promoter’s channels before a general public on-sale date.

The bill is due to be sent to the provincial Legislature in the first days of August 2026. —Target Markets. The measure targets international tourism from the United States, Europe, Asia, Israel, Brazil, and Chile. —Existing Benefit. Argentina’s Río Negro province is moving to make its tourism sector more attractive by eliminating a key provincial tax for foreign visitors. Governor Alberto Weretilneck announced the plan as part of a broader push to position Bariloche and the region as a more competitive destination in Latin America.

The Exemption Proposal

The government of Río Negro is preparing a bill that would exempt international tourists from paying the provincial Gross Income tax, known as Ingresos Brutos, on their purchases and services. Governor Alberto Weretilneck confirmed the initiative, stating that it aims to lower the cost of visiting the province and draw more foreign visitors.

If approved, the exemption would apply to a wide range of tourist spending, complementing an existing VAT refund program already available to non-resident travelers. Weretilneck emphasized that no other Argentine province has adopted such a measure, putting Río Negro at the forefront of a fiscal strategy designed to bolster international tourism.

Legislative Calendar

The draft law is scheduled to be presented to the provincial Legislature during the first days of August 2026, according to the governor’s office. Once submitted, it will enter the regular legislative process for debate and possible amendment before a final vote.

Officials are targeting the second half of the year for the measure to take effect, aligning with the peak season for international arrivals. The timeline reflects an urgency to capture demand from key long-haul and regional markets as global travel continues to recover.

Competitiveness Play

Bariloche and the wider Río Negro region face direct competition from neighboring Chile and other Latin American destinations that often lure visitors with lower tax burdens or promotional incentives. By removing the Ingresos Brutos charge, the province hopes to level the playing field and make its lakes, mountains, and ski resorts more price-attractive to foreign travelers.

The effort specifically names origin markets such as the United States, Europe, Asia, Israel, Brazil, and Chile as priorities. Weretilneck’s administration sees the tax exemption as a concrete tool to increase market share in the highly competitive international tourism sector.

Stacking Incentives

Foreign tourists in Argentina already benefit from a value-added tax (VAT) refund on certain purchases, a federal program that reduces the effective cost of goods and services. The proposed provincial exemption would layer additional savings on top of that refund, effectively lowering the total tax bite on a tourist’s spending inside Río Negro.

The combined fiscal incentives are designed to send a clear signal that Río Negro is open and committed to offering a high-value experience. Tour operators and hospitality businesses in Bariloche are expected to watch the legislative process closely, as the change could reshape local pricing strategies for foreign guests.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Gross Income tax (Ingresos Brutos) that tourists currently pay?

It is a provincial tax levied on gross revenue from sales of goods and services, which is typically passed on to consumers in the final price. The proposed exemption means foreign visitors would no longer bear this cost for qualifying purchases inside Río Negro.

Which foreign tourists would qualify for the exemption?

The measure is intended for international tourists arriving from abroad, with a particular focus on travelers from the United States, Europe, Asia, Israel, Brazil, and Chile. Details on eligibility documentation would be specified once the bill is introduced.

When could the exemption actually take effect?

The bill is set to be sent to the Legislature in early August 2026, with the aim of implementing the change in the second half of the year. The exact start date depends on how quickly lawmakers debate and approve the legislation.

World.title: Argentina Honors Gardel, Yupanqui and Piazzolla’s Living Legacy
World.content:
Cultural Heritage

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —Gardel’s legacy. Argentina marks Tango Day on 11 December, Gardel’s birthday, and maintains a house museum and subway station in his name. —Yupanqui’s centenary. A six-CD project replicated his complete guitar works, while state media and theatres continue to programme dedicated homage concerts. —Piazzolla’s centenary. Buenos Aires reopened the Teatro Colón in 2021 for his 100th-birthday programme and scheduled an Obelisk concert to close the year. —Institutional permanence. A Piazzolla homage was performed in 2024, and La Plata’s Teatro Argentino houses the Sala Astor Piazzolla. —Global reach. Ensembles such as Tango Buenos Aires tour internationally with Gardel programmes, and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra honoured Piazzolla’s centennial.

Argentina channels significant public and private resources into honouring Carlos Gardel, Atahualpa Yupanqui and Astor Piazzolla, treating the trio not merely as musicians but as foundational assets of the country’s cultural brand and soft power.

Gardel: the eternal voice that built a national myth

Carlos Gardel died in a plane crash in 1935, yet Argentina has spent nearly a century turning his memory into a permanent civic institution. His repatriated body lay in state at Luna Park, where tens of thousands queued through the night while radio stations broadcast his voice across the country.

The state later renamed a Buenos Aires subway station “Carlos Gardel” and converted his former home in the Abasto neighbourhood into a national historic monument and museum. Every 11 December, Argentina celebrates Tango Day on his birthday, a date that now anchors a calendar of concerts, exhibitions and tourism promotion.

For the 90th anniversary of his death, public bodies mounted the exhibition “Gardel, el cantor eterno” with photographs, letters and personal objects. The ritual at his Chacarita cemetery tomb—where visitors still place a lit cigarette between the fingers of his statue—shows how Gardel operates as a living cultural asset rather than a historical figure.

Yupanqui: the deep voice of Argentina’s land

Atahualpa Yupanqui occupies a different register: the rural, indigenous and social conscience of Argentina. Public Television Argentina has produced dedicated programmes marking the 25th anniversary of his death, framing his songs as “profoundly linked to identity, memory and the country’s cultural roots.”

For the centenary of his birth, guitarist Carlos Martínez recorded the complete works for guitar across six CDs, a discographic tribute that replicated Yupanqui’s technique with scholarly precision. Buenos Aires folklore cycles have been organised under themes such as “La voz profunda de nuestra tierra,” presenting Yupanqui as an emblematic figure of national folklore.

Government cultural portals describe him as a “wise and generous man” who helped construct Argentine identity. These tributes position Yupanqui as the soul of the creole guitar, a moral and poetic reference that anchors Argentina’s rural heritage in the national story.

Piazzolla: from tango killer to national treasure
