Astor Piazzolla’s trajectory within Argentina’s cultural memory is the most dramatic. Once derided as a “tango killer” for injecting classical and jazz elements into the genre, he is now treated as a national treasure whose centenary in 2021 triggered a year-long programme of state-backed events.

Buenos Aires reopened the Teatro Colón after pandemic closures specifically to feature Piazzolla concerts. The Kirchner Cultural Centre dedicated a special programme, and planners scheduled a large outdoor concert at the Obelisk so the city would “end the year to the sound of Piazzolla’s music.”

The institutionalisation continues: a Piazzolla homage was performed in the National Auditorium in 2024, and La Plata’s Teatro Argentino operates a permanent Sala Astor Piazzolla. An asteroid, (12102) Piazzolla, carries his name into the cosmos, a gesture that underlines how Argentina treats its cultural icons as assets of permanent global relevance.

Why Gardel, Yupanqui and Piazzolla matter as a trio

Argentina groups these three figures because together they cover the full spectrum of the country’s musical identity. Gardel represents the golden age of tango and the romantic urban myth of Buenos Aires; Yupanqui embodies the countryside, indigenous heritage and social conscience; Piazzolla stands for innovation, cosmopolitanism and the transformation of tango into a concert art form.

The state’s investment in their legacies—museums, subway stations, theatre halls, commemorative stamps, asteroid names and annual festivals—functions as cultural infrastructure. It supports tourism, fuels the country’s soft power abroad and provides a stable narrative of national identity that transcends Argentina’s frequent economic and political volatility.

The soft-power and market read-through

For investors and expats, Argentina’s sustained cultural spending on these figures signals something practical: the country’s brand equity in music and the arts remains a reliable export. Ensembles such as Tango Buenos Aires tour internationally with Gardel programmes, while orchestras from Chicago to Berlin programme Piazzolla, generating touring revenue and keeping Argentina in the global cultural conversation even when its macroeconomic indicators deteriorate.

The tributes also anchor domestic tourism. The Carlos Gardel House Museum, the Chacarita tomb ritual, the Sala Astor Piazzolla in La Plata and folklore cycles in Buenos Aires all draw visitors year-round, creating a cultural economy that operates independently of the peso’s fluctuations.

What to watch next is whether the Milei administration’s austerity drive touches cultural programming. So far, the institutional tributes—orchestral concerts, museum exhibits and anniversary events—have continued, suggesting that even in a fiscal squeeze, Argentina’s political class views the Gardel-Yupanqui-Piazzolla triad as untouchable national capital.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Argentina celebrate Tango Day on 11 December?

Argentina chose 11 December because it is the birthday of both Carlos Gardel and bandleader Julio de Caro. The date anchors a national calendar of concerts, exhibitions and tourism promotion centred on tango as a cultural export.

How did Astor Piazzolla go from being criticised to becoming a national treasure?

Piazzolla was initially attacked by tango purists for incorporating classical and jazz elements, earning the label “tango killer.” Over decades, his work gained international acclaim, and by his 2021 centenary Argentina was treating him as a heroic moderniser whose nuevo tango now defines the country’s contemporary musical identity abroad.

What is the economic value of Argentina’s tributes to these three musicians?

The museums, festivals, touring ensembles and commemorative events generate cultural tourism and soft-power dividends that operate independently of Argentina’s macroeconomic cycles. International orchestras programming Piazzolla and tango companies touring Gardel shows keep Argentine cultural exports earning foreign currency even during domestic downturns.

World.title: Rincón de la Vieja volcano raised to caution level after 38 eruptions
World.content:
If you have a Rincón de la Vieja hike or a hot springs day trip on your calendar, the volcano’s official activity level went up last week — and the change is worth not only knowing about but understanding before you drive out there.

The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVISCORI) moved Rincón de la Vieja from warning to caution on 24 July, the third rung on a four-step scale. Since 2 July the observatory has counted 38 phreatic eruptions at the crater. Three of them sent lahars down the northern flank. The strongest, on 20 July, was the most energetic eruption the volcano has produced all year.

Volcanologist Geoffroy Avard said the decision rested on more than the eruption count. Seismic activity has picked up. The shape of the volcano itself is changing measurably and to get technical, the Sulphur dioxide output is up. Put together, those three signals point the same direction, and the observatory said further eruptions of equal or greater intensity are possible. In a nutshell, this is not a report that something happened but a report that something is more likely to happen again.

What caution actually means

Costa Rica’s volcano scale runs from one to four. Level one is calm. Level two, warning, is where Rincón de la Vieja has spent most of the last several years — small eruptions, gas, hot springs bubbling harder than usual, mild swelling of the summit. Ash falls lightly if it falls at all.

Level three, caution, is a step up in what the volcano is capable of on short notice, not a declaration that it is erupting now. It means bigger explosions are on the table, rocks can be thrown further from the crater, ash can travel, and lahars are an expected consequence rather than a surprise. Level four is reserved for a major eruption in progress.

Nothing about level three closes the area, cancels flights or triggers evacuations. What it does is shrink the margin for error close to the crater, which is exactly where the hardest hiking in the park goes.

Why the rivers turn grey

Those downhill from the volcano reported the Azul and Pénjamo rivers running a milky grey earlier this month after eruptive episodes. That color is the most reliable early warning system in the area, and it is worth knowing what it signals.

Rincón de la Vieja has an acidic lake sitting inside its active crater. A phreatic eruption happens when groundwater or lake water hits something hot enough to flash it to steam, and the pressure blows out through the top. There is no lava involved. What comes out is steam, gas, rock and a great deal of water and sediment.

That water and sediment goes somewhere. The crater’s northern rim is the lowest, so the flow spills that way and races downhill as a lahar — essentially a fast-moving slurry of water, ash, mud and rock with the consistency of wet concrete. It picks up more material from the riverbed as it goes. By the time it reaches the lowland farming communities on the Upala side, the river is grey, smells of sulphur and is running higher than it was an hour earlier.

Rain makes this worse rather than better, which is important to know in late July. Heavy rain at the summit mobilizes loose volcanic material that is already sitting on the slopes, so a lahar can come down without a fresh eruption to announce it.

The historical record shows what these flows can do. In November 1995 a lahar took out the bridge over the Pénjamo entirely. In 2019 the same river rose more than four metres (13 feet) in minutes and widened by six metres (20 feet) on each bank. Dead fish have turned up in the Río Niño, 15 kilometres (nine miles) from the crater, after past events.

If you are near one of these rivers and the water changes color, rises or starts to smell of sulphur, get away from the channel and onto higher ground. Do not wait to see how big it gets. That is the whole safety rule, and it works because lahars travel much faster than people can outrun them along a riverbed.

What is open in the park

Rincón de la Vieja National Park covers 14,300 hectares (35,300 acres) and is the busiest protected area in the Guanacaste Conservation Area. It sits about 23 kilometres (14 miles) from Liberia, which is why it shows up on so many itineraries. Visitation splits between two sectors, Las Pailas and Santa María.

The Active Crater trail — eight kilometres one way, 16 kilometres (10 miles) round trip, climbing roughly 1,000 metres (3,300 feet) — has been closed for years. Volcanic activity and unsafe crater gases keep it shut, and last week’s level change does nothing to reopen it. Anyone selling you a summit hike is selling you something the park is not permitting.

The Las Pailas loop is the main draw and the reason most visitors come. It runs three kilometres (1.9 miles) on a circuit past fumaroles, boiling mud pots and steam vents that sit between 78 and 106 degrees Celsius (172 to 223 degrees Fahrenheit). It is well marked and partly paved. The waterfall trails to La Cangreja, five kilometres (3.1 miles) out, and Catarata Escondida, 4.3 kilometres (2.7 miles), are longer and harder.

Confirm the day before you go. Area and trail closures at this park have historically arrived with no notice, sometimes on the morning of, and travelers have turned up at the gate to be told a trail shut days earlier. Park staff at the entrance know the current status. A tour operator’s website from last season does not.

All tickets must be bought in advance through the park service’s online reservation system. There is no cash or card payment at the gate.

What closes first if the level rises

The pattern here in Costa Rica is consistent, and it works outward from the crater. Summit and crater-adjacent trails go first — those are already shut here. Next come the longer backcountry trails that put hikers hours from an exit, which is where the waterfall routes sit. Then the visited sectors themselves close, sometimes one at a time, sometimes both.

Hot springs resorts and private reserves on the volcano’s flanks operate independently of the park and make their own calls, so a park closure does not automatically mean your hot springs booking is cancelled, or the reverse. Full closures of an entire area have happened repeatedly at active volcanoes and have lasted anywhere from a day to several weeks. Build that possibility into a tight Guanacaste itinerary rather than assuming a single fixed day at the park will hold.

Poás is active too

Rincón de la Vieja is not the only volcano the observatory is watching. Poás, far more accessible from the Central Valley and San José, is producing low-intensity eruptions of its own. Poás has its own history of abrupt closures over gas emissions and ashfall, including multi-week shutdowns. If you are choosing between the two on a short trip, check both before committing.

Where to check

The observatory monitors Rincón de la Vieja continuously through seismic stations, gas-measuring equipment, cameras and field observation, and publishes changes as they happen. Level changes in either direction are announced rather than quietly applied — the volcano was moved down from caution to warning in a previous cycle, and it could go either way again.

The behavior on display now is not new for this mountain. Rincón de la Vieja has run through active phases and quiet ones since 2011, with stretches of daily small eruptions followed by months of little. What the level change records is that the current stretch is more energetic than the last one, and that the instruments suggest it has further to run.

World.title: Costa Rica Investigated Possible Drug Money Inside Soccer Club
World.content:
Costa Rican investigators examined whether money from an alleged international cocaine-trafficking organization was invested in Puerto Golfito F.C., a former second-division soccer club based in the country’s Southern Zone. The allegations form part of the Distrito organized-crime case, which is scheduled to go to trial on August 3.

The proceedings are expected to continue through late 2027, as prosecutors present telephone recordings, surveillance reports, photographs and extensive financial records. One of the main defendants is businessman Rehan Fraile Pérez, known as “Rey.” Investigators allege that Fraile received money connected to the criminal organization and moved it into businesses and sports projects, including Puerto Golfito F.C. and a soccer training operation called Premier Academy CR.

Fraile is accused alongside Hilary Walker Fowlker, known as “Hilario,” whom investigators identified as the suspected leader of the organization. A confidential Judicial Investigation Agency report included in the case file says Fraile maintained relationships with Puerto Golfito players and officials. Some of those individuals were suspected of having links to the alleged trafficking network, although the accusations have not been proven in court.

Investigators also documented meetings in Golfito and San José between Fraile and a club official identified by the surname Barquero and the nickname “Ceviche.” Undercover officers reportedly saw Fraile repeatedly at Fortunato Atencio Stadium, where Puerto Golfito played its home matches.

The investigation also recorded several trips by Walker to Costa Rica’s Southern Zone to meet Fraile. Prosecutors contend that these contacts formed part of a broader effort to move and disguise money generated by cocaine trafficking. The criminal case also examines Premier Academy CR. Investigators allege that former judicial employee Steven Mesén Bolaños acted as an intermediary between Fraile and Walker, helping arrange meetings, transfer money and handle matters connected to the academy.

Authorities say Mesén also collected two foreign visitors from Juan Santamaría International Airport and took them to facilities associated with the soccer project. During an August 2022 search of a gym linked to Fraile, investigators seized documents involving Puerto Golfito’s debts, academy employment contracts, accounting books and administrative records. Those materials are expected to be examined during the trial.

Prosecutors allege that the wider trafficking organization obtained cocaine along Costa Rica’s Pacific and Caribbean coasts before moving it into the Central Valley. The drugs were then allegedly shipped to the United States and Europe inside contaminated cargo containers and modified machinery.

The case has been linked to the seizure of 1,263 kilograms (2,784 pounds) of cocaine in Belgium and another 1,200 kilograms (2,646 pounds) in England. Costa Rican authorities also discovered vehicles with hidden compartments containing 33 kilograms (73 pounds) and 269 kilograms (593 pounds) of cocaine.

Puerto Golfito F.C. later became involved in a separate controversy over match-fixing. In March 2024, Costa Rica’s soccer federation banned the club and three senior officials from all federated soccer activities for 10 years. The officials sanctioned were club president Roy Telles Campos, majority shareholder Deivis Antonio Barquero and sporting director Arturo Alberoni Palma Fallas. The disciplinary proceeding began after suspicious betting activity was identified and reviewed through soccer integrity monitoring systems.

That disciplinary ruling was administrative and separate from the Distrito criminal case. However, the criminal file reportedly includes communications between Barquero and individuals accused in the trafficking investigation. The upcoming trial will determine whether prosecutors can prove that Fraile and the other defendants participated in the alleged trafficking organization and whether soccer projects were used to conceal or legitimize illegal profits.

The claims against Fraile, Walker and the other defendants remain allegations. None of the accusations involving the financing of Puerto Golfito F.C. has been proven in court.

World.title: High Court dismisses Nimrod Tillett’s constitutional challenge; extradition case to resume – Apologizes to DPP after Judge noted him staring ‘menacingly’
World.content:
High Court dismisses Nimrod Tillett’s constitutional challenge; extradition case to resume – Apologizes to DPP after Judge noted him staring ‘menacingly’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The High Court has dismissed a constitutional challenge filed on behalf of Orange Walk resident Nimrod Tillett Catzim, clearing the way for extradition proceedings requested by Mexican authorities to resume in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court.

Justice Derick Sylvester dismissed the claim on Monday after Tillett’s legal representatives acknowledged that they had been unable to obtain evidence supporting their argument that extraditing him to Mexico would violate his constitutional rights. The court made no order as to costs.

Tillett is wanted in Quintana Roo, Mexico, in connection with the alleged 2019 killing of a woman described as his former companion. Previous reports alleged that the woman’s body was discarded in a garbage container and that aspects of the incident were captured on surveillance footage.

Mexican authorities initially obtained a provisional arrest warrant against Tillett in October 2023, followed by a formal extradition request. The substantive proceedings were later interrupted after English barrister Tim Prudhoe raised questions concerning Tillett’s medical condition, the availability of specialist treatment in Mexico and conditions within the Mexican prison system.

The constitutional claim alleged that sending Tillett to Mexico could expose him to cruel and inhumane treatment, contrary to Section 7 of the Belize Constitution. The matter was consequently referred from the Magistrate’s Court to the High Court.

Director of Public Prosecutions Cheryl-Lynn Vidal, SC, told Breaking Belize News that the court established deadlines for Tillett’s attorneys to submit medical reports, witness statements and other evidence concerning Mexican prison conditions. However, several deadlines and extensions passed without the required documents being filed.

Two scheduled hearing dates were reportedly vacated because the evidence had not been submitted. Vidal said Tillett’s representatives informed the parties only last week that they had no evidence with which to substantiate the constitutional claim, but did not have instructions to withdraw or discontinue it. The issue was therefore left for Justice Sylvester, who dismissed the proceedings.

Vidal stressed that Monday’s ruling does not mean that Tillett has been ordered extradited. The High Court dealt only with the constitutional question, while the actual extradition application must now continue before the Chief Magistrate.

The State will present the High Court’s dismissal order to the Magistrate’s Court and request a date for the resumption of the extradition hearing. Tillett has not consented to surrender to Mexican authorities.

The DPP also expressed concern about the length of the delay, saying the Mexican authorities have repeatedly requested progress reports since making their request nearly three years ago. She clarified, however, that Mexico has not complained or threatened any consequences.

Rather, Vidal said the inability to report meaningful progress had become embarrassing for Belize and could reflect poorly on the country’s justice system. She maintained that the delay was caused by the claimant’s failure to file the evidence, rather than by the court, which she said had provided more than sufficient time for Tillett to substantiate his case.

Monday’s brief hearing also included an unusual courtroom intervention after Justice Sylvester observed Tillett staring “menacingly” at the DPP. The judge reminded Tillett that Vidal was acting professionally on behalf of the State and had nothing personal against him.

Tillett subsequently apologized. His extradition matter is expected to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, but no new hearing date has yet been announced.

World.title: Shyne Barrow launches 2622 LGND tour
World.content:
Shyne Barrow launches 2622 LGND tour

By Zoila Palma: Former Leader of the Opposition and rap artist Shyne Barrow has announced the launch of his “2622 LGND” tour, bringing together iconic names from Hip Hop and Reggae for a celebration of music’s golden eras.

The tour will feature reggae icon Barrington Levy and rap legend Lil Cease, with performances planned across the United States and Canada before expanding to international markets.

Shyne, who rose to prominence with his commanding baritone and gritty lyrical style, released his platinum-certified self-titled debut album in 2000, followed by the gold-certified “Godfather Buried Alive” in 2004.

Over his career, he has sold more than 40 million records as a performer, writer and producer, with credits involving artists including Usher, Lil Wayne and The Notorious B.I.G.

Announcing the tour on social media, Shyne said the upcoming shows will continue the legacy of his return to the stage. “Since my historic return to the stage on May 2 at the Kings Theatre I had to take a little time before we continued the World Tour to ensure I got the iconic Barrington Levy to clear his calendar so the people can get one of the most legendary Rap/Reggae collaborations ever live on stage in the U.S. and Canada before we go to Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, UK, Latin America, the Caribbean and finish in Belize!” he wrote.

Shyne added, “Beyond excited to announce the celebration of the legacy continues this fall with the 2622 LGND tour with my very special guests the iconic Barrington Levy and my brother lil Cease plus other surprises……can’t wait to see you.” The tour is expected to showcase classic hits from the artists while bringing together generations of fans across multiple musical genres.

The announcement comes as Shyne continues to build on a career that has spanned more than two decades and has included a transition from international music star to political figure.

World.title: International News: Pardoned by Trump, Former Honduran President Hernández returns home to face charges
World.content:
International News: Pardoned by Trump, Former Honduran President Hernández returns home to face charges

By Zoila Palma: Former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández returned to Honduras on Sunday, four years after he was extradited to the United States to face drug trafficking charges, following his release from prison after receiving a presidential pardon from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Hernández, who led Honduras from 2014 to 2022, was sentenced to 45 years in prison in the United States before Trump pardoned him in December, saying he had not received a fair trial.

Hernández now faces corruption charges in Honduras linked to the Pandora I case, which alleges that former senior officials participated in the distribution of more than 288 million lempiras ($10.8 million) in public funds to various foundations.

Prosecutors allege Hernández benefited from the scheme, receiving at least 62 million lempiras ($2.3 million) for his political campaign through shell companies, intermediaries and fictitious contracts.

The former president was welcomed at Palmerola International Airport by his family and supporters from his National Party. His return comes amid concerns from human rights advocates and legal experts that Honduras’ justice system may fail to hold him accountable.

In June, a judge suspended his arrest warrant and an international Interpol red notice, and Hernández has agreed to appear before a judge on August 3 for his arraignment.

World.title: International News: Infantino slams critics for spreading hate during World Cup 2026
World.content:
International News: Infantino slams critics for spreading hate during World Cup 2026

By Zoila Palma: FIFA President Gianni Infantino has criticized the World Cup 2026 tournament’s detractors, accusing them of “spreading hate” and missing the joy and unity surrounding the global football event, Yahoo reports.

In a lengthy social media post following the conclusion of the tournament, Infantino said critics were so focused on negativity that they failed to appreciate families and fans coming together to celebrate the sport.

“To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents, and parents come together for the beautiful game, I say sorry that the matches are now over and sorry that you missed all that joy and togetherness,” Infantino wrote.

“Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all.” He also appeared to criticize journalists and commentators, saying: “To those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours, I want to say that while you are sitting behind, we at FIFA are on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering the best show in the world.”

Infantino went on to defend the tournament’s message of unity while addressing criticism over refereeing and disciplinary decisions. “While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate,” he wrote, adding, “Our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning.” He also said, “It’s not about politics. Football is about unity, not division. Football is bigger than hate and discrimination.”

The FIFA president also defended what he described as “’arguable’ referees’ decisions” and “’strange’ disciplinary rulings,” saying such incidents are common in major football leagues.

World.title: Belize is about to license the fishermen while the trawler sails away untaxed
World.content:
Belize is about to license the fishermen while the trawler sails away untaxed

By Horace Palacio: Let me begin with a declaration of interest, because honesty is the price of your trust.

The proposed new Broadcasting Act, revealed this week, would expand the definition of broadcasting to cover the internet. Online outlets and creators earning advertising or sponsorship money from Belizean audiences would need a licence, or an official exemption, from the Belize Broadcasting Authority. That net catches podcasters, news pages, entertainment channels, and yes, the very publication carrying this column. I am inside the net I am about to discuss. Judge my argument on its merits.

And let me be fair before I am fierce, because the drafters are not villains. The online space has real problems. Defamation flows freely. Misinformation spreads faster than truth. There are no standards where standards sometimes matter. The attorney explaining the bill was careful to say the casual user going live for friends is not the target, only the regular commercial broadcaster. Fine. The instinct to bring order is not evil.

But the aim is backwards. And I can prove it with one question.

Who is the biggest broadcaster in Belize?

It is not any radio station. It is not any television house. It is not this publication or any local page. The biggest broadcasters in Belize, by audience, by hours consumed, by advertising dollars collected, are Meta, Google, and TikTok. Foreign platforms that reach more Belizean eyes every single day than every licensed Belizean broadcaster combined.

Now follow the money, because the money tells the whole story. Every time a Belizean business boosts a post, every sponsored ad served to a Belizean screen, that money leaves this country. It flies to California and Singapore. The platforms harvest Belizean attention, sell that attention back to Belizean businesses, and pay Belize nothing. No licence. No GST collected on the sale. No fee. Not one dollar to the treasury of the country whose citizens generate the value.

And into this reality walks a bill pointed at whom? At the Belizean podcaster. The Belizean news page. The young creator who figured out how to earn a living from a phone and a ring light.

Picture it plainly. A foreign supermarket sets up in the middle of every town at once, pays no rent, collects no GST, holds no licence, and sells to every Belizean household daily. And our response is to demand permits from the vendors selling tamales on the sidewalk outside. We are licensing the fishermen while the factory trawler empties our waters untaxed.

The world has already run this experiment, both ways, and the results are in.

France chose to aim upward. In 2019 it imposed a three percent tax on the revenue the digital giants earn from French users. Washington threatened tariffs. Paris held its ground. Today France collects hundreds of millions every year from the platforms, and here is the part that matters most, French creators were left completely alone. Britain did its own version at two percent. The principle is simple and just. You earned it from our people, you owe our treasury.

Uganda chose to aim downward. In 2018 it taxed its own citizens for the act of using social media, a daily fee just to open the apps. The result was a national self-inflicted wound. Millions of Ugandans simply went offline or escaped through VPNs. Small businesses that lived on those platforms bled. The revenue never came close to projections. By 2021 the government quietly abandoned the scheme. Burden your own users and creators, and you shrink your own economy while the foreign giants feel nothing at all.

Two roads, fully tested. One taxes the harvest of the giants. The other taxes the hustle of the citizens. And Belize’s draft, as revealed, starts down the Ugandan road.

There is a second danger in this bill, and it is heavier than any fee. A licence that can be granted can be denied. A licence that can be denied can be dangled. This column has already documented how advertising gets pulled in this country to punish inconvenient coverage. Now imagine every online news outlet, every commentator, every critic, holding a licence that some authority, under some administration, red or blue, must periodically renew, using criteria that live partly in official discretion. You do not need to revoke a single licence to change a country’s journalism. The mere possibility does the work. Every hard story gets weighed against the renewal date. That is not regulation. That is a leash. And a democracy should be very slow to braid one, even with good intentions.

So here is the constructive path, because this column does not tear down without building.

First, make the giants collect GST. Dozens of countries, including our Caribbean neighbours, already require foreign platforms to register and charge sales tax on digital services sold to their citizens, the subscriptions, the advertising. This is not radical. It is standard global practice, administratively proven, and it can be done here without touching a single Belizean creator. Start there, this year.

Second, study a modest digital services tax on the ad revenue the platforms extract from Belize, with eyes open. Honesty requires the caveat, such taxes have drawn American trade pressure, and Belize is small. Which is exactly why we should move with CARICOM, a coordinated regional levy that no one can bully one small island out of. Alone we whisper. Together the region speaks.

Third, flip the pipeline. Whatever Belize collects from the giants should seed a Belizean creators and local journalism fund, training, equipment, grants. Let the money extracted from Belizean attention finally return to build Belizean voices.

Fourth, fix the bill itself. Keep real standards for real harms, defamation, election integrity, child protection, but achieve them through simple registration and laws of general application, not discretionary licensing. Write every criterion into the statute, leave nothing to mood, make exemption the default and licensing the rare exception, and build a press-freedom firewall no future government can quietly remove.

Because understand what our online creators actually are. They are the seedlings of Belize’s digital economy, young people who built audiences and incomes from nothing, exporting Belizean culture and stories to the world. In every other column I write, we beg for exactly this, Belizeans producing, earning, building. Now that they exist, our first regulatory instinct is paperwork for them and a free pass for the billion-dollar platforms above them.

Tax the harvesters. Free the growers. That is the whole principle, and the world has already shown us it works.

The national conversation on this bill is just beginning, and it deserves vigour. Let this column open it with one sentence every lawmaker should tape above the draft.

Before Belize puts a single form in front of a Belizean with a microphone, send the bill to the giants who have been broadcasting to us, and billing us, for fifteen years, free of charge.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Department of Youth, in collaboration with UNDP, advances Girls in ICT course
World.content:
Department of Youth, in collaboration with UNDP, advances Girls in ICT course

The Department of Youth, in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), highlighted the progress of the Girls in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Course, delivered by Pixel Pro Media as part of a practical training programme designed to equip young women with skills for the digital economy.

The course is implemented through UNDP’s “Strengthening Youth Governance and Institutional Resilience for Peacebuilding in Belize” project and supports national efforts to expand inclusive access to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) opportunities. The programme targets 30 female participants aged 14 to 21 and provides hands-on learning in digital literacy, graphic design, artificial intelligence (AI), website publishing, digital research, digital safety, and presentation readiness.

Through guided instruction, practical exercises, mentorship, and access to technical resources, participants are developing market-relevant outputs, including graphic design assets and digital portfolio websites. The course places strong emphasis on responsible technology use, safe online publishing, creativity, innovation, and the confidence needed to pursue further education, entrepreneurship, and leadership opportunities in Belize’s growing digital economy.

Speaking about the programme’s impact, Mr. Gabriel Casey, Lead Instructor and Owner of Pixel Pro Media, highlighted the course’s transformative value. “This is exactly why programmes like this are so important. These young women are not only learning technical skills, but they are also gaining the confidence and independence to build, promote, and grow their own businesses in today’s digital world.”

Throughout the course, participants have demonstrated enthusiasm, creativity, and determination as they apply new digital tools to real-world ideas and personal projects. Their progress underscores the importance of investing in young women and ensuring equitable access to training, mentorship, and technology that can support their success in the digital age.

The Girls in ICT Course reaffirms the Department of Youth’s commitment, alongside UNDP, to creating inclusive opportunities that empower young people, strengthen digital capacity, and contribute to sustainable development, resilience, and peacebuilding in Belize.

World.title: Gunman kills one twin, wounds the other in Unitedville night attack
World.content:
Gunman kills one twin, wounds the other in Unitedville night attack

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Saturday night spent socializing with family ended in tragedy in Unitedville Village, where a 25-year-old man was shot and killed and his twin brother wounded in a sudden attack that has the Cayo community on edge once again.

Police report that around 8:30 p.m., the brothers, both of Belize City, were on the roadside with another man in the Spanish Town area, in front of a residence, when a lone gunman stepped out of a bushy lot nearby. Dressed fully in black with a green camouflage BDF style jacket, the attacker allegedly opened fire without warning.

The 25-year-old went down under multiple shots, and police say the gunman then reportedly stood over him and fired again before disappearing into the bushes.

A neighbor rushed both men to the Western Regional Hospital. Officers arriving there met a heartbreaking scene: the victim lying motionless in the bed of a black pickup truck, held by his wounded twin. Doctors pronounced him dead on arrival. His brother, shot once in the right buttock, was treated and is in stable condition.

Investigators recovered several 9mm shell casings from the scene, and the search for the gunman is on. It marks another murder for Unitedville, a village that has seen too much of this.

Anyone with information that can help identify the shooter is urged to contact the nearest police station or reach out confidentially. A family is grieving, and a killer is still out there.

World.title: Justice Godfrey Smith of Belize to lead Guyana ferry inquiry
World.content:
Justice Godfrey Smith of Belize to lead Guyana ferry inquiry

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The full weight of the MV Barima disaster is now coming into focus. Seventy-three bodies have been recovered from Guyana’s ferry tragedy, with 30 people still unaccounted for, as President Irfaan Ali names a five-member international Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Justice Godfrey Phillip Smith of Belize, to establish how the catastrophe happened.

The toll rose again on Friday, when a body was recovered from inside the MV Barima during diving operations. Of the 73 recovered, 69 have been positively identified and 63 released to their families. Authorities have confirmed 76 survivors, and based on the government’s estimate that 179 people were aboard, far more than initially reported, 30 remained unaccounted for after Friday’s recovery. Officials continue reconciling the names of survivors and the recovered with the vessel’s manifest.

The recovery operation itself remains immense. More than a week in, 14 vessels and three aircraft are supporting the effort, with divers battling poor underwater visibility as the ferry lies on its side, complicating the search of its interior and preparations for a possible righting operation.

Against that grim backdrop, President Ali on Sunday formally named the Commission of Inquiry into the July 18 capsizing on the Georgetown to Port Kaituma route. “The members have been carefully selected for their independence, technical expertise, and proven ability,” Ali said.

At its head sits a Belizean. “The CoI will be chaired by Justice Godfrey Phillip Smith of Belize. He currently serves as the CARICOM High-Level Representative for Law and Criminal Justice and as an Ad Hoc Justice of the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal,” the President announced. Smith, a former Attorney General of Belize, will lead a panel spanning naval architecture, marine engineering, vessel surveying, maritime law, and security: Dr. Andrzej Jasionowski of Poland, a naval architect and marine engineer; Captain Hamada Fouda, Senior Maritime Surveyor and Compliance Auditor at the Maritime Authority of Jamaica; Nyree Dawn Alfonso of Trinidad and Tobago, an attorney with expertise in Admiralty and Maritime Law; and Rear Admiral (Ret’d) Hayden Pritchard of Trinidad and Tobago, an expert in maritime operations and security.

The commission’s mandate reaches into every corner of the disaster: the vessel’s loading, passenger boarding procedures, onboard conditions, seaworthiness, maintenance history, and compliance with maritime laws and safety standards, along with the conduct and competence of the master and crew, passenger management, and lifesaving arrangements. It will also review the coordination and effectiveness of the search, rescue, and recovery operation, and will determine its own procedures and method of work.

Most consequentially, the panel is empowered to determine whether negligence, misconduct, dereliction of duty, or institutional failures contributed to the tragedy, to recommend accountability, and to propose legislative, regulatory, institutional, or operational reforms aimed at preventing another disaster.

For Belize, Justice Smith’s appointment places a national son at the centre of the Caribbean’s search for truth, and for the families of Guyana, that search now has its instrument. Seventy-three recovered, thirty still missing, and one question the region needs answered: how was this allowed to happen?

World.title: Sitting duck
World.content:
The 10 per cent General Consumption Tax that had softened the blows suffered by tourism activities is expected to move to the standard 15 per cent, effective next year April

ATTENTION will turn this Wednesday to a crucial meeting between the finance ministry and anxious tourism leaders fearing that a General Consumption Tax (GCT) increase being proposed for the sector will badly hurt its viability for the immediate future.

Nervously awaiting the outcome of the discussions also are sectors like domestic agriculture and manufacturing — broken down into produce, poultry, dairy, juices, sauces, water, electricity, packaging, furniture, uniforms, amenities, and transport and services, for which tourism is the anchor customer.

The tourism industry and its spin-off entities have been fretful in recent years over its future profitability after a series of financial shocks, mostly stemming from natural weather events, left the sector reeling.

Sector leaders interviewed by the Jamaica Observer for this story said Hurricane Melissa caused more than US$8 billion in physical damage, pointing out that rebuilding room stock, restoring attractions, and repairing the infrastructure that moves visitors around the island is not a one-season exercise. Much of that work is still under way.

Industry-wide, it was accepted that the Andrew Holness Administration was bound to ask the sector to help carry the burden of funding the expansive post-Hurricane Melissa recovery, as has always been the approach by governments after major disasters.

But when Finance Minister Fayval Williams tabled revenue measures in this year’s budget, she shook the tourism sector by announcing that the 10 per cent GCT, that had softened the blows suffered by tourism activities would move to the standard 15 per cent, effective next year April.

Williams said the one-year notice would give the tourism sector itself more time to recover from Melissa. What the finance minister’s calculations did not factor in, however, was the flow of earnings from the sector.

Notably, most rates were already negotiated and inked with overseas partners like tour operators. Jamaica’s tourist entities were, therefore, being asked to pass off a 50 per cent rate increase where other sophisticated tourism markets are fighting for the same global tourism traveller.

Passing on GCT increases would, at best, be impossible without doing further critical damage to the sector and leaving it naked and exposed to its overseas competitors, the leaders concurred.

“For the most part, hotel room sales are contracted often 18 months to two years in advance with tour operators and wholesalers in source markets,” said new Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brien Heron when queried by the Observer.

“It means that a contract signed with a tour operator or wholesaler in 2026 involves a significant share of the room nights that will be sold in the 2027 season [and beyond] at the current 2026 room rates, inclusive of GCT.

“…Those contracts cannot be reopened just because Jamaica’s tax rate changed, which means that the local hotel or attraction will have to absorb the difference between the old and new GCT rate through to the end of the current contract period,” he added.

Moreover, industry leaders insist recovery is not the only pressure that has intensified since the measure was announced. Energy costs have soared, exacerbated by war in the Middle East that has pushed up global oil prices from roughly US$60 a barrel in December 2025 to near US$100 by March 2026.

Jamaica generates much of its electricity from imported fuel, so that increase passes almost directly into the cost of running a hotel.

“It lands on an industry that was already paying among the highest electricity rates in the hemisphere,” added the JHTA head. “Business electricity in Jamaica runs well above the global average — a structural disadvantage that has nothing to do with how well any individual property is managed.

“For a resort, electricity is not overhead at the margin. Air conditioning, refrigeration, laundry and water production run 24 hours a day, every day, whether the room is occupied or not,” he explained.

Heron roundly disagreed with government number crunchers’ description that it was “a five-percentage-point increase”, reiterating that it was a 50 per cent GCT increase — from 10 to 15 per cent.

“What is at stake here is the economic fabric of tourism, and tourism is the engine that drives Jamaica’s economy,” he said. “When you compress this sector you do not compress one industry. You compress the farmer who supplies it, the manufacturer who packages for it, the transport operator who moves its guests, and the worker whose household depends on it.”

Speaking for the small hotels, JHTA past President Evelyn Smith stressed the struggles facing the sector after being hit by significant disasters like the COVID-19 pandemic, hurricanes Beryl and Melissa; a northerly that threw up angry waves that badly damaged some Negril beachfront properties; and the recent water problem that “forced us to pay huge sums of money to have water trucked to the properties”.

“During these disastrous events, some properties had to shut down altogether; others remained open but retained staff at tremendous sacrifice,” said Smith.

“Negril is well known as having the largest collection of small hotels. We have kept the life of Negril going during these many shocks, especially after Melissa, the worst hurricane to hit Jamaica. We kept our doors open even as cash depleted.”

Smith said she strongly disagreed with the Government that the industry has matured.

“Tourism is an export industry, so our competition is overseas, and we can’t just pass on any increase. Our rates are already set. Our revenues are already very thin, and now we are being asked to absorb further increases. Something is going to have to give.

“This significant increase will hit what we have to do in order to simply remain alive,” she reasoned.

The JHTA’s present leadership is also worried about the dim prospects facing the allied sectors, such as ground transportation and attractions, said Nadine Spence, the 4th vice-president.

“While we fully appreciate the Government’s responsibility to generate revenue to fund national development, timing is critical. The transportation, attractions, and allied sectors are still recovering from Hurricane Melissa and a challenging tourism environment,” Spence pointed out.

“A 50 per cent increase in the GCT applied to hotel accommodation risks weakening Jamaica’s competitiveness at a time when every visitor matters. We depend directly on hotel occupancy, and any decline in arrivals or visitor spending flows immediately through our sector, affecting jobs, investment, and small businesses across the island,” she argued.

“If higher taxes reduce arrivals or visitor spending, transportation and attractions businesses immediately feel the impact. A tax on hotels inevitably becomes a tax on the wider tourism value chain.

“Furthermore, this tax proposal comes at the worst possible time,” she suggested. “An industry facing this level of compounding strain requires temporary relief, incentives, and structural support to rebuild, not an aggressive tax hike.

“Taxing local businesses into submission during a recovery period will only push more players out of the formal market and exacerbate the very revenue shortfall the Government is trying to solve.

“If Jamaica wants a sustainable, high-yielding tourism sector… we need policies that nurture Jamaican-owned ground transport and attraction businesses, enabling them to build domestic wealth that stays right here in the economy.

“An increase in GCT at this critical time is not good for a sector on the rebound, especially when arrivals are down 30 to 40 per cent… Lower pricing will increase volumes which will increase traffic and that means additional revenue,” said Spence.

Martin Zsifkovicks, co-chair of the association’s linkages and agriculture committees, cautioned about the indirect harm threatening agriculture.

“The GCT increase will not automatically damage agriculture fruits, vegetables, as most agricultural inputs remain GCT-free, which is fundamentally important. However, the mechanism runs through hotel profitability rather than the tax code directly,” he suggested.

“When hotels come under margin pressure, procurement is historically one of the first places operators look to cut, precisely because it’s a variable cost that can be scaled up or down quickly, unlike staffing contracts, utilities, or debt service. We have already seen how directly that plays out for farmers: During COVID, when hotel demand collapsed, Government had to step in with a buy-back scheme because produce already planted for the hotel trade had nowhere to go.”

Zsifkovicks agreed that the timing of the increase was bad, saying that close to 5,000 rooms remain off stream since Hurricane Melissa hit in October 2025, and hurricane recovery of this scale typically takes years, not months.

“That means the industry is already absorbing pressure on revenue and cash flow before the GCT increase even takes effect. Layering a tax increase on top of a sector that hasn’t yet returned to full inventory only adds to that strain, and procurement is likely to be one of the first places it shows up.

“A GCT-driven margin squeeze is a different kind of shock than a pandemic shutdown, but the transmission line is the same — pressure on hotel revenue shows up quickly in what and how much hotels are willing to commit to buying from local farmers. That’s the risk worth watching, even though the produce itself isn’t being taxed,” he said.

President Heron also warned that absorbing a tax increase does not simply reduce profit but reduces the cash available for everything that sits below the operating line, like debt service, refurbishment, and reinvestment.

“Most properties in this market are carrying storm-related capital expenditure and, in many cases, related borrowing. Compress operating earnings and the first casualties are not investor dividends. They are the deferred room refresh, the delayed energy-efficiency retrofit, the postponed hire.

“An industry that defers reinvestment does not announce a crisis. It simply becomes gradually less competitive, and the consequences arrive later, when they are far more expensive to reverse,” charged Heron.

He said that when hotel margins compress, procurement is one of the first places operators look to trim costs. And the path of least resistance begins with buying harder. That means suppliers will feel the squeeze through both rate and volume pressures. Not out of any lack of national commitment, but because a buyer under margin pressure buys on price.

“This is where the policy tension becomes difficult to ignore. The Government’s own Tourism 3.0 and Local First agenda commit to prioritising Jamaican farmers, artisans, manufacturers, and micro-entrepreneurs as first suppliers to hotels and attractions. That is a genuinely good policy, and the industry supports it.

“… There is also a principle worth stating plainly. Under Jamaica’s own GCT Act, exports are zero-rated. Tourism is an export industry — it earns foreign exchange and it is consumed primarily by non-residents. By that logic, the tax code, fairly applied across all exporters, tourism services should also be zero-rated.

“Successive government administrations have repeatedly accepted this fact and, while some adjustments have been made to the GCT rate differential, the principle supporting tourism having a lower rate than the national rate is well documented and, up ’til now, was assumed a settled matter,” he added.

Heron said that what the industry is asking for is to be in a position to show the Government the disastrous implications expected to tourism businesses by the proposed change.

Heron confirmed that the JHTA would be meeting with the finance minister this week and that work is under way to put independent evidence in front of Government.

“Tourism’s bottom lines to watch is not only about the hotel’s. It is also the farmer’s, the manufacturer’s, the worker’s, and the country’s. That is precisely why the timing, and the terms of this increase are worth getting right — together,” he said.

World.title: The spy, the specialist and the thief
World.content:
For the second time in a week, police cordoned off Horseshoe Curve on Caledonia Road in Mandeville on Saturday.

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Police here say they are determined to dismantle a network of criminals, particularly those involved in the robbery of bars, during which poker boxes are mainly targeted.

This follows Saturday’s triple fatal shooting by cops on Caledonia Road in Mandeville, involving three suspects with connections to criminals in neighbouring parishes who police said targeted bars across Manchester.

“The group that was involved in the shoot-out, we have been tracking them for some time and, based on intelligence, we even recovered stolen items, including poker box parts at three premises two Fridays ago, tied to these three people,” a police source said.

Police named those fatally shot as Lester Morris, Travis Baker and Sutania Boothe, otherwise called Chun Chun. Two firearms were reportedly seized during Saturday’s alleged shoot-out.

Police said about 4:00 pm they were alerted to a robbery spree and subsequently intercepted a vehicle near Horseshoe Curve.

A highly placed police source said the occupants of the intercepted vehicle opened fire on cops, who returned gunfire. A shoot-out ensued resulting in a prolonged stand-off.

Boothe, Morris and Baker, according to the police, were taken from the intercepted vehicle and rushed to hospital where they were pronounced dead on arrival.

The incident happened in proximity of last Saturday’s double murder in which nursing student Deenekia Pounall and Sadefa Henry were gunned down in a taxi by a gunman posing as a passenger.

Baker and Morris were well known to the police, having both been previously arrested and charged for several offences, including praedial larceny and robbery.

Police described Baker as a third-generation thief in February 2024, when he was arrested a week before his father, Neville, was detained. At that time, the younger Baker was among three men arrested and charged with praedial larceny offences following a high-speed chase in Newport, Manchester. A ram goat was recovered from the trunk of a Toyota Axio in which Baker was travelling.

The elder Baker was subsequently arrested when police caught him and two other men with more than 600 pounds of stolen carrots and Irish potatoes in Kingsland near Mandeville.

A year later, on March 2, 2025, Neville Baker was gunned down in his car at the entrance to the community of Hatfield in Manchester. He had also previously served prison time for firearm offences.

In relation to Morris, police described him as “a poker box specialist” in robbing and dismantling the popular gaming equipment.

In 2022, police in neighbouring St Elizabeth said upscale gaming boxes, including those with touch screen technology, were worth as much as $500,000 each and were in demand, while older versions can be sold for up to $300,000.

Police accused Boothe, the woman killed in the triple fatal shooting, of being integral in robbery sprees.

“She would be the lookout and the spy for the group. She would go into bars and scope out the place and then call in her cronies,” a senior police source alleged.

“These criminals are not just based in Manchester, it is a network of them spanning multiple parishes. We have reason to believe [that] this team may be connected to the multimillion-dollar robbery heist in Red Bank near Junction, St Elizabeth, last month, in which two of their cronies perished in a fiery crash while trying to elude the highway patrol team,” added the police source.

Police theorise that a Toyota Noah motor vehicle, which burst into flames killing its two occupants when it crashed on the Williamsfield highway in the wee hours, was used as the getaway vehicle by thieves who had targeted the St Elizabeth establishment on June 27.

Police said they will continue to pursue criminal suspects linked to a series of robberies.

“There are others of them out there and we will not relent until the criminal network is dismantled,” said a senior police source.

World.title: Families abandon relatives in hospital while occupying their homes
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton addressing a media briefing at Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover on Friday. Photo: Anthony Lewis

WITH hundreds of medically discharged patients continuing to occupy public hospital beds across Jamaica, Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says the Government is looking at the law to determine how relatives who abandon loved ones in hospital can be held accountable.

He also revealed that some relatives continue to live in homes owned by the very people they have neglected.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer after last Thursday’s Health Hurricane Response Programme (HHRP) working breakfast, Tufton said social cases currently account for between five and 10 per cent of the country’s roughly 4,000 public hospital beds.

He said the problem has become particularly acute in western Jamaica, where he believes the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa may have worsened an already strained situation.

He warned that the growing number of patients who no longer require medical treatment but remain in hospital is reducing bed availability for people awaiting admission.

“We’re doing another census, because it’s a moving target, and I’ve asked for that information to be granted, but we are really under pressure when it comes to social cases. Like I said at Savanna-la-Mar Hospital [last] week, I checked, there were 26. Now, when you have a hospital with 150, 160 beds and you have 26 [social cases], and you have 30, 40 people waiting for a bed, you understand that problem would have been much less,” Tufton said.

However, the minister said the challenge extends well beyond Savanna-la-Mar Public General Hospital.

“The truth is that the infirmaries seem to be crowded… [and] what is happening is that there’s a gradual creep that is taking place, where health now is becoming a provider of social [services] for the infirm. We’re already doing it unofficially, but practically, yes, in the hospitals; because I think we have, in western region alone — and this could be wrong — in western region alone, maybe because of Melissa, I think we have in excess of 100 social cases.

“And when you contact the families, they say they’re not willing to take the person because they can’t manage them and all of that, while some of them don’t even respond,” he said.

Social cases are individuals who have been medically cleared for discharge but remain in hospital because they have nowhere suitable to go or because family members are unwilling or unable to care for them. Health officials have long argued that these cases place additional strain on an already stretched public health system by occupying beds needed for acutely ill patients.

During a media briefing following a tour of Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover last Friday, Tufton provided a breakdown of social cases currently occupying beds across the island’s four regional health authorities:

* Southern Regional Health Authority currently has 44 cases: 12 at Mandeville Regional Hospital, seven at Percy Junor, Black River has one, Lionel Town has four, and May Pen Hospital has 20;

* South East Regional Health Authority has 89 beds taken up with social cases: Bustamante Hospital for Children and Linstead Hospital have eight each, Spanish Town has 37, Sir John Golding has two, Kingston Public Hospital has 22, and Princess Margaret has 12;

* ​North East Regional Authority, which is the smallest region, currently has 29 social cases: Port Maria Hospital has four cases, Port Antonio has six, St Ann’s Bay Regional has nine, and 10 are at Annotto Bay Hospital.

* Western Regional Health Authority has 98 cases on record. The 360-bed Cornwall Regional Hospital currently has 62 cases while Savanna-la-Mar has 27, and Falmouth and Noel Holmes hospitals have four cases each.

Last Thursday, Tufton told the Observer that the ministry is pursuing several approaches to reduce the numbers, including engaging social workers to reunite patients with relatives, training unpaid caregivers to care for incapacitated family members at home, and expanding community support.

However, he indicated that legal intervention is also under consideration following advice from the Attorney General’s Chambers.

“The third is to look at the laws, which I have spoken about, but our laws don’t currently give us that authority and we are told by the AG to literally take people to court when they have abandoned their loved ones, and there’s clear evidence that they can take care of them because, in some cases, some of these social cases own homes and homes are occupied by relatives,” he said.

Pressed on that assertion, Tufton maintained that some relatives continue living in properties owned by patients who remain in hospital.

“When they die, people come to claim the death certificate in order to get the benefit, so that’s not all the cases but there are some of those cases. So what is happening is that we are really plagued by that, and it puts added pressure on the system and prevents the people who really need a bed from benefiting from a bed,” he said.

According to the health minister, the impact is felt most sharply in hospital emergency departments, where patients often wait hours or days for admission because in-patient beds remain occupied by people who no longer require acute medical care.

Meanwhile, at the media briefing last Friday, Tufton pointed out that the primary role of the Government is to finance public health-care facilities, cover staff salaries, and supply medication, but the social cases crisis has forced his portfolio ministry to step outside its original mandate.

In response, the ministry has partnered with the Ministry of Local Government, providing more than $100 million to fund the build-out of additional space at the St James Infirmary.

“Health [Ministry] has had to commit, not just to building, but also to committing to staff and meals, I believe, for two-plus years. And normally the parish councils are just not able, or that’s the word, to take the additional social cases. So, you know, we really have a problem,” stated Tufton.

When asked by Deputy Mayor of Lucea Andria Dehaney Grant whether Hanover could get similar help, Tufton said, while this is not the norm, the ministry is willing to provide help.

“We have done it because we really have a crisis and we have to try and correct the crisis. That’s not to say we mustn’t work together, and that’s what we’re doing. Where there is a need, and we can help, then we are more than willing to help. If the mayor has an issue and we think we can provide some support, we’re willing to look at it and we’d be happy to discuss it,” assured the minister.

World.title: Blvk H3ro, Yungg Trip embrace Phemomenal
World.content:
Blvk H3ro and Yungg Trip shoots some visuals.

Following a run of standout releases, Jamaican artiste Blvk H3ro returns with Phenomenal, a high-energy anthem produced by Yungg Trip that radiates confidence, resilience, and pure feel-good energy.

Built around an irresistible hook and infectious groove, Phenomenal blends modern reggae with dancehall swagger, delivering a bold celebration of self-belief and unstoppable momentum.

Blvk H3ro’s sharp lyricism keeps it authentic, while the song’s driving rhythm makes it one that seems set to move crowds.

Produced by Yungg Trip, the track pairs powerful messaging with massive festival-ready energy, making it one of Blvk H3ro’s most explosive releases yet.

As his global profile continues to rise, Phenomenal proves once again that Blvk H3ro knows how to balance substance with undeniable vibes; creating music that hits just as hard on the stage as it does in your headphones.

Blvk H3ro is at the forefront of Jamaica’s new wave of reggae, blending roots foundation with dancehall and global influences into a sound that feels both authentic and forward-thinking.

Hailing from Portmore, he’s built a growing international presence, performing across North America, Europe, and Africa while delivering music rooted in discipline, growth, and real-life experience.

A Grammy-nominated artiste and recipient of the Dennis Brown Award for Most Promising Entertainer at the International Reggae and World Music Awards (IRAWMA), among his releases are On A Mission and Winnah.

World.title: Golding denies leaked audio reflects PNP policy
World.content:
A screen grab of People’s National Party President Mark Golding taken from the video released by the Opposition party after its National Executive Council meeting at the University of the West Indies, Mona, in St Andrew, on Sunday.

People’s National Party (PNP) President Mark Golding on Sunday sought to distance the Opposition party from controversial leaked voice notes discussing strategies against the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA), insisting the recordings reflected the personal views of individuals and not official party policy.

However, the party’s explanation came only in a recorded video statement after a highly anticipated opportunity for the PNP to answer questions from the media vanished when it cancelled its planned post-National Executive Council (NEC) press briefing on Sunday.

Speaking in the video released following the NEC meeting, Golding said the party had withheld comment until it had completed its own review of the matter.

“Our review is now complete and it established three things,” Golding said.

“Firstly, the conversation in which those leaked recordings took place did not happen in any official party forum. Secondly, no party officer, no officer of the party participated in that discussion, and thirdly, the PNP has no official NEC or executive WhatsApp group. That doesn’t exist, and certainly not where party policy is made,” he said.

He further maintained that the conversations were not representative of the Opposition’s official position.

“This was a WhatsApp group formed by individuals within the party, and the views expressed were their personal views. So those recordings do not represent the official position of the PNP or any policy of the PNP,” Golding said.

“The PNP takes responsibility for its official positions. Those are set by our constitutional organs, such as this National Executive Council or the Executive Committee of the party, and those that are communicated by our authorised representatives and shown through our public actions or through our public media outlets, social media outlets, and so on,” he added.

The video statement came after journalists arrived at The University of the West Indies (UWI), Mona, for what had been billed as a post-NEC media briefing featuring Golding, party Chairman Dr Angela Brown Burke, General Secretary Dr Dayton Campbell, and other senior leaders. The briefing had been scheduled for 3:30 pm following the executive council meeting.

Instead, members of the media were informed of a two-hour delay and were advised that the planned press briefing had been cancelled, with the party indicating that a video statement would be issued instead.

The cancellation meant the Opposition missed what many had viewed as its first major opportunity to directly answer questions about the leaked recordings that have dominated the political landscape for much of the past week.

The recordings, which have circulated widely on social media and whose authenticity has not been independently verified, allegedly capture two members of the PNP discussing political strategies surrounding NaRRA, the agency established by the Government to coordinate Jamaica’s recovery and reconstruction following Hurricane Melissa.

One of the recordings appears to suggest that the authority should be viewed through a political lens because of the electoral benefit it could bring to the governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), while another discusses ways to undermine public confidence in NaRRA Chief Executive Officer Major General (Ret’d) Antony Anderson despite acknowledging his credibility.

The recordings have prompted sharp criticism from the governing JLP, which accused the Opposition of placing partisan interests above the country’s recovery efforts. Jamaicans For Justice was the only civil society group to have weighed in, urging the PNP to distance itself from any suggestion that politics should interfere with national reconstruction.

Against that backdrop, Sunday’s NEC meeting had been expected to provide clarity on the party’s position and whether it intended to investigate the circumstances surrounding the leaked conversations.

Ahead of the meeting, the PNP had advised that the post-NEC briefing would provide “updates from the NEC and address recent reports circulating in the public domain”, adding that members of the media would have an opportunity to pose questions to the party’s leadership on those matters and other issues.

World.title: INTO THE SPOTLIGHT!
World.content:
Jamaica’s Romaine Beckford (Photo: AFP)Photo: AFP

Jamaica’s medal chase in track and field at the Commonwealth Games will start at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, with the finals of two events — the 110m hurdles and men’s high jump — scheduled to be contested.

National champions Demario Prince, in the hurdles, and Romaine Beckford, in the men’s high jump, are expected to lead the medal chase.

Technical leader Maurice Wilson said all was well in the camp except the withdrawal of men’s sprinter Nishion Ebanks, a loss which could have repercussions for the relays.

“We are settled in and expectations are high despite the cold weather,” Wilson said. “However, we had a late pull out, Nishion Ebanks, which affects the 4x100m relay pool.”

Ebanks was set to contest the individual men’s 100m, along with Ackeem Blake and Rohan Watson. He was expected to form part of the sprint relay team.

Watson will be the only Jamaican competing in the first round of both the men’s and women’s 100m, with the rules allowing the top eight to advance to the next round. Blake and women runners Jonielle Smith and Jodean Williams will sit out the first rounds as a result.

Prince is the leader in the Commonwealth Games 11om hurdles rankings with his personal best 13.01 seconds set at the Prefontaine Classic two weeks ago, while Jerome Campbell is ranked ninth. Both will hope to qualify for the final.

Beckford, who was eighth at the Commonwealth Games four years ago, is ranked third in the men’s high jump. He is to face off against top-ranked Kimani Jack of England and Sarvesh Anil Kushare of India, both of whom have cleared 2.31m this season.

Two-time World Athletics Indoor Championships bronze medallist Raymond Richards of Jamaica and defending champion Hamish Kerr of New Zealand are also down to compete.

Also on Monday, Adelle Tracey, who switched allegiance from England to represent Jamaica four years ago but was not allowed to compete at the 2022 Commonwealth Games because required documentation had not been completed, will make her debut in the women’s 800m. She is to be joined national champion Kelly-Ann Beckford in the first round.

The women’s 800m will be one of the most anticipated events, at least on the opening day of track and field, since a number of top athletes, including England’s Georgia Hunter-Bell, Scotland’s Jemma Reeki and Shafiqua Maloney of St Vincent and the Grenadines, are expected to be in the medal hunt.

Former world champion and Olympic Games medallist Tajay Gayle will hope to improve on his fourth place at the 2018 Commonwealth Games when he takes part in the first round of the long jump. Jordan Turner is also down to compete.

They will go up against top-ranked Sreeshankar of India, Liam Adcock of Australia, Kelsey Daniel of Trinidad and Tobago and Stephen McKenzie of Scotland.

Six-time national champion Nayoka Clunis, a medal contender in the women’s hammer throw, is expected to advance from the first round.

Clunis, who extended her national record to 72.03m this year, is ranked fifth. She is to face top-ranked Canadian Camryn Rogers, New Zealand’s Lauren Bruce and England’s Charlotte Payne.

World.title: Failing the boys
World.content:
Chairman, Education Transformation Oversight Committee (ETOC), Dr Adrian Stokes, gives an update last Thursday, during the ETOC Press Conference for year four, quarter one, at The University of the West Indies Regional Headquarters in St Andrew. Photo: JIS News

DESPITE steady improvements in overall Primary Exit Profile (PEP) performance, Jamaica remains without a clear solution to the long-standing underachievement of boys in schools, prompting Education Transformation Oversight Committee (ETOC) Chairman Dr Adrian Stokes to warn that “a lot more” must be done to close a gender gap that continues to favour girls.

Stokes issued the warning at ETOC’s quarterly press conference at The University of the West Indies’ Regional Headquarters last week.

He argued that one of the country’s most persistent education challenges remains unresolved — boys continue to trail girls in key areas despite years of research into the problem.

This year’s mathematics results underscored the disparity. While 64.9 per cent of girls achieved the “proficient” level, compared with 57.2 per cent of boys, girls also edged boys at the highest achievement level, with 8.3 per cent classified as “highly proficient” compared with 7.7 per cent of boys. Boys, meanwhile, accounted for a larger share of students in the lower achievement categories.

Stokes said the gap could no longer be viewed as simply another statistic.

“The girls continue to outperform the boys in statistically significant ways. It’s not even close. The [Orlando] Patterson report highlights this issue, and indeed, all the entities that have taken a deep dive looking into the Jamaican education system — like the UNICEF report, the 2022 report — point out that Jamaica is one of the few places globally where girls outperform boys in mathematics, for example,” he said.

He noted that the Orlando Patterson-led education review had carefully examined the issue and identified several social and psychological factors affecting boys, but said Jamaica has yet to develop targeted interventions capable of reversing the trend.

“The Patterson report argued that the root cause was not favouritism. It’s not like girls are being given some advantage, knowingly. Rather, what the report highlights is that our boys, through social circumstances, or their abusive upbringing, cultural norms, but generally, let’s say, psychosocial issues that are putting our boys at a disadvantage… So the bottom line is, we have more work to do to find solutions that can close the gender performance gap,” he added.

Although the Ministry of Education recently announced plans to establish a committee to examine how boys are educated, Stokes suggested that would not, on its own, be enough.

“We need to do a lot more than that… Let’s say that’s a first step, hopefully, to something meaningful… We need real initiatives. We need to pilot different ideas. As I said, I am not certain that anyone has a full slate of answers… The question is, how do we respond? Or, how do we modify or evolve the education system to accommodate these psychosocial issues that are playing out in society? So, hopefully, it’s a step in the right direction, but I’m not expecting, just from that committee, to see significant change, a lot more needs to happen,” Stokes noted.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information Dr Kasan Troupe agreed that the education system must now adopt more targeted approaches for boys, arguing that biological and social differences influence how they learn.

She said the ministry has already begun examining changes to teaching methods, classroom environments and teacher training.

“So, particularly, we have been talking about how we socialise our boys. Boys learn differently, boys like competition, and so that means our teachers have to be retooled. They have to be trained — we need the bingos, we need the dominoes, we need movements. There’s a whole raft of measures that we have to look at as it relates to how we are going to support our boys,” she said.

State minister Rhoda Moy Crawford struck a more optimistic tone, expressing confidence that the proposed committee would produce tangible results, pointing to the work already undertaken by ETOC since its establishment.

She also argued that the latest PEP results showed there was reason for hope.

“I know this committee that will be put in place to examine what we can do differently to benefit our boys, I know it will be a solid committee…and I’m also motivated by the fact that when we look at our recent PEP results, our top 10 students, out of those 10 students, seven were boys. So all is not lost,” she said.

World.title: Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton: Helping to shape Jamaica’s digital future
World.content:
Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton.

“I’VE always believed that technology should never be an end in itself. Its true purpose is to improve lives, create opportunities and remove barriers.” For more than three decades, that philosophy has shaped every stage of Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton’s career.

From leading complex banking technology transformations to shaping regional telecommunications policy, her career has been defined by one consistent goal: Using technology to improve people’s lives. Today, as managing director of Spectrum Management Authority (SMA), she is helping to position Jamaica at the forefront of spectrum management and digital innovation. Her leadership has also earned regional and international recognition through roles with the Caribbean Telecommunications Union (CTU) and the Inter-American Telecommunication Commission, where she contributes to shaping the future of global radiocommunications policy.

Yet titles have never been what motivated her.

“When I started my career, I wasn’t chasing titles or recognition,” Myers-Hamilton reflects. “I was fascinated by solving problems. Every role presented a new challenge and another opportunity to learn. Looking back, I realise those experiences were preparing me for leadership — not simply because of the technical knowledge I gained, but because they taught me resilience, adaptability, and the importance of making decisions that affect people’s lives.”

Long before entering telecommunications regulation, Dr Myers-Hamilton built her career in Jamaica’s financial sector, where technology had to be dependable, secure and resilient.
