The second would return Queensland to the situation before the ban, where treatment was provided through the Queensland Children's Gender Service. The review said this option may be beneficial for young people but also carried risks, including a limited evidence base for the medication.

The third would allow the treatment to be delivered within a public statewide system of care, with additional safety measures to help ensure and monitor quality of care and mitigate risks. The review said that option would "support more robust research and reporting to inform the evidence base".

The Queensland government stopped short of fully implementing the first option, instead choosing to continue the pause until 2031, while awaiting the results of the upcoming UK clinical trial.

That decision went "beyond" the review, according to professor of endocrinology at the University of Melbourne, Ada Cheung, who supports the use of puberty blockers where appropriate.

"The Vine Review did not advocate for restricting care," she said.

" The Vine Review put forward three options and the government chose the option that provided no benefit but significant risk, which is concerning. "

Ethical dilemmas

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRHa), or puberty blockers, pause aspects of physical development by suppressing sex hormones. (ABC News: Nico White)

A complicated combination of ethical and practical limitations around the way research is conducted means puberty blockers are caught in a conflict of methodology.

The gold standard of scientific studies is known as the randomised controlled trial, which compares two groups randomly selected. One is given the treatment and the other is given something else, like a placebo, or even the same treatment at a different time.

In the case of puberty blockers, that approach raises ethical concerns, because it can mean delaying or withholding treatment for children.

When neither the participants nor the researchers know who is in which group, that is called a double-blind trial — a method used to prevent bias.

However, because the drugs stop physical changes like menstruation or voice deepening, patients and doctors can guess if they are in the group receiving treatment, so double-blind trials are not possible with puberty blockers.

That has left a reliance on so-called observational studies, where scientists observe and track individuals without manipulating the environment.

These studies are not considered to be as high quality as randomised controlled trials because without comparison, researchers cannot be sure what impact the treatment itself has had.

Endocrinologist Professor Ada Cheung says the limited evidence around puberty blockers doesn't mean there's evidence of harm. (ABC News: Nico White)

In addition, because only a small proportion of the population is trans or gender dysphoric, the available studies have small sample sizes.

The available evidence is interpreted differently by each side of the debate.

Professor Cheung argues that a burden of proof has been put on puberty blockers that has not been placed on other forms of healthcare.

"This level of evidence is very common for other areas of paediatrics and for surgery and so it's the norm, not the exception … and it's not dissimilar to other areas of health like, for example, ADHD," she said.

" There are many areas of medicine where we may not have the highest quality of evidence, but it doesn't mean an absence of evidence, and it doesn't mean evidence of harm. "

However Gold Coast paediatrician Dylan Wilson says he does not believe the benefits outweigh the risks.

"The fact that this has been subjected to systematic reviews shows that the evidence at the moment is poor," he said.

"That doesn't mean that because other treatments don't have that same standard that we should continue with this treatment."

'Pulled the rug out from under them'

Dr Fiona Bisshop treats children with gender dysphoria. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Queensland's effective ban has led many children with gender dysphoria to Brisbane GP Fiona Bisshop.

Dr Bisshop, a past president of the Australian Professional Association for Trans Health, now administers puberty blockers to patients paying about $3,000 a year to purchase the medication privately.

She says the impact of the ban was profound and immediate.

"Our phone lines were ringing off the hook with worried parents," she said.

"There were many young people who were about to start puberty blockers through the clinic, and it pulled the rug out from under them.

"For many of them, they don't know where else to go. So there are definitely going to be people out there who are missing out."

Dr Bisshop says puberty blockers have been used since the 1980s to treat young children who go through puberty early, which is also known as precocious puberty.

"It is a double standard to say that you can use this treatment for one condition of childhood but not for another … transphobic discrimination is what it is," she said.

Dr Fiona Bisshop says the Queensland government's effective ban on puberty blockers is "transphobic". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Dr Bisshop says puberty blockers have benefits that outweigh the risks for many young people, and minimise the need for future medical intervention for those who decide to continue with their gender-affirming care.

"My adult trans patients who never had puberty blockers, they are now undergoing surgeries," she said.

"Some of them are undergoing top surgery to remove breast tissue. Some of them are undergoing surgery to get rid of their Adam's apple to try and change their voice and make it lighter and higher.

"These things — the voice, the hair — are key identifying features out in society. So if you walk down the street and you've got a deep voice and facial hair, people are immediately going to gender you as male, it doesn't matter what you're wearing and how you present yourself.

"These are the sorts of things that we can prevent. And the ultimate saving in mental health and in costs to our patients is enormous."

Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls defended his government's decision.

"We owe it to children to ensure health care is based on robust evidence and delivered with caution to ensure their safety and wellbeing," he said in a statement to 7.30.

How many children on puberty blockers?

The Queensland government has restricted public access to puberty blockers for children with gender dysphoria. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Clinicians prescribing puberty blockers argue only a small portion of patients referred to gender clinics go on to puberty blockers.

However, finding out exactly how many children are on puberty blockers for gender dysphoria is difficult, and has meant people are debating an issue without relevant data.

7.30 contacted every state and territory for the figures, however most declined to provide the information citing privacy concerns, even though the data could be provided without naming individual children.

Perth Children's Hospital's Gender Diversity Service is treating 58 children on puberty blockers, while Queensland's Children's Gender Service — which is not taking new patients — is treating 77 patients with puberty blockers.

Dr Wilson says the lack of transparency around how many children are on puberty blockers nationwide is problematic.

"It's very frustrating," he said.

"Having clear transparency of these numbers would allow us to look at what's happening in those trends."

Paediatrician Dr Dylan Wilson says puberty blockers should not be prescribed to children with gender distress. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The Australian Medical Association (AMA) supports the use of puberty blockers for children with gender dysphoria.

Dr Wilson is among those who believe they should not be used.

"I think children should be allowed to grow and develop, become who they really are, allow themselves and their identity to mature, allow their bodies to grow and mature, be helped and supported and loved through that difficult period of time with the appropriate mental health support that they need, without making any permanent irreversible decisions about their bodies," Dr Wilson said.

While the available studies indicate puberty blockers are reversible, Dr Wilson points to international research and anecdotal evidence in Australia which suggests the majority of children who start on puberty blockers choose to go on to hormones like oestrogen or testosterone.

"It's only reversible if they are actively reversed. So children have to come off them and allow that time for the body to resume normal puberty in order for that to happen," he said.

As the name suggests, for puberty blockers to be as effective as possible they need to be taken before the onset of puberty — for some children that happens as early as age 10.

Psychiatrist Professor Philip Morris has concerns about the ability of children to consent to puberty blockers and potential side effects. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Psychiatrist Philip Morris questions whether a child so young could appropriately consent to treatment.

"It's just impossible for a child at that age to be able to make decisions about their future that will be affected substantially by the medications," Professor Morris said.

"If you stop them, puberty might return to some degree or it might come back, but the child has gone through maybe one, two or three years where they haven't had the other hormones that are being produced by the ovaries or by the testes."

Professor Morris is president of the National Association of Practising Psychiatrists (NAPP), a group which has written a guide for clinicians advocating for puberty blockers to be "second-line" treatments, with psychotherapy to be used as a "first-line" intervention.

"We look at a much more down the middle of the road approach so that doctors can be comfortable with what they're doing and they can fulfil their obligations, both in terms of their ethics and their professional obligations when they're looking after young people," Professor Morris said.

Laying groundwork for national standard

National guidelines on puberty blockers are due in 2028. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

As it considers the patchwork of policies and processes both internationally and at a state level, the federal government has asked the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) to develop new national treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse youth in Australia, including around the provision of puberty blockers.

The final guidelines are due in 2028, with an interim report due in a matter of weeks.

Those guidelines will likely not have the power to override state decisions and some advocates told 7.30 they are concerned that as a result, they will not lead to certainty or consistency.

Dr Bisshop says while the guidelines were unlikely to change the trajectory in Queensland, she is hopeful they would support the use of puberty blockers.

"What I'm really hoping for is some scientific integrity and that they will use proper science to look at the evidence we have and understand what grade of evidence is acceptable in this field," she said.

Dr Wilson says the federal government should consider permanently banning the medication.

"When you look at the evidence as a cold hard fact, there's not much to back up the use of the treatment," he said.

"What I would hope is they produce a moderate guideline that suggests that we should be cautious about what we're doing."

In a statement, a federal government spokesperson told 7.30 the "issues should be nationally consistent" and will be driven by the NHMRC.

"The [health] minister is confident state and territory governments will give proper consideration to that advice."

Political involvement 'disrespectful'

The lack of access to puberty blockers impacted Ashton's mental health. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Ashton came out as trans at 14, but said his parents did not let him use puberty blockers because they wanted to avoid medical intervention.

The 20-year-old is one of many in the transgender community frustrated at the politicisation of the debate.

"I honestly think it's quite disrespectful to have politicians trying to involve themselves in discussions about puberty blockers when they have no experience in the field," he told 7.30.

" I think it should be left up to doctors and the actual patient and the family, not just politicians to decide medical care. "

Ashton says not taking puberty blockers left him contending with the unwanted consequences of puberty.

Ashton says he faces expensive medical bills for surgery that could have been avoided if he'd accessed puberty blockers. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"If I'd been able to access puberty blockers I wouldn't have to get top surgery in the future, which would cost me about $10-20,000 out of pocket," he said.

"So it's going to take a very long time to save up for and it also would have helped my mental health a lot.

"I ended up at 14 attempting suicide, which resulted in an ICU admission.

"After that I just went through cycles of hospital admissions — I'd get out for a few weeks and then I'd be back in hospital and that happened until I was 18, which then it got a bit better because I started testosterone."

Conversely for Kassie, two years of puberty blockers have given her time and space to work out her next steps.

Kassie is worried for children who are unable to access puberty blockers. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

But the politicisation of the deeply personal is difficult to understand.

"I love the people of this country and to think that some of them refuse to give little kids life-saving care that they need to effectively function and feel comfortable or just time to stop and breathe for a second," she said.

"It's really sad and I feel these poor kids have to go through so much more added trauma that isn't necessary."

Last year Kassie had her final shot of puberty blockers, and her first shot of oestrogen — the next stage in the process of transitioning.

"If I hadn't had this medication, my life would be so much darker and bleaker," she said.

" I'm probably going to have to go through so [many] more struggles … but I'm happy to live. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Can't stop spending? These approaches can help curb impulse buying
World.content:
We're living through a cost-of-living crisis, but that doesn't mean we're always good at curbing our spending.

This can be especially tricky with impulse shopping, or for things we don't really need.

"Shopping can become a way of regulating uncomfortable emotions or creating a brief sense of control, comfort or reward," says Lea Clothier, a behavioural money coach and former financial adviser.

She says financial stress can also create a scarcity mindset, where our brains become more focused on immediate relief rather than long-term outcomes.

"That's one reason people sometimes continue spending even when they know it isn't helping their financial situation," Ms Clothier says.

If you'd rather be saving than shopping, but are struggling to switch gears, there are ways to change your habits.

Why it's hard to stop shopping

Jonathan David, from the Department of Psychology at York University in Canada, focuses his research on addiction, compulsive buying and hoarding.

Dr David, who completed his PhD in psychology at Macquarie University, says for people who struggle to control their shopping, financial pressure doesn't necessarily stop them from spending more.

"Financial pressure can often come along with job stress, or family stresses, so going on your phone to shop can be an escape.

"But making a purchase or adding the item to your cart only relieves stress in the short term."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

He says cutting back on shopping is also hard because it's something we can't completely avoid.

"[With] addictive behaviours and substances, it's often easier to change the habit if you abstain completely rather than try moderation management.

"But most people can't completely abstain with shopping — we all need to buy groceries on a regular basis and occasionally we need things like clothes or homewares."

That means shopping addicts are often near their triggers, making it easier to indulge.

Ms Clothier says we're also up against external influences such as advertising.

"Retailers are incredibly good at creating urgency through limited-time offers, personalised advertising and one-click purchasing.

"They make buying feel effortless while reducing the space we have to make intentional decisions."

And we're constantly exposed to curated versions of other people's lives, leading to the comparison trap.

"[It] can subtly influence what we think we need in order to feel successful, happy or enough," Ms Clothier says.

Five shopping goals to curb impulse purchases

1. Create an urge log

Because it's hard to change habits, Dr David says you should give yourself credit for realising your shopping is a problem.

Moving overseas helped me change my shopping habits Amid all the adventure and growth, I've noticed a surprisingly quiet shift I didn't expect: my relationship with shopping.

"One of the best tools is keeping an urge log. This involves writing down when you get an urge to shop or make purchases outside your means."

Write down what you were feeling at the time, what you were thinking, and the situation you were in.

"This can give you a game plan to think of ways you can approach that situation differently in the future, so you don't give into the impulse next time," Dr David says.

2. Introduce mindfulness to your shopping

Many impulse purchases aren't really about the item itself, explains Ms Clothier, but an attempt to change how we're feeling.

Creating a small pause using mindfulness helps us to separate our emotion from our intention.

In practice, Ms Clothier says it can be as simple as pausing before you purchase and asking yourself a few questions:

What am I feeling right now?

What am I hoping this purchase will give me?

Will this still matter to me next week or next month?

Does this purchase move me towards the life I'm trying to create?

"Sometimes you'll still decide to buy it, and that's perfectly OK. Mindfulness doesn't mean never buying anything.

"The difference is that you're making the decision intentionally rather than emotionally."

3. Impose a 24-hour rule

Another simple practice is creating a waiting period to avoid reacting to that sense of urgency scarcity marketing creates, says Ms Clothier.

"For non-essential purchases, leave it in your online cart for 24 hours.

"If it still feels like a good decision after the emotion has settled, you'll probably feel much more confident about buying it."

Even waiting an hour can allow the emotional intensity to settle, she adds.

4. Compare your values to your purchases

If you know what really matters to you, Ms Clothier says you can instead spend money on the life you're intentionally creating.

"Before making a purchase, ask whether it moves you closer to what you genuinely value.

"If you value connection, adventure, health, creativity or freedom, does this purchase support those things, or is it simply offering a temporary emotional lift?"

She recommends creating a list of your five core values.

"Then, over the next month, simply notice where your money is actually going. At the end of the month, compare your spending with your values."

She says that awareness can shift spending habits without needing strict rules or budgets.

5. Make room for joy without guilt

Improving your financial wellbeing doesn't have to be about deprivation, says Ms Clothier.

Five simple steps to saving cash Saving money is not about beating yourself up. It's also not about depriving yourself of all sources of joy.

"When people try to eliminate all discretionary spending, they often end up rebounding into even bigger impulse purchases."

She says we've been taught that good money management is about discipline.

"In my experience, it's actually about awareness.

"When we understand what we're feeling, what we value, and what we're really trying to buy, we make better financial decisions almost effortlessly."

What to do if you regret an impulse purchase

If you've made a regrettable purchase, Ms Clothier says to respond with curiosity rather than criticism.

"Many people immediately blame themselves, but guilt rarely creates better financial habits. It usually creates shame, which can actually lead to more emotional spending."

She says to instead ask, "What was happening for me when I bought this?"

"Were you stressed? Lonely? Tired? Celebrating? Looking for comfort? Trying to fit in?

"Every purchase teaches us something about ourselves if we're willing to pay attention."

Dr David recommends making steps to return the item and get your money back, if possible.

"If that isn't possible, then hopefully you can find a thrift shop to donate it to, or someone else who needs the item."

He then says to plan to reward yourself with an activity you enjoy that isn't shopping related.

"You're slowly breaking habits, so keep finding other ways to reward yourself for the hard work you're doing."

World.title: UK PM Burnham meets Zelenskyy and vows 'unwavering' support for Ukraine
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has met new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a visit to the UK, as the two allies vow to continue working closely on defence and military manufacturing.

The Ukrainian president's trip to a naval base in Portsmouth marked the first foreign leader visit since Mr Burnham was sworn in as prime minister last week.

It also came hours after Russia carried out ballistic missile strikes on the Ukrainian capital.

"You are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office, and that is no accident," Mr Burnham told Mr Zelenskyy.

" It is intended to send a very clear message: we are with Ukraine 100 per cent, I am personally with you 100 per cent, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full. "

Mr Burnham said Britain would provide new, home-grown jamming technology to protect Ukrainian drones in the war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is the first foreign leader visit since Andy Burnham was sworn in as UK prime minister. (Aaron Chown via Reuters)

During the visit, Mr Burnham and Mr Zelenskyy were due to meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel and sailors who have spent the past three weeks in Britain taking part in Exercise Sea Breeze, a maritime security and counter-mine exercise designed to prepare participants for future missions in the Black Sea.

Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the UK's total support for Ukraine has reached £25 billion ($47.5 billion), including £16 billion in military assistance and £5.6 billion in non-military support, according to Downing Street.

It added the meeting was designed to underscore the UK's steadfast support for Ukraine.

Mr Burnham is the fifth British prime minister Mr Zelenskyy has dealt with since Russia launched the war in 2022.

Speaking with Sky News UK before the meeting, Mr Zelenskyy said former UK prime minister Sir Keir Starmer had promised to him that the UK would remain a close ally of Ukraine under Mr Burnham.

"We are ready to share all of our experience with the UK, and I hope the UK will do the same, so we need to make this drone deal be very strong," he said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shows no signs of ordering his forces to back down. (Reuters/Sputnik: Vyacheslav Prokofyev)

Mr Zelenskyy also touched on what he had previously labelled as Ukraine's "long-range sanctions" against Russia, taking the form of continuing drone strikes against the country's oil and gas refineries and distribution centres.

"We started to do everything to respond and to bring this war back to Russia, where it came to us," he said.

"It gives us the possibility to be more strong — Russia and Putin do not respect weak."

Mr Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer visited Kyiv days before he stood down earlier this month, where he pledged €300 million ($488 million) to help equip Ukraine with a squadron of 16 Swedish-made Gripen fighter jets.

Sir Keir also helped form the Coalition of the Willing in 2025 with France and Germany in a bid to better support Ukraine, defend Europe’s freedom and work with the US on a peace deal for Ukraine.

The meeting came a day before Mr Zelenskyy was expected to visit US President Donald Trump in Washington.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Australian clean sweep in women’s 100m free as golden wave hits pool
World.content:
All right, enough about the splashers. Things have started at the aths track with Sarah Billings running a very impressive 800m heat.

She won comfortably in 2:01.51, though the time is sort of irrelevant given the first three across the line and the three next fastest times after that go through to the finals.

While the quality of some Commonwealth Games events can be questionable, there is nothing soft about this event. Billings has Kenya’s reigning world champion Lilian Odira and England’s world silver medallist from last year Georgia Hunter-Bell to get past. Odira and Hunter-Bell both won their heats easily.

BIllings, though, looked good, and will fancy her chances of a place on the podium if she can get the right race.

The stadium for the first night session is a wee ripper. No rain, good atmosphere albeit it is small and boutique, and the stands are virtually full.

World.title: Inflation spike: Oil prices could derail economy, Treasury warns
World.content:
Treasury has warned the Australian economy could be hit by an inflation spike and slower growth through the second half of the year as America’s war against Iran, Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, and Ukraine’s assault on Russian oil refineries upend the global petroleum market. Amid forecasts from the chief economist of the nation’s biggest bank that the “clock was ticking” on oil spiking towards $US150 a barrel, Treasury is increasingly worried of a price crunch as nations run down their oil reserves, and supplies out of the Middle East and Russia dry up. Ships like these remain anchored outside the Strait of Hormuz with the war between the US and Iran escalating over the past fortnight. Getty Images Brent crude eased to $US85 on Monday after hitting $US100 a barrel late last week on concerns the renewal of hostilities between the United States and Iran will leave oil refiners struggling to get adequate supplies in coming months. Retail prices have now climbed to their highest level since early June. Over the past week, the national average price for unleaded rose by 9.5¢ to 182.3¢ a litre. Retail prices lifted by 8.9¢ in Sydney to 178.7¢ a litre, while they jumped by 10.1¢ in Melbourne to 181.7¢ a litre.



In formal advice to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, his department – which in the May budget released worst-case modelling of what would occur if oil prices reached $US200 a barrel – warned a series of factors meant the cost of oil was likely to stay elevated, hurting the domestic economy. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At the start of the war in March, members of the International Energy Authority committed to release 400 million barrels of their strategic reserves. About 290 million barrels of that reserve has been drawn down, leaving little to boost global supplies. The move by Houthi rebels to target oil movements through the Red Sea has added to global price pressures. Although oil can still be moved out of Saudi Arabia through the Suez Canal, it adds time and cost to shipping expenses. A new and unexpected development has been the success of Ukraine in using drones to attack Russian oil refineries. A strike last week on a Siberian refinery, almost 2000 kilometres from Ukraine, and a separate facility in the Caspian Sea caused extensive damage.



The attacks have not only forced Russia, one of the world’s largest oil producers, to impose restrictions on domestic use. Exports of diesel have now been banned, depleting global supply. Treasury warned that “upside risks to oil prices” would build if the current state of affairs did not change. Loading Chalmers said the increase in global prices caused by the ongoing turmoil in the Middle East could have a detrimental impact on the global and domestic economy. “The recent escalation of tensions in the Middle East poses a substantial threat to global inflation. There is still so much uncertainty about this war and its ongoing costs and consequences,” he said.



“Like the rest of the world, we are monitoring day-to-day developments very closely because so much hinges on a proper ceasefire and the permanent reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. “From an economic point of view, a proper and permanent end to the war can’t come soon enough.” Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman said markets believed just a few weeks ago there was a good chance of a global over-supply of oil that would bring prices down to between $US60 and $US70 a barrel. Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman says the clock is ticking on oil prices moving towards $US150 a barrel. Alex Ellinghausen But he said the fresh hostilities, on top of the Houthi attacks, the war in Russia and the rundown in global reserves meant there was a real chance oil could hit up to $US150 a barrel within eight to 10 weeks.



“The clock is ticking,” he told this masthead. Yeaman said a surge in oil prices would force up domestic inflation, which by itself would likely prompt an increase in official interest rates by the Reserve Bank. But the bank could then find itself cutting rates to deal with a slowing economy. Related Article Analysis

Trade Donald Trump’s trade war is costing the world a fortune – and the cost is going up “You could see a stagflation impulse, with higher inflation in the short term, but then growth comes down below potential,” he said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will on Tuesday announce $4 million in federal funding for a pre-feasibility study into an oil refinery plant in Western Australia to be built by energy and fertiliser firm Perdaman. The nation has just two refineries – in Queensland and Victoria – with no new ones established since the 1960s.



“The longer war in the Middle East goes on, the greater the impact on Australia will be, and my government will continue to do everything we can to shield Australia from the worst effects – and set us up for the future,” he said. While petrol prices are poised to climb, the electricity market is providing some reason for optimism as renewable energy and batteries decouple Australia’s power prices from the volatile global energy market. Coal-fired power fell to its lowest point on record in the second quarter of the year, and gas hit a 20-year low, as renewable energy generation and in particular battery output grew, according to the latest report by the Australian Energy Market Regulator. As a result, the past quarter’s wholesale price, which is the cost for retailers to buy electricity, was down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year. A big shift in the electricity market during past year is the rise of batteries, including grid-scale and household installations, which has boomed under the Albanese government’s rebate scheme.

World.title: ‘Plainly unfair’: Rohan Browning slams 100m qualifying rules at Commonwealth Games
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games ‘Plainly unfair’: Rohan Browning slams 100m qualifying rules at Commonwealth Games Michael Gleeson July 27, 2026 — 11:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Sprint champion Rohan Browning slammed the 100m qualifying at the Commonwealth Games as “plainly unfair” and manufactured to get certain runners into the finals. Runners with the eight fastest times in the first half of this calendar year have automatically been placed in the semi-finals without having to run heats. Only the 17 fastest times in the heats will advance to the semi-finals in Glasgow. Ordinarily, the first two finishers in each heat, and then two or three of the next fastest runners across all heats, would advance. Unhappy: Gun sprinter Rohan Browning has expressed his displeasure with the new finals format. Getty Images “It’s an unheard-of progression. It’s extremely weird,” said Browning, an Olympic and world championships semi-finalist.



“I mean, it’s gusty out there. So when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of the field goes through like on the time trial rather than, you know, first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will get better conditions than others. So I don’t know what’s going on. Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Australian clean sweep in women’s 100m free as golden wave hits pool “I think when you turn up to a championships, you’re prepared to run three rounds, and the reality is you’ve got to run hard for all of them. So, you know, I felt like I was running hard out there, even if it also felt a little awkward.” Browning qualified for the semi-finals, placing second in his heat with a time of 10.24s. “Of course, it’s not fair. Clearly, it’s not fair,” Browning said of the fact eight athletes had automatically advanced to the semi-finals without running a heat.



“Like it’s clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever’s motivated that decision, I don’t know what it is or if it’s reasonable or not. But clearly, it’s not fair. I think everyone would agree on that. “You would expect to [advance after automatically finishing second] but it’s possible that people might get a slow heat and nobody might go through from that heat. “Look, at the end of the day, this sport is meritocracy at its finest. If you’re quick enough, you go through. “So I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place through the season. In all likelihood, they’re probably the guys who are going to make the final, regardless. But you just don’t know … some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. ” Further to Browning’s point, for the final heat of the morning, there was a big +3.9m/s tailwind which would make any time illegal, as far as records go. But there was no adjustment for the wind in any of the heats.

World.title: Three storeys everywhere: The radical plan to drive down house prices
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Three storeys everywhere: The radical plan to drive down house prices Shane Wright July 27, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s sprawling suburbs of single-storey homes would be transformed under a plan from the Productivity Commission to make the property market affordable, with three-storey developments allowed everywhere and high-rise apartment blocks built near train, tram and bus stations. Declaring state and local government planning regulations a key reason for Australia having some of the most expensive homes in the world, the commission also wants the minimum size of home lots to be reduced while allowing more European-style mixed commercial and residential developments. Single-block homes would be replaced by three-storey townhouses under a plan to reduce the cost of housing across Australia. Getty Images Commission chair Danielle Wood said regulation was the handbrake on new homes, with the time needed to save for a deposit climbing by almost 30 per cent over the past 20 years. “When people can’t live near work or family the economy and the community suffers. We cannot solve our housing affordability problem unless we build more homes where people want to live,” she said.



The commission has been charged by Treasurer Jim Chalmers to examine the nation’s building approval process, land use, access to infrastructure and construction methods. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent The government, which in the budget committed $2 billion towards states and councils for housing-related infrastructure, is more than 100,000 properties behind its own target of building 1.25 million homes between mid-2024 and mid-2029. Despite a slowdown in the nation’s property market since February, house prices are still at record levels of unaffordability. Median house prices in some cities are still climbing, with Perth up 87 per cent since 2020 and in Brisbane up by 92 per cent. In its interim report, the commission said state and territory governments should allow three-storey developments on all residential land, with exceptions only for environmental factors, particular hazards or heritage listings where benefits of protection outweighed the costs.



State and council planning schemes would allow four- to nine-storey and high-rise apartments in high-demand areas with existing transport infrastructure, or where it could be quickly upgraded. Minimum lot sizes on new developments should be cut, especially in designated high-demand areas. Commercial zones that effectively prohibit residential development should also be overhauled to enable mixed-use areas. Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood says the country has to build more homes where people want to live. Eamon Gallagher Commissioner Alison Roberts said there were far too many regulations that had driven up the cost of building or reduced supply. “Regulation is essential – particularly where it ensures buildings are safe and built to a high standard. But too often, other rules are making it illegal or unviable to build the kinds of homes people need in the places they want to live,” she said.



“The kind of rules that stop you adding a granny flat in your garden or replacing a single home with townhouses are at the core of our housing challenge.” The commission said the surge in the cost of housing had led to an almost 18-percentage-point drop in the number of people between 25 and 34 with their own home between 1981 and 2021. Australian mortgage debt is among the highest per person in the developed world. In a bid to reduce construction costs, the commission recommends car parking requirements be reduced or axed completely, especially in areas where there is evidence that off-street parking is not being used or there are high levels of public transport. Loading Broad heritage listings would be replaced by more specific protections that had gone through a cost-benefit analysis. Instead of blanket heritage protections, specific buildings or small areas would attract heritage listings, with more options to delist buildings.



A constant complaint from the housing sector is the imposition of developer contributions for new projects. The Urban Development Institute of Australia estimates developer fees can make up to 20 per cent of the cost of bringing a new lot to market. Related Article Analysis

Property market Saying there’s an upside to falling house prices is sacrilege. But Labor needs to admit it The commission found developer contributions should be used where there is a “close nexus” to the proposed development and local infrastructure needs. Estimates of developer fees should be made before the release or rezoning of land, with proponents given the option to make the payments over a period of time or later in the development process. Under the commission’s proposals, current restrictions in areas such as minimum dwelling and balcony sizes and storage requirements for apartments would be axed. Current dwelling and bedroom size requirements differ between states and territories.



The commission said “state, territory and local governments should avoid regulating observable characteristics that do not negatively affect the wider community”. Restrictions on housing types would also be ditched. Another area targeted by the commission is the time many authorities take to approve new housing. Wood said in one case, a developer spent an extra three years on reports and waiting for approvals for a 1600-lot development on Melbourne’s urban fringe. The commission’s final report is due by March next year. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: The true meaning of flying economy
World.content:
“ABC TV 24 News recently ran a story about Qantas adding an additional “20 litre” fuel tank to make the AU-Europe trip in one hop,” notes David Southwell of Pymble. “Not one, but two of the seemingly oblivious presenters read this same story. Ron Burgundy moments, or does Qantas have the most fuel-efficient jet ever? I guess one of the crew has to fill the jerry can with Avgas on the way to work.”

Jo Rainbow’s West Berkshire experience (C8) continues: “In Oxford we drove past Toot Hill Butts. I wonder if it is an effluent area.”

“My first movie (C8) was a charity screening of Jedda in 1959,” recalls Andrew Cohen of Glebe. “There was a garden party afterwards. I was traumatised, terrified, and I recall several stark images that I can’t exclude even now as to how fearful I found them. I recall that director Charles Chauvel sat me on his knee, trying to console me. I wasn’t sobbing but describing at high volume what was scary. I was four and haven’t seen it again.”

George Zivkovic of Northmead perceives that “Roy Masters, in his column, suggested allowing one attacking kick, or forward pass to an offside receiver, per set of six tackles will perhaps achieve ‘global domination’ for rugby league”. Sorry, Roy, but that’s already been happening in the games I’ve been watching this season, along with attackers in front of kickers, dubious play-the-balls and Clayton’s scrums.”

Shout-out to the Manly Observer, an independent publication bucking the trend by adding a print edition along with a real-time digital presence and, as Allan Gibson of Cherrybrook points out, is a dab hand at alliteration, with the headline, “Baby-faced booze bandits busted by bystander”. We give it a B+.

World.title: ‘Really devastated’: Saints coach Lyon reveals King’s anguish after another injury blow
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Max King suffered a season-ending hamstring strain on Sunday.

Brisbane’s Ty Gallop will face a serious misconduct charge.

St Kilda’s Darcy Wilson has re-committed on a new two-year deal. St Kilda coach Ross Lyon maintains the club is committed to keeping Max King at Moorabbin, revealing the injury-prone forward was “really devastated” and asked if the club had had enough of him. The 26-year-old has been put in cotton wool for the rest season but St Kilda stresses the 84-gamer is “incredibly important” to the Saints and they’re determined to get him back playing senior footy. King will not play again until at least next year after it was confirmed on Monday he suffered a season-ending left hamstring strain in his return AFL game against North Melbourne on Sunday. Lyon spoke about the extent of King’s frustration and disappointment, with the Saint seeking assurances that they would still back him as an AFL player.



Max King during his comeback game. Getty Images Tied to the Saints until the end of 2032 after signing a six-year contract extension two years ago, King faces a huge challenge to overcome his injury woes. “His concern was he’d let the club and a lot of his team down,” Lyon said on Fox Footy. “And shame is too strong a word, but [he was] probably embarrassed. “Like [he was] saying, ‘Have you guys had enough of me?’ And I said, ‘Hang on here. We’re in.’”



King’s season-ending left hamstring strain is a devastating blow for the Saints and King, who had not played at AFL level for 757 days before his latest setback, and has now suffered hamstring injuries twice this year. Lyon is adamant the Saints did everything in their power to ensure King was fit enough to return to senior football. Loading “Every parameter … was really strong. I mean he got to half-time [on Sunday] healthy. Anyone who thinks it’s fatigue [is off the mark],” he said. “There’s nothing on the parameters [we look at] or the demand of the game that caused this.”



Lyon had already defended the club’s decision to play King in the senior side and bypass the VFL this time, but the star forward will now have played just once in three seasons after a torturous run that includes injuries to both knees and calf issues. Max King gets a kick away against the Kangaroos. AFL Photos King left Sunday’s 31-point win over North Melbourne midway through the third quarter and did not return. He started each term on the bench and played in six-minute stints, but managed just one kick and one handball while playing at different times on Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr. Saints football boss Lenny Hayes said the club would “wrap our arms” around King.



“It’s an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return,” said Hayes. “He’s an incredibly important part of our football club. We’ll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback. “Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027.” King signed a six-year contract extension in October 2024 that ties him to the Saints until the end of the 2032 season. His horror injury run started about three months before he inked that deal, when he sustained a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide.



King also hurt his right knee in a pre-season game mere months later that ultimately required three separate surgeries and wiped out his 2025 season. After a delayed start to the past off-season, a new calf problem sidelined him again. King made it back from that setback, only to suffer a hamstring strain in his second VFL game in May. The 26-year-old went into an extended rehabilitation period after that, including spending time on the Gold Coast with his twin, Suns focal point Ben, who is expected to sign as a restricted free agent with Hawthorn. Lyon said St Kilda’s high-performance team was satisfied that King had proven he was ready with a significant volume of running, including at high speeds and game-like intensity.



“We stand by our decision to play him,” Lyon said on Sunday. There are still six seasons left on King’s deal, and he will be desperate to repay the Saints’ faith in him to avoid becoming the poster child for how long-term contracts can go wrong. King won’t play again until the 2027 season. AFL Photos The No.4 pick from the 2018 AFL draft displayed his immense potential in a career-best 52-goal season in 2022. St Kilda are clinging to a wildcard berth with a month to go in the home-and-away season, with matches to come against Sydney, Carlton, Richmond and Gold Coast, all of which will be played in Melbourne.



In positive news for the Saints faithful, it was confirmed on Monday evening that Darcy Wilson has committed to the club on a new two-year deal. The hard-running midfielder had attracted plenty of rival interest after a breakthrough season. The 20-year-old, who was drafted at pick 18 in the 2023 draft, will remain at the club until the end of the 2028 season. The Saints made a splash in last year’s player movement period, recruiting Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Sam Flanders and Liam Ryan, after making Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera the league’s first $2 million-a-season man. St Kilda’s big spending has so far delivered only a mediocre return, worsened by Flanders suffering a season-ending Achilles injury. De Koning also missed games with broken ribs and a punctured lung, but demonstrated what he could bring in a strong performance against the Roos on Sunday.



Lion straight to tribunal on misconduct charge Brisbane youngster Ty Gallop has been sent straight to the AFL tribunal for shoving Port Adelaide’s Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf. Gallop has been charged with serious misconduct for the incident in the second quarter of Brisbane’s win over Port at the Gabba on Sunday. The 20-year-old rolled Georgiades in a heavy tackle but has come under scrutiny for his actions off the ball immediately after. As the Lions swept downfield, Gallop lifted Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.



Depending on how the tribunal sees the incident, Gallop could face multiple weeks on the sidelines. “It wasn’t a great look, but I’m on the other side of it,” Port Adelaide coach Josh Carr said. “They’re a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There’s not much more to say.” Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.



Gallop’s choice to hit out at Georgiades was described as “a stupid action” by former Brisbane great Alastair Lynch. “We’ve been singing the praises of Ty Gallop over the last half a dozen weeks particularly,” Lynch said on Fox Footy. “But that’s just a stupid action. We don’t want to see that. Mitch has had some problems with concussion. AAP and Scott Spits Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Australian clean sweep in women’s 100m free as golden wave hits pool
World.content:
All right, enough about the splashers. Things have started at the aths track with Sarah Billings running a very impressive 800m heat.

She won comfortably in 2:01.51, though the time is sort of irrelevant given the first three across the line and the three next fastest times after that go through to the finals.

While the quality of some Commonwealth Games events can be questionable, there is nothing soft about this event. Billings has Kenya’s reigning world champion Lilian Odira and England’s world silver medallist from last year Georgia Hunter-Bell to get past. Odira and Hunter-Bell both won their heats easily.

BIllings, though, looked good, and will fancy her chances of a place on the podium if she can get the right race.

The stadium for the first night session is a wee ripper. No rain, good atmosphere albeit it is small and boutique, and the stands are virtually full.

The nation’s sprawling suburbs of single-storey homes would be transformed under a plan from the Productivity Commission to make the property market affordable, with three-storey developments allowed everywhere and high-rise apartment blocks built near train, tram and bus stations. Declaring state and local government planning regulations a key reason for Australia having some of the most expensive homes in the world, the commission also wants the minimum size of home lots to be reduced while allowing more European-style mixed commercial and residential developments. Single-block homes would be replaced by three-storey townhouses under a plan to reduce the cost of housing across Australia. Getty Images Commission chair Danielle Wood said regulation was the handbrake on new homes, with the time needed to save for a deposit climbing by almost 30 per cent over the past 20 years. “When people can’t live near work or family the economy and the community suffers. We cannot solve our housing affordability problem unless we build more homes where people want to live,” she said.



The commission has been charged by Treasurer Jim Chalmers to examine the nation’s building approval process, land use, access to infrastructure and construction methods. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent The government, which in the budget committed $2 billion towards states and councils for housing-related infrastructure, is more than 100,000 properties behind its own target of building 1.25 million homes between mid-2024 and mid-2029. Despite a slowdown in the nation’s property market since February, house prices are still at record levels of unaffordability. Median house prices in some cities are still climbing, with Perth up 87 per cent since 2020 and in Brisbane up by 92 per cent. In its interim report, the commission said state and territory governments should allow three-storey developments on all residential land, with exceptions only for environmental factors, particular hazards or heritage listings where benefits of protection outweighed the costs.



State and council planning schemes would allow four- to nine-storey and high-rise apartments in high-demand areas with existing transport infrastructure, or where it could be quickly upgraded. Minimum lot sizes on new developments should be cut, especially in designated high-demand areas. Commercial zones that effectively prohibit residential development should also be overhauled to enable mixed-use areas. Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood says the country has to build more homes where people want to live. Eamon Gallagher Commissioner Alison Roberts said there were far too many regulations that had driven up the cost of building or reduced supply. “Regulation is essential – particularly where it ensures buildings are safe and built to a high standard. But too often, other rules are making it illegal or unviable to build the kinds of homes people need in the places they want to live,” she said.



“The kind of rules that stop you adding a granny flat in your garden or replacing a single home with townhouses are at the core of our housing challenge.” The commission said the surge in the cost of housing had led to an almost 18-percentage-point drop in the number of people between 25 and 34 with their own home between 1981 and 2021. Australian mortgage debt is among the highest per person in the developed world. In a bid to reduce construction costs, the commission recommends car parking requirements be reduced or axed completely, especially in areas where there is evidence that off-street parking is not being used or there are high levels of public transport. Loading Broad heritage listings would be replaced by more specific protections that had gone through a cost-benefit analysis. Instead of blanket heritage protections, specific buildings or small areas would attract heritage listings, with more options to delist buildings.



A constant complaint from the housing sector is the imposition of developer contributions for new projects. The Urban Development Institute of Australia estimates developer fees can make up to 20 per cent of the cost of bringing a new lot to market. Related Article Analysis

Property market Saying there’s an upside to falling house prices is sacrilege. But Labor needs to admit it The commission found developer contributions should be used where there is a “close nexus” to the proposed development and local infrastructure needs. Estimates of developer fees should be made before the release or rezoning of land, with proponents given the option to make the payments over a period of time or later in the development process. Under the commission’s proposals, current restrictions in areas such as minimum dwelling and balcony sizes and storage requirements for apartments would be axed. Current dwelling and bedroom size requirements differ between states and territories.



The commission said “state, territory and local governments should avoid regulating observable characteristics that do not negatively affect the wider community”. Restrictions on housing types would also be ditched. Another area targeted by the commission is the time many authorities take to approve new housing. Wood said in one case, a developer spent an extra three years on reports and waiting for approvals for a 1600-lot development on Melbourne’s urban fringe. The commission’s final report is due by March next year. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
