World.title: The true meaning of flying economy
World.content:
“ABC TV 24 News recently ran a story about Qantas adding an additional “20 litre” fuel tank to make the AU-Europe trip in one hop,” notes David Southwell of Pymble. “Not one, but two of the seemingly oblivious presenters read this same story. Ron Burgundy moments, or does Qantas have the most fuel-efficient jet ever? I guess one of the crew has to fill the jerry can with Avgas on the way to work.”

Jo Rainbow’s West Berkshire experience (C8) continues: “In Oxford we drove past Toot Hill Butts. I wonder if it is an effluent area.”

“My first movie (C8) was a charity screening of Jedda in 1959,” recalls Andrew Cohen of Glebe. “There was a garden party afterwards. I was traumatised, terrified, and I recall several stark images that I can’t exclude even now as to how fearful I found them. I recall that director Charles Chauvel sat me on his knee, trying to console me. I wasn’t sobbing but describing at high volume what was scary. I was four and haven’t seen it again.”

George Zivkovic of Northmead perceives that “Roy Masters, in his column, suggested allowing one attacking kick, or forward pass to an offside receiver, per set of six tackles will perhaps achieve ‘global domination’ for rugby league”. Sorry, Roy, but that’s already been happening in the games I’ve been watching this season, along with attackers in front of kickers, dubious play-the-balls and Clayton’s scrums.”

Shout-out to the Manly Observer, an independent publication bucking the trend by adding a print edition along with a real-time digital presence and, as Allan Gibson of Cherrybrook points out, is a dab hand at alliteration, with the headline, “Baby-faced booze bandits busted by bystander”. We give it a B+.

World.title: ‘Really devastated’: Saints coach Lyon reveals King’s anguish after another injury blow
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Max King suffered a season-ending hamstring strain on Sunday.

Brisbane’s Ty Gallop will face a serious misconduct charge.

St Kilda’s Darcy Wilson has re-committed on a new two-year deal. St Kilda coach Ross Lyon maintains the club is committed to keeping Max King at Moorabbin, revealing the injury-prone forward was “really devastated” and asked if the club had had enough of him. The 26-year-old has been put in cotton wool for the rest season but St Kilda stresses the 84-gamer is “incredibly important” to the Saints and they’re determined to get him back playing senior footy. King will not play again until at least next year after it was confirmed on Monday he suffered a season-ending left hamstring strain in his return AFL game against North Melbourne on Sunday. Lyon spoke about the extent of King’s frustration and disappointment, with the Saint seeking assurances that they would still back him as an AFL player.



Max King during his comeback game. Getty Images Tied to the Saints until the end of 2032 after signing a six-year contract extension two years ago, King faces a huge challenge to overcome his injury woes. “His concern was he’d let the club and a lot of his team down,” Lyon said on Fox Footy. “And shame is too strong a word, but [he was] probably embarrassed. “Like [he was] saying, ‘Have you guys had enough of me?’ And I said, ‘Hang on here. We’re in.’”



King’s season-ending left hamstring strain is a devastating blow for the Saints and King, who had not played at AFL level for 757 days before his latest setback, and has now suffered hamstring injuries twice this year. Lyon is adamant the Saints did everything in their power to ensure King was fit enough to return to senior football. Loading “Every parameter … was really strong. I mean he got to half-time [on Sunday] healthy. Anyone who thinks it’s fatigue [is off the mark],” he said. “There’s nothing on the parameters [we look at] or the demand of the game that caused this.”



Lyon had already defended the club’s decision to play King in the senior side and bypass the VFL this time, but the star forward will now have played just once in three seasons after a torturous run that includes injuries to both knees and calf issues. Max King gets a kick away against the Kangaroos. AFL Photos King left Sunday’s 31-point win over North Melbourne midway through the third quarter and did not return. He started each term on the bench and played in six-minute stints, but managed just one kick and one handball while playing at different times on Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr. Saints football boss Lenny Hayes said the club would “wrap our arms” around King.



“It’s an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return,” said Hayes. “He’s an incredibly important part of our football club. We’ll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback. “Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027.” King signed a six-year contract extension in October 2024 that ties him to the Saints until the end of the 2032 season. His horror injury run started about three months before he inked that deal, when he sustained a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide.



King also hurt his right knee in a pre-season game mere months later that ultimately required three separate surgeries and wiped out his 2025 season. After a delayed start to the past off-season, a new calf problem sidelined him again. King made it back from that setback, only to suffer a hamstring strain in his second VFL game in May. The 26-year-old went into an extended rehabilitation period after that, including spending time on the Gold Coast with his twin, Suns focal point Ben, who is expected to sign as a restricted free agent with Hawthorn. Lyon said St Kilda’s high-performance team was satisfied that King had proven he was ready with a significant volume of running, including at high speeds and game-like intensity.



“We stand by our decision to play him,” Lyon said on Sunday. There are still six seasons left on King’s deal, and he will be desperate to repay the Saints’ faith in him to avoid becoming the poster child for how long-term contracts can go wrong. King won’t play again until the 2027 season. AFL Photos The No.4 pick from the 2018 AFL draft displayed his immense potential in a career-best 52-goal season in 2022. St Kilda are clinging to a wildcard berth with a month to go in the home-and-away season, with matches to come against Sydney, Carlton, Richmond and Gold Coast, all of which will be played in Melbourne.



In positive news for the Saints faithful, it was confirmed on Monday evening that Darcy Wilson has committed to the club on a new two-year deal. The hard-running midfielder had attracted plenty of rival interest after a breakthrough season. The 20-year-old, who was drafted at pick 18 in the 2023 draft, will remain at the club until the end of the 2028 season. The Saints made a splash in last year’s player movement period, recruiting Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Sam Flanders and Liam Ryan, after making Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera the league’s first $2 million-a-season man. St Kilda’s big spending has so far delivered only a mediocre return, worsened by Flanders suffering a season-ending Achilles injury. De Koning also missed games with broken ribs and a punctured lung, but demonstrated what he could bring in a strong performance against the Roos on Sunday.



Lion straight to tribunal on misconduct charge Brisbane youngster Ty Gallop has been sent straight to the AFL tribunal for shoving Port Adelaide’s Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf. Gallop has been charged with serious misconduct for the incident in the second quarter of Brisbane’s win over Port at the Gabba on Sunday. The 20-year-old rolled Georgiades in a heavy tackle but has come under scrutiny for his actions off the ball immediately after. As the Lions swept downfield, Gallop lifted Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.



Depending on how the tribunal sees the incident, Gallop could face multiple weeks on the sidelines. “It wasn’t a great look, but I’m on the other side of it,” Port Adelaide coach Josh Carr said. “They’re a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There’s not much more to say.” Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.



Gallop’s choice to hit out at Georgiades was described as “a stupid action” by former Brisbane great Alastair Lynch. “We’ve been singing the praises of Ty Gallop over the last half a dozen weeks particularly,” Lynch said on Fox Footy. “But that’s just a stupid action. We don’t want to see that. Mitch has had some problems with concussion. AAP and Scott Spits Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Experts call for more water infrastructure investment as report reveals 'severe' pressure
World.content:
Experts are calling for more investment in water infrastructure, after a report revealed the country averaged 31 wastewater overflows a day.

The Water Services Authority published the first national picture of water networks on Monday.

It showed there were "severe" pressures on water infrastructure, leading a third of councils to have at least one drinking water network with "very high" leakage levels by international standards.

Dr Mike Joy, a freshwater ecologist at the Victoria University of Wellington, said the report confirmed his concerns about water infrastructure.

"We've known for a long time that our wastewater systems are failing."

He said the network was run down and unfit to handle growing demand and strain from climate change.

"We're getting overflows, we're getting sewage going into the environment - and it's going to get worse because we have failed infrastructure."

Joy said water investment had been put off by local governments as it was not a "sexy" issue.

"It's not something that you get voted in on. It's not something that's popular and we have a lot of pressure on councils to reduce rates."

He said there needed to be stricter regulations and enforcement.

The report found that a fifth of wastewater treatment plants operated on expired consents; Joy said this was symptomatic of a lack of proper enforcement.

Te Tahi wastewater treatment plant in Waikato heavily damaged from a storm. Waipa District Council

He said councils would be reluctant to fine plants which they owned themselves as it would effectively be a tax on ratepayers.

He said as a result there was no pressure on councils to address problems.

"They just get a sad face stamp from the authorities if they fail these things," he added.

The risk of failing infrastructure, he said, was the contamination of drinking water - which could spread disease.

During heavy rain and floods, rainwater could overflow into the sewage system, overloading the network.

"The treatment plant has no storage opportunity, so it has to just open the gate.

"And a lot of the water treatment - killing pathogens - happens with ultraviolet systems. And as soon as the water becomes too dirty or the flow's too high, they stop working and it's just discharging raw sewage into the environment."

Raw sewage could then find its way into drinking water catchments, he said.

"If we want to be able to swim in our beaches and rivers, then we have to make sure that we're not polluting them with human waste. It's really, really basic, really simple."

Industry group Water NZ said the report highlighted the need for more investment in water infrastructure.

Chief executive Gillian Blythe said councils needed to spend the money ringfenced for water projects under Local Water Done Well.

"It's critical that we understand the need to invest for our future climate, for our future populations and for the natural hazards that are faced across New Zealand," she said.

Water New Zealand chief executive Gillian Blythe. RNZ / Niva Chittock

Looking to the future, she called for stronger protection of water drinking sources.

"Whether that's a river, a lake or an aquifer - because that is the most effective and most cost-efficient way to ensure reliable drinking water supplies for communities," she added.

She said protecting source water would cost less than having to treat contaminated drinking water.

World.title: Guidelines for AI use in courts need updating, some academics say
World.content:
Experts say guidelines for AI use in New Zealand's courts need to be updated, but the courts say a cautious approach is still needed.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use in New Zealand's legal system is continuing to increase, a fact the Office of the Chief Justice has acknowledged.

But the judiciary's guidelines for AI use were last updated in 2023.

Matt Bartlett, a lecturer at the University of Auckland's Law School, said other judiciaries around the world were updating their guidance far more frequently than New Zealand.

"They're out of step with the capabilities, the risk profile, and frankly the practice overseas," he said.

Dr Joshua Yuvaraj, a senior lecturer at the University of Auckland's Law School, said the technology was evolving so quickly that the guidelines should be reviewed regularly to ensure they remained fit for purpose.

Dr Joshua Yuvaraj, a senior lecturer at the University of Auckland's Law School. Supplied / University of Auckland

"Three years is a very long time in the technology space," he said.

Technology, he said, had moved beyond just generative AI technologies to agentic AI, where AI systems could automate tasks such as organising workflows, responding to emails and other administrative work.

He said these developments warranted some attention in the court's guidelines. He also wanted to see continual emphasis on the privacy and confidentiality risks associated with using AI tools.

Auckland barrister Josh McBride said while the guidelines were now a few years old, they had largely stood the test of time.

"I've looked at them recently, and in fairness, they do a pretty good job," he said.

"The problem with getting prescriptive and being detailed about what tools are okay and which aren't, and what uses are okay and which aren't, is that you are having to literally update these every few weeks, which is a very, very difficult task.

"I think all that the courts can do, and I think they're doing this in New Zealand really well, is to say, 'proceed with extreme caution if you're using these tools in this context. You are responsible for the material that goes into the court. You can't blame a robot if it goes wrong, and we expect you to comply with all of the ethical obligations'."

More transparency needed

Typically AI use did not need to be disclosed, and Bartlett said that made it difficult to understand the extent to which AI was already influencing the justice system.

He said courts overseas were already experimenting with AI, and it would be naïve to assume New Zealand judges would not use similar tools.

His greatest concern was the possibility of AI being used to help draft judicial decisions.

Matt Bartlett, a lecturer at the University of Auckland's Law School. Supplied / University of Auckland

"The danger with an AI is that it undermines what we currently have from judges, which is them explaining their reasoning.

"They're writing their judgments. They are explaining how they arrived at their legal conclusions. If you have an AI that is writing the judgment, you're undermining the explanatory process of how a judge arrived at their decision, which is just core to how the whole common law, our whole constitutional structure operates."

Bartlett questioned whether overseas AI models could adequately account for New Zealand's unique legal and constitutional context.

"They will place no particular emphasis on New Zealand-specific constitutional factors."

He noted the judiciary's own guidance already warned that GenAI chatbots did not adequately account for New Zealand's cultural context or the specific cultural values and practices of Māori and Pasifika.

Yuvaraj said if AI use wasn't disclosed then people didn't know how much it had been used and therefore whether it had any potential impact on the outcome of a case.

"We want to make sure that the judge has read everything that's relevant rather than just outsourcing that, because then we can't be sure that the judge has administered justice fully."

McBride meanwhile did not believe AI use should necessarily have to be disclosed.

However he said he had seen instances where litigants armed with AI tools were producing disproportionate volumes of AI generated material for what the case entailed.

He said there was a benefit in clearer rules being developed around the volume of AI-generated material people could file, along with clearer warnings that litigants were responsible for verifying anything AI produced before submitting it to the court.

Auckland barrister Josh McBride. Supplied / Richmond Chambers

Courts taking cautious approach

In response to questions from RNZ a spokesperson from the Office of the Chief Justice said while the judiciary recognised the opportunities created by AI to support access to justice and the timely, efficient and proportionate administration of justice, it was taking a cautious approach to the exploration and adoption of Generative AI (Gen AI) to support the work of the courts.

"At present, a limited number of judges and their support staff are trialling some Gen AI tools overseen by the Judicial AI Advisory Group. The trials start from the premise that a judgment is a reasoned human decision made by a judge drawing on the evidence, submissions, pleadings, charges, and applicable law. Judgment writing is a fundamental responsibility of the judge - that responsibility cannot be delegated to other people, or to AI."

The spokesperson said the guiding principles for the trials were that Gen AI tools must not be used for judicial reasoning or decision-making, and must not be used in a way that replaces, compromises, or obscures the essential human task of judging.

"The trials are testing responsible use cases of AI, and are being used to refine the existing Guidelines for Judicial Use of AI - these were issued in 2023 and need updating.

World.title: Bill Hammond painting expected to sell for up to $1.8m at auction
World.content:
An iconic New Zealand painting by artist Bill Hammond is expected to fetch up to $1.8 million when it goes under the hammer tonight.

Zoomorphic Lounge III was painted by Lyttelton artist Bill Hammond in 1999, and features surreal humanoid creatures on an emerald green background.

An art historian said the bird-like creatures, which were common in the artists work, were symbols of New Zealanders and their place in the world.

Linda Taylor, a professor in the Art History department at the University of Auckland, said a key moment in Hammond's career was his visit to the sub-antarctic Auckland islands in 1989.

"What struck him there was it was a bird-land. It was like New Zealand before human beings arrived and his art was very markedly changed after that moment. He became a little bit bird obssesed."

That motif could clearly be seen in Zoomorphic Lounge III.

Bird-like and horse-like figures were depicted in human-like activities across the canvas - playing in a band, hula-hooping, smoking, drinking at a bar.

"He's not exactly reproducing birds. But he's using the bird as a symbol - as an iconic symbol to stand in for New Zealanders and who we are and where we are in the world."

The painting's set on an emerald green background, with long lines dripping their way down the canvas, and some of the animals have barcodes tattoed on their bodies.

Auctioneer Webb's estimated the work will sell for between $1.4 million and $1.8 million.

The sheer size of the work and the fact the artist was dead made it valuable, Taylor said.

"If you create scarcity, which artists dying does, it limits the supply of artworks from them. Then it makes the commodity more valuable and because it's such a good example and in such great condition it's liable to get at the high end of their estimates."

Lytellton-based Poet and broadcaster Gary McCormick was a friend of Bill Hammond's and often spent time with him in the local bar The Civil & Naval.

"You didn't have to talk to Bill and Bill didn't have to talk to you. He was the sort of guy that, if he wanted to be silent for an hour and a half he would. And if he wanted to speak he'd speak... I guess you do tend to find that with creative people in the sense that they're busy creating in their own minds."

The painting in question was "spooky" to him, McCormick said, but captured something unique about New Zealand that few other artists had.

"Obviously the forest green type cover for the whole painting in which there are all these bird like creatures. That says New Zealand for me. And there is this slight lurking menace which I think is also part of New Zealand life."

He hoped it would be bought by a New Zealand gallery, so that future generations could see it.

Webb's art department manager Megan Shaw said Hammond was one of New Zealand's most important artists.

"This work was in Bill's own collection for many years and when our collector came upon it, it was then loaned to a few public art galleries... so I think it's already been recognised that this painting is highly significant."

Another of Hammond's paintings - called Melting Moments - sold for $1.7 million in 2023.

The most expensive New Zealand painting ever sold was Thoughts of a Tohunga by Charles Frederick Goldie which went for $3.75 million.

World.title: Who's offering more generous paid parental leave?
World.content:
What if you don't want a slice of the AI hype? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

National may be proposing to increase the amount of paid parental leave that new parents are allowed to take, but about half of all New Zealand employers are already offering more than the statutory minimum.

National said at the weekend it would extend the paid parental leave period from 26 weeks to 30, if it was re-elected.

Primary carers are eligible for 26 weeks of paid leave and another 26 weeks unpaid, at their normal rate of pay but capped at $811 a week.

Some employers are already offering significantly more generous leave policies. Kiwibank tops up employees' leave to 100 percent of their normal salary for 26 weeks plus offers an extra six weeks' paid leave when they return to work. Law firm AJ Park offers 18 weeks paid at 100 percent of salary plus another eight weeks topping up the government payment. Another law firm, Mayne Wetherell, offers up to 26 weeks at 100 percent pay with significant flexibility around the timing of the leave.

Within government, ministries tend to offer a one-off payment equivalent to six weeks' pay when staff go on leave.

Teachers receive a similar payment.

Members of Parliament receive their normal remuneration while on parental leave.

Otago University associate professor Paula O'Kane, said for most people, the availability of additional parental leave perks was something that was a pleasant surprise when they came to use it.

"Not a lot of people will be looking at it whenever they are thinking about going in and working with an employer."

But she said the Parental Leave Register, which is administered by Crayon, was a good tool for people to look at potential employer policies, or even those of their current workplace.

O'Kane said employees would value a top-up to 100 percent of their salaries because the parental leave rate was a significant pay cut for many people.

"The more you're paid, the bigger cut you're taking when you go off on parental leave."

Otago University associate professor Paula O'Kane. Dave Bull

She said it tended to be bigger companies that were able to offer more, but most New Zealand businesses were small.

"It's much trickier to top up those different elements of that parental leave package. That's where the government really becomes an important player to be able to support those smaller organisations."

She said the minimum government payment should be higher. "I think if they were more generous you would give parents and children a better start in life."

She said other things would matter, too, like work flexibility when someone returned.

Shannon Barlow, managing director of Frog Recruitment, said extended paid parental leave was viewed positively by jobseekers, but it was not a deal breaker in the current market.

"It's been a difficult couple of years for many job seekers. With unemployment still relatively high and competition for roles remaining strong, we're seeing more people take a 'bird in the hand' approach. If they've found a role that offers career progression, stability and a good manager, they're less likely to hold out for an employer with a slightly more generous parental leave policy.

"Our latest market report reflects that. Career opportunities, work-life balance, management support and trust, and job security are the biggest drivers for candidates this year. Extended parental leave is appreciated, but it sits well behind those broader workplace factors in terms of what influences someone's decision to join or stay with an employer.

"That said, any additional benefit is viewed favourably, particularly one that supports employees through a major life event. It's the sort of initiative that can strengthen an employer's reputation and reinforce that they genuinely invest in their people, even if it isn't the deciding factor when someone accepts a role."

Shannon Barlow, managing director of Frog Recruitment. Supplied/ Frog Recruitment

She said the employers that would stand up were those who did not wait for legislation.

"They look at what their people value and build benefits that strengthen their employee value proposition, whether that's enhanced parental leave, higher KiwiSaver contributions, paid life or longevity leave, or paying a living wage rather than simply meeting the minimum wage. Those initiatives help differentiate an employer in the market and demonstrate a genuine commitment to supporting their people, rather than just meeting the statutory minimum.

"It also keeps New Zealand moving in the same direction as Australia. Australia has just expanded its government-funded Paid Parental Leave to 26 weeks from July this year, with reforms designed to increase support and flexibility for families. So anything that gives us an edge over the Aussies is a good thing! National's proposal to move New Zealand to 30 weeks would continue that trend of gradually strengthening parental leave rather than being a dramatic shift."

Research for the Ministry of Social Development in 2021 showed women who were working before having children preferred to take 69 weeks of leave on average. People who were self-employed or working part-time were more likely to want to take less.

Just over half said they expected to get less leave than they wanted. More than half returned to work within nine months.

World.title: What if all you have to do is ask for a better deal?
World.content:
What if you don't want a slice of the AI hype? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

What if all you had to do to get a better deal was to ask?

Bargaining is something that doesn't come naturally for lots of people, but experts say you may be able to negotiate the price of anything from your electricity to your new dining table, if you try.

Here are a few things for which it might be worth giving it a shot.

Your mortgage rate

Banks will often negotiate with customers, particularly if they say they are thinking about moving to a competitor.

"If you're looking at switching your mortgage, give your existing mortgage broker a call and say 'look I'm out of here unless you match the guys down the road'," Consumer NZ chief executive Jon Duffy said.

"Quite often you'll be able to get a deal that's better than the headline advertised deal."

Consumer NZ chief executive Jon Duffy. Supplied / Consumer NZ

Glen McLeod, head of Link Advisory, said banks generally had two tiers of pricing.

"The first is the advertised or 'carded' rate, which is publicly available on the bank's website. The second consists of special rates that may be available to borrowers with a loan-to-value ratio (LVR) below 80 percent. Many borrowers aren't aware that these lower rates may exist, which is why it's important to ask whether there are any better rates available. Simply asking the question can provide valuable insight into the most competitive options on offer."

He said mortgage advisers received weekly pricing schedules and banks were becoming less flexible about offering any lower, but it was always worth trying.

"Importantly, the conversation is no longer just about securing the lowest interest rate. We're seeing a growing trend where borrowers who are refixing a loan at the end of a fixed-rate term may also be eligible for retention incentives, such as cashback offers or retention payments.

"As a result, the best outcome is often determined by the overall package on offer-not just the interest rate, but also any financial incentives that can improve the client's position and reduce the overall cost of borrowing."

Jeremy Andrews, of Key Mortgages, agreed cash payments were a good option to ask for. You could try to negotiate this from another lender, or your existing bank.

He said banks were offering up to 1 percent cashback in some cases, particularly for people with new or larger loans.

Your income

Just under half of New Zealand workers say they've never even asked for a pay rise.

Although the labour market has been a bit weaker lately, you may still be able to make a case to increase your income. Experts say it usually helps to go into a meeting about a pay rise with a clear idea of what you're achieving in your job and what you're generating for the business. Make your case for why you deserve more money, not just tell your boss you want some.

You can also look at what other roles similar to yours are paying. There are salary surveys available each year from organisations such as Hays and Robert Walters and you may also be able to get an idea from looking at sites such as Seek.

Purchases for your house

If you're considering a purchase such as an appliance, whiteware or a new piece of furniture, you may be able to get a better deal if you can show a competitor is offering a lower price. Take your phone with you when you're shopping and google anything you're considering. Sites such as PriceSpy will show you what price it is selling for elsewhere.

Consumer NZ points out that Briscoes and Rebel Sport will offer a discount of 10 percent on a lower price from a competitor while Bunnings and Mitre 10 offered 15 percent. "JB Hi-Fi, Noel Leeming and The Warehouse will match the cheaper price, but don't offer a further discount."

It said people could also get prices matched at Chemist Warehouse and Bargain Chemist.

Even if a shop doesn't advertise that it has a price match policy, you may be able to get a discount by pointing out that an item is cheaper elsewhere. Duffy said sometimes there would be other inducements that were offered instead. "Get a free toaster with your fridge or something like that."

Power

Shopping around on your power can help you get a better price. Sites like Billy and Powerswitch allow you to compare what's on offer. If you find something that looks like a better deal, you could ask your current provider to match it.

Duffy said that was something people often did on Powerswitch.

"Often people will compare prices, then go back to their existing provider and say, 'well, I can see that there's two different power companies that are offering a cheaper rate than you. Give me your best deal or I'm leaving'. And that feels kind of acceptable in the services space, similarly with broadband.

"By making a comparison, sometimes you can go back to your current provider and say, I'm out of here. And we know that the big broadband providers all have retention teams who you'll get transferred to, and those people are specifically tasked with getting you a deal that will keep you."

Buying a house

One of the areas where a lot of New Zealanders expect to negotiate is in buying a house.

Duffy said most people would not take the first price offered to them. "There's an aggressive negotiation process where buyers and sellers need an intermediary in there to kind of be a referee to get the final price."

Data from Realestate.co.nz showed that house sellers were accepting prices about $30,000 lower than their first asking price in the first quarter of this year.

World.title: 'The most loving, laziest dogs': Greyhound-owner wants others to adopt as 1500 lose homes
World.content:
An Upper Hutt mum who adopted two greyhounds in the past month is encouraging others to do the same, with almost 1500 race dogs set to lose their homes next week.

Greyhound racing will be banned on Saturday, and a massive rehoming project aims to find families for the ex-racers over the next five years.

Julia Gray called Sam her "gateway drug".

Her family adopted the dog from Nightrave Greyhounds last month.

"It was one of those things where we went and I said 'we're only looking', but I'm a very impulsive person and Sam ended up coming home with us a week later," she said.

Not long after adopting Sam, Gray said her family met Dream at the same agency.

"Next thing you know the car's getting packed up for two dogs to come home with us, and we're picking out collars and we're picking out jackets, and now we have Dream who has been with us for a week," Gray laughed.

"Life has just been amazing with them and I don't know why I've left it so long."

Sadie the greyhound is seeking a new home after the end of racing in NZ. Supplied / The Greyhound Rehoming Project

Rachel Rae, the co-director of Nightrave, said hundreds of dogs like Sam and Dream would be looking for new homes.

"We believe there's going to be about 1500 to rehome, they're all going to be out of a job so the lives they've had up to now will absolutely disappear," Rae said.

"The transition agency has a brief to last five years, so that's how long we've got to home the dogs. We think it will probably be done in a shorter time period than that, probably three years."

She said greyhounds remained a popular breed, and demand was high for the lazy and well behaved animals.

"They are very well suited to pet life, particularly in our modern busy lives, they're quite a calm and lazy dog, they very much enjoy laying around," she explained.

"If you're a time-poor family with children and lots of school activities, that could be a very good option to have as a family dog."

Gray said Dream was a former racing dog, while Sam lived a quiet life.

"Dream has raced over a hundred times and won 13 races, something like that," she said.

"Sam... I like to say he didn't think running was for him. He was too slow apparently, so he's never raced."

She said Dream was still adjusting to life as a family dog.

"Sam settled a lot faster than Dream has," she said.

"Sam walked into this household and commanded it as his own, he knows this is his home and that he's loved. Dream on the other hand is a lot more timid, a lot more wary, it's going to take a lot more time with her."

Marcus Jackson's greyhound Ben. Supplied / Marcus Jackson

Wellingtonian Marcus Jackson adopted former racing greyhound Ben last week, and said he was easing him into life as a pet.

"Everything is new... There's this whole 3-3-3 rule, so for three days you keep their world quite small and then gradually introduce them to stuff," he said.

"He still gets a little startled by things, like buses. He still hasn't quite cottoned onto buses."

Jackson said styling Ben was another perk of adopting a greyhound.

"It's definitely not a reason to buy a greyhound, but it is a very fun aspect that you get to do a lot of shopping," he laughed.

"In our house he's pretty much in what I guess is essentially a t-shirt most of the time, and when he goes outside he's got a full-on coat. He doesn't have a raincoat yet but we're getting him a raincoat.

"You have to figure out his style, you know. We don't want to put him something he wouldn't put himself in."

Gray urged other families to consider adopting a greyhound.

"They are the most loving, laziest dogs you will ever take in in your entire life, they barely shed which has been amazing, they never bark, and all they do is sleep and they're happy with a 20 minute walk, I cannot find any negatives about having a greyhound," she said.

World.title: Residents fear Auckland sinkhole a sign of wider problem with old infrastructure
World.content:
The sinkhole that appeared on a street in Auckland's St Mary's Bay could take up to two months to repair, Watercare says.

Residents are concerned what the large sinkhole will do to ageing water infrastructure below.

The hole emerged on Thursday evening and is about 5m long, 3m wide and over a metre deep in parts.

Watercare said fixing it could take up to two months.

A heavy stream of water could be seen flowing through the hole, located in a dip on Hackett St.

Suction hoses were on Monday working hard to remove water pooling in the large hole in the middle of the road but water continued to gush down into a large gap space beneath the tarmac.

The section of road was damaged in the Auckland Anniversary floods in January 2023, after which it was covered by a metal plate.

On Monday workers were using suction hoses to remove water pooling in the large hole. Nick Monro

On Thursday, the road appeared to have collapsed, with some residents reporting losing water for several hours.

Tony Skelton has lived in the area for 53 years.

"So for three years it's been lying in a condition which clearly shows that there are some infrastructural issues that could cause serious damage if left unattended," he said.

He's particularly concerned about what the sinkhole and flow of water with a 126-year-old emergency overflow point, or EOP, located beneath it.

"If there is further damage to the EOP that could undermine our properties, it could cause considerable problems."

Tony Skelton has lived in the area for 53 years. Nick Monro

Of particular concern is what would happen during the next heavy rain event.

"We are very concerned about it and we have been for years. The infrastructure here is a major concern to this suburb and no-one is listening to us about this."

John Hill from the St Mary's Bay Association said nobody knew the extent of the damage to the infrastructure since the Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods.

"We are seriously concerned with this old infrastructure. We've had collapses in other parts of St Mary's Bay -- it's 126-years-old -- and it all arrives here at this EOP which is way down, it's seven metres down.

Hill said the issue demonstrated why the recently-approved Plan Change 120, which would allow for housing intensification in inner-Auckland suburbs, was a bad idea.

"They're zoning the whole of St Mary's Bay for six-storey buildings and they're planning to put it on old infrastructure," he said.

"This is a horrible indication that warns everybody that it can't be done."

John Hill from the St Mary's Bay Association. Nick Monro

Watercare chief operations officer Mark Bourne said it was investigating what caused the section of road to collapse above the pipes.

Water and wastewater services would remain online while the repair work was carried out .

Hackett St would be closed at the site of the hole, however, residents would still be able to access their properties.

World.title: Freezing start for much of New Zealand as bitter cold snap continues
World.content:
Much of the country had a frosty start with a second day of cold early morning temperatures.

MetService meteorologist Ashlee Parkes said some of the coldest temperatures in the North Island, seen around 5am Tuesday morning, included southern Waioru at -7.7C and the Desert Road at -6.8C.

The South Island also didn't completely escape the cold with MetService recording -4.5C at Pukaki Airport and -3C in Alexandra.

"Most places are not as cold this morning [as] they were yesterday morning," Parkes said.

"The one exception to that that I could find was Hamilton Airport, which was -3.2C at 5am this morning and that is their coldest temperature measured this year."

She said a front approaching on Wednesday would see a slight warming of temperatures, especially for the South Island.

Tuesday's chill follows a cold and frosty morning around the country on Monday, with Taupō falling to -5.6°C and Christchurch reaching -4.7°C.

MetService said it expected the frosty mornings to continue through the first half of the week, especially across the North Island.

Meteorologist Devlin Lynden earlier said the cold start was being driven by clear skies and light winds.

"With calm, clear nights, heat escapes easily into the atmosphere, allowing temperatures to plummet before sunrise. Sheltered inland valleys become even frostier as cold air settles into low-lying areas."

While there was another cold start on Tuesday morning, overnight temperatures later in the week should be warmer as northerly winds develop.

The South Island has also seen frosty mornings, although increasing northerly winds have prevented temperatures from dropping too harshly.

Those winds should strengthen through Tuesday and Wednesday ahead of a front bringing a change in the weather toward the rest of the week.

Power demand surges

Transpower NZ said the cold weather this week was leading to record electricity demand, with Monday's peak demand of 7141 MW an all-time record.

Transpower - which is responsible for maintenance and transmission of the electric power grid - said it was working with the electricity sector to increase the amount of electricity that is available.

World.title: Aussie Rohan Browning clips 'unfair' 100m surprise sprung on sprinters
World.content:
Just a day or two before the start of the athletics program at the Commonwealth Games, the public was made aware that the top eight 100 metre sprinters in the rankings would be given a free ticket into the semifinals in a break from tradition.

It left the rest of the field, including Australians Rohan Browning and Eddie Nketia, to duke it out in a mass time trial across 11 heats.

It was a significant change to the usual system where everybody runs the heats and the top two in each race are automatic qualifiers, with the remaining runners trying to get through on times.

Both Australians finished second in their heats, but Browning could not enjoy the moment after going through in 10.24 seconds in heat seven with four more to come.

Browning said the new rules were as much of a surprise to him as they were for the rest of us.

Glasgow 2026 day four live The athletics program starts on day four of the Commonwealth Games, marking the first of three days that feature swimming as well as track and field.

"It's an unheard of progression, it's extremely weird. It's really hard to know, I have no idea what times have been run, I have no idea where I sit in the placings," he said, asking reporters to clue him in on where he sat in the standings.

"It's gusty out there, so when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of us goes through on a time trial rather than first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will have better conditions than others, so I don't know what's going on."

Browning made the cut in 16th as the second slowest qualifier and compatriot Eddie Nketia was fourth fastest overall with his 10.07

Browning, who was a controversial inclusion in the team ahead of Josh Azzopardi, said he always turns up prepared to run three rounds but the other folks, including countryman Lachie Kennedy, do not have to.

Eddie Nketia looked powerful as he finished second in his heat. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"It's not fair, clearly it's not fair," he said.

"It's clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever's motivated that decision, I don't know what it is or if it's reasonable or not, but clearly it's not fair. I think everyone would agree on that."

Nketia said it was out of his control so he was not going to worry too much about it, and Browning acknowledged the best response is probably to just run fast.

Aussie sprinter feels 'robbed' Josh Azzopardi opens up after missing out on selection as a 100 metres runner in Australia's athletics team for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

"At the end of the day this sport is meritocracy at its finest; if you're quick enough you go through, so I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place," he said.

"In all likelihood they were probably the guys paying the best odds to make the final regardless, but you just don't know. Some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. I don't even know when they took the performances from."

National record holder Torrie Lewis is experiencing both sides of the coin in the women's events, running the heats in the 100m but granted the automatic progression in the 200m.

"Having a day off in the middle is perfect, so I'm really happy with that," he said after winning her heat in 11.15 seconds to finish as the second-fastest qualifier.

"It would've been better if it was first [past the post], just to eliminate the wind because it's so gusty going around, but what can you do? Just be the fastest no matter what."

World.title: Live: Harris claims gold as Aussies sweep medals in 100m free
World.content:
Commonwealth Games debutant Briseis Brittain is a Gunalbingu & Njebbana woman from Ramingining & Maningrida.

Hailing from the Northern Territory, the 18-year-old is not loving the weather, which turned from a gorgeous summer to decidedly Scottish the moment the Games started.

(ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It's really freezing here," she says.

"Because I'm from Darwin, it's too freezing. I hate it."

But the weather aside, Brittain is loving life, qualifying alongside Ella Pardy, who is 17 years her senior.

"I just can't believe that I just came third in the heat," Brittain says.

"It was really huge. This is my first commonwealth games, it's really good experience for me. I hope I hit a PB in the final."

Rhiannon Clarke stormed to victory in the second heat, going through to the final as the second-fastest qualifier, but leaving plenty in the tank.

"Feeling really good, nice easy run, easy enough to get into the final. so I'll take it," she says.

(ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I know I can go way faster in the final, just need to make sure I catch my start and I know I've got that top end speed as well. Just got to put it all together.

"It was enough to get into the final, so might as well do that rather than push myself too hard."

As for the weather, the 24-year-old West Australian isn't fazed by anything, be it cold or unpredictable swirling winds.

"It's fine, it is definitely a bit cold but in Australia at the moment it's colder so I think we've actually had it a bit lucky to have that winter season to prepare," she says.

"We had a nice legal tailwind, which I'll take, but anything can happen. I'm from Perth, we've had +4 tailwinds, we've had lots of crazy winds.

"I feel like it's nice, it makes your legs feel like they can turn over faster."

Clarke, Brittain and Pardy will run in the women's 100m T38 final at 4:50am AEST.

World.title: Max King's season is over after first AFL game in two years
World.content:
Luckless St Kilda spearhead Max King's season is over after confirmation the key forward suffered a hamstring injury in his first AFL game in two years.

King left the field in the third quarter of the Saints' 13.15 (93) to 8.14 (62) win over North Melbourne, his first AFL appearance in 757 days, due to hamstring tightness.

Scans confirmed a strain to King's left hamstring, with St Kilda drawing a line through his season on Monday.

"It's an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return," general manager of football Lenny Hayes said.

"He's an incredibly important part of our football club. We'll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback.

"Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027."

Saints coach Ross Lyon had defended the decision to play King in his first AFL game since June 30, 2024, having battled knee injuries as well as soft-tissue concerns.

The 26-year-old played two VFL games earlier in the year and suffered a hamstring injury in one of those, pushing his comeback past the two-year mark.

King is on a monster contract until the end of the 2032 season, but has largely been unable to play since signing it.

The 10th-placed Saints remain firmly in the finals wildcard mix, but losing King is a blow to their September hopes.

There was also bad news for GWS dynamo Finn Callaghan, who will require season-ending ankle surgery.

The exciting midfielder sprained his ankle late in the derby loss to Sydney.

"Following scans and a specialist consultation, Callaghan and the club's medical team have opted for surgery to repair the damage," the Giants said.

"Callaghan is expected to be sidelined for approximately 12 weeks."

GWS sit 12th, a win and significant percentage outside the wildcard places.

World.title: Disgruntled Tiger Doueihi expected to return to training
World.content:
Adam Doueihi has smoked the peace pipe with Wests Tigers powerbrokers and is expected to return to training on Tuesday.

Doueihi and his manager Isaac Moses met coach Benji Marshall, chief executive Shaun Mielekamp and football manager Pat Richards at the club's Concord headquarters on Monday morning to thrash out their differences.

Mielekamp emerged from the crisis talks claiming the meeting was "positive" after weekend fears Doueihi had played his last game for the Tigers.

Luai joins Parramatta, Marshall slams relationship breakdown rumours Benji Marshall has slammed "bull**** rumours" claiming a fractured relationship with Jarome Luai contributed to the star five-eighth's early exit from Wests Tigers.

Contracted until the end of the 2029 NRL season, Doueihi was said to have fallen out with Marshall after making himself unavailable for Saturday's 56-10 loss to Canberra.

The playmaker was upset about being asked to move from halfback to lock to make way for rookie debutant Javon Andrews.

But the 27-year-old could now even be rushed back for Sunday's clash with Parramatta following Monday's clear-the-air meeting.

"It was a very positive and productive meeting," Mielekamp read from a brief prepared statement.

"Adam will be at training tomorrow, which is a very good sign."

Asked to elaborate on Monday's talks, Mielekamp was tight-lipped.

"What was said in the room will stay in the room," he said.

"That's important for us as a club. We're all doing what's best for the club."

The Doueihi drama is the latest controversy to hit the embattled club after superstar playmaker Jarome Luai recently signed a one-year deal with the Eels ahead of his arrival at the PNG Chiefs for their 2028 entry to the competition.

After briefly sharing top spot on the table this season, the Tigers have dropped to second-last and out of finals contention for a 15th consecutive season.
